Isaacman said the “new space race” to land astronauts on the moon — racing against China now versus the Soviet Union during the Apollo era — will be “much closer than it ever needed to be” because of slow going in past years.

But the space agency is now accelerating its pace, he noted, eliminating endless meetings and bureaucratic inertia, as SpaceX, Blue Origin and other companies scramble around the clock to meet the deadlines and NASA bolsters its workforce.

Adopting Apollo's urgent and intense approach from 1968 through 1972, a period which saw 24 astronauts fly to the moon and 12 land on it, is not “tech industry pixie dust or some new management philosophy,” Isaacman said.

“It's about our own history. It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months,” he said during a news conference at Kennedy Space Center.

Both landers will be launched next summer for docking practice by the three NASA astronauts and one Italian who will blast into orbit aboard NASA's Orion capsule. The mission will require three launches in quick succession from Cape Canaveral. Orion will dock first with Blue Origin's Blue Ghost about 270 miles (435 kilometers) above Earth, then with SpaceX's Starship in a slightly lower orbit.
“As a rocket nerd, it's going to be pretty awesome,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA's associate administrator.

NASA's planned moon base near the moon's south pole — nowhere near Apollo's more equatorial locales — should see its first launch by year's end. The Pittsburgh company whose first lunar landing mission fizzled in 2024 will attempt a “take two,” this time aiming for the moon's south polar region with a rover and other experiments. More landers, rovers and orbiters will follow, so many that by the time the first Artemis moonwalkers arrive, their moon car will already be there waiting for them, according to officials.

To speed up and reduce risk, the initial moonwalkers will wear a lighter, less complex spacesuit than the one still under development by Axiom Space for longer, later excursions. Axiom will test these new so-called “sortie suits” on the International Space Station next year.
Setting up a long-term presence is what makes this so much more challenging than the Apollo-style commuter flights, said NASA astronaut Frank Rubio, who is part of the Artemis III crew.
“It is incredibly ambitious,” Rubio told The Associated Press earlier this month. “One thing I’ve always believed and learned is don’t bet against America.”

title: Mississippi DEI ban can go into full effect after Fifth Circuit reversal
summary: The U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower-court ruling that prevented portions of a Mississippi ban on diversity, equity and inclusion from being enforced
story: The U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower-court ruling that prevented portions of a Mississippi ban on diversity, equity and inclusion from being enforced

JACKSON, Miss. -- Portions of a Mississippi ban on diversity, equity and inclusion practices in public schools can go into effect after the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court's ruling that blocked sections of the law from being enforced.

The parts of the law in question prevent public schools from requiring diversity training and maintaining DEI-related programs, courses and offices. It also bans public schools from discussing a list of “divisive concepts” related to race, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, religion, ethnicity and national origin. Public schools that violate the law could lose state funding.
The ban passed in April 2025 and is being challenged by a group of educators, students, parents and activists who say the law violates their First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.

The plaintiffs have several weeks to file a petition for rehearing with the Fifth Circuit. The law would take effect seven days after the petition deadline passes or if a petition is denied, according to McKenna Raney, an attorney representing the plaintiffs.

The Fifth Circuit also ordered that the case be reassigned to a different district court judge after U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate issued a “botch job” temporary restraining order that contained artificial intelligence hallucinations, according to the Thursday ruling. The TRO predates Wingate's August 2025 preliminary injunction, which the Fifth Circuit overturned.
Additionally, the ruling provides clarity on the scope of the law, which opponents have criticized as overly vague.

The law does not apply to scholarly activities, student activities and groups or creative engagements, according to the Fifth Circuit. The court also said concerns raised by the plaintiffs that the law would ban discussions of civil rights, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., the Ku Klux Klan, the Fourteenth Amendment, Juneteenth and “Of Mice and Men” are incorrect.

“It is heartening to know that at the very least these specific iterations of classroom discussions that have been happening for years in Mississippi are exempted and they can continue unimpeded," said Raney, an LGBTQ Justice Project staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of Mississippi. However, Raney said the types of discussions allowed under the law are still “murky.”

The Mississippi Attorney General's Office, which represents the defendants, did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment on the court's ruling. The office's attorneys have previously argued that public employees do not have First Amendment rights when acting in a professional capacity.

title: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
summary: President Donald Trump says U.S. warships returning from Iran could stop in Cuba
story: President Donald Trump says U.S. warships returning from Iran could stop in Cuba

FORT MYERS, Fla. -- President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.

Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the U.S. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership — was “deep into negotiations with Cuba,” saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal,” adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States.
Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C., and can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP. AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed from Washington.

title: Trump, seeking to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins, exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs
summary: President Donald Trump is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer
story: President Donald Trump is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30.
The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.''

Collins, locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, issued a statement saying she'd spoken with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.''

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said.
She said she asked for tariff relief for such products “and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families.”
Collins said she'd seek "additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”

Trump started a trade war with America’s longstanding ally and northern neighbor, reaching back to a Depression-era trade law to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. He charged that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly lashed back with tariffs of 15% to 50% on American products, matching Trump’s import taxes dollar for dollar.
Trump ratcheted the dispute up from there last month by imposing a flat-out ban on $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.

The U.S. president has claimed that foreign countries pay his tariffs. In fact, U.S. importers do. And they often face the tough choice of having to pass along the higher costs to their customers or absorb them.

As the Nov. 3 midterm elections approach, many Americans are furious about the cost of living. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll of 2,140 U.S. adults, conducted Sept. 24-28, found that 65% now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high prices more than factors outside of his control, signaling weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and unhappiness with the war with Iran, which has driven up the price of gasoline.

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement, “Trump’s desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies.”

Collins complained that Trump’s levies were hurting Maine farms and businesses that rely on Canadian imports when U.S.-made alternatives are not available. Her office cited the example of Maine wild blueberry growers who need specialized harvesting boxes from Canada that work with their processing equipment.

title: Man who killed school shooter says he regrets there were children he didn't save
summary: The Oregon man who fatally shot a teenage gunman to end a rampage at an elementary school says he was the children's “last line of defense.”
story: The Oregon man who fatally shot a teenage gunman to end a rampage at an elementary school says he was the children's “last line of defense.”

The Oregon man who fatally shot a teenage gunman to end a deadly rampage at an elementary school last week says he was the children's “last line of defense” and that he regrets not arriving soon enough to save them all.
Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary, where the Oct. 15 attack occurred, said he feels like he failed the families of those who died.

“I want to apologize for not saving their babies, that’s probably the biggest thing for me right now,” Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting in an interview published Friday. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome. But there were ones that I didn’t save.”

Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the school in Bend, Oregon, last week when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.
Police say another teacher threw her phone at the attacker and wrestled with him before Giamanco shot and killed him after following the gunman into the building.

Giamanco said he dropped off his daughters at the school that morning before driving to work. A few hours later, the 36-year-old carpenter was passing the school again as he was heading home for lunch.

He said he spotted someone wearing black and carrying a long gun fire shots into a pickup truck and at a person mowing the school's lawn before the shooter climbed a fence and headed toward the school building.

Giamanco said “panic fled into my brain.” He grabbed a .40-caliber handgun from his truck's center console and went after the gunman as he dialed 911. He asked the dispatcher to send help before hanging up his phone.
“I said 'I’m sorry I have to go in. People are going to die,'” Giamanco said in the interview.
As he got closer to the building, Giamanco said, he lay on his stomach and used his elbows to crawl across the ground.

“That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives,” he said. “And then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster. And I told myself: 'This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.'”

Giamanco said he entered the school through a window that had been shot out. Peeking into a nearby classroom, he saw a teacher grappling with the shooter. He said he faced them both in profile, giving him an open shot.
“I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children,” Giamanco said.
He swung the door open, stepped into the room and fired his gun.
Both the gunman and the teacher dropped to the floor. The teacher bolted from the room as the shooter reached for his shotgun.
“He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.”

Police have said Giamanco was carrying his gun legally in his truck and have credited him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving lives. A day after the shootings, President Donald Trump said that Giamanco was a “great hero” who “took care of business.”

A second teacher in the classroom, Becky Drury, said in a statement Wednesday that she lay on the floor, helplessly playing dead, after being struck at close range by a shotgun blast that nearly severed her left hand.
The teacher who struggled with the shooter hasn't been publicly identified. Giamanco told the public broadcaster that she's “a real true hero” whose actions gave him an opening to kill the attacker.

“I can’t tell you what it feels like to take a life … but I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there,” Giamanco said. “If I wasn’t there, I just don’t know what would have happened.”
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

title: Ohio mayor says employee error caused chemical leak, lifts evacuation orders
summary: Officials in northeast Ohio said a chemical tank leak earlier in the week was caused by an employee error
story: Officials in northeast Ohio said a chemical tank leak earlier in the week was caused by an employee error

TOLEDO, Ohio -- Officials in northeast Ohio said Friday that a chemical tank leak earlier in the week was caused by a chemical reaction resulting from an employee error and lifted all remaining evacuation orders.

Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said during a news conference that the venting of the tank that ruptured at MC Tank Terminal on Tuesday was finally completed late Thursday night, allowing a hazmat team to enter the site and test safety levels.
“At this time, we do feel confident that the site is safe," Toledo Fire and Rescue Battalion Chief Blake Molnar said.

The rupture happened late Tuesday night. MC Tank Transport, the owner of the site, said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.” Hundreds of people were initially forced from their homes and 57 were treated at hospitals.

The chemical leak happened when an employee of the company “introduced a temperature level to the tank in the process of trying to transfer the liquid" that caused a chemical reaction, the mayor said. The company has “accepted responsibility” for what happened, he said.

“There was no fire, there was no explosion. There was a very serious chemical reaction, which now happily has run its course, and we’re now finally able to return to some level of normalcy here in our community," Kapszukiewicz said.
There are questions that remain unanswered, and the investigation is ongoing, he said.

title: Severe flooding in the Four Corners region triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation orders
summary: Severe flooding in the Four Corners region has led to water rescues and impassable roads
story: Severe flooding in the Four Corners region has led to water rescues and impassable roads

FORT COLLINS, Colo. -- Severe flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues — some from rooftops — and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado and New Mexico and others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.

It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees onto houses and downed power lines in Arizona. At least one person was injured.
An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued Friday by New Mexico Guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, San Juan County spokesman Devin Neeley said.
“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4 feet (1-1.5 meters) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.
Skies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.
“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.
Some 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.
“We are kind of all hands on deck,” Intoppa said.
Farmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the U.S. where four states — Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah — come together.
In southern Colorado, flooding was even worse than forecast and a full 3 feet (1 meter) higher than a 100-year flood on the San Juan River only a year ago.
Before midday, rescuers in a state helicopter were trying to reach two people who were stranded in a motor home after trying to escape floodwaters, Archuleta County Sheriff Mike Le Roux said.
“We have two adult people and we’ve got three dogs that are as well as they can be, being perched in the middle of a river in a vehicle that’s somewhat submerged,” Le Roux said.
Authorities were meanwhile assessing who else needed help, including many whose homes weren’t flooded but cut off by floodwaters.
“We have widespread catastrophic infrastructure damage across state infrastructure, county infrastructure, private infrastructure. The volume of water has been unprecedented,” Le Roux said.
Le Roux was not aware of any deaths or serious injuries as of midday Friday, he said, “the best news that we can hope for.”
In nearby Rio Grande County, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the southwest part of the state.

The city of Hurricane in far southwestern Utah was cleaning up after declaring a state of emergency Thursday. Reddish-brown floodwater lapped into and around 80 homes in a neighborhood and 50 recreational vehicles in an RV park.
Surreal scenes included a shipping container drifting slowly down a street.

The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the Southwest are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.
Still more rain was forecast through the weekend.
“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed to this story.

title: Jordanian government spokesperson says 6 killed, 28 wounded in church shooting in Karak
summary: Jordanian government spokesperson says 6 killed, 28 wounded in church shooting in Karak
story: Jordanian government spokesperson says 6 killed, 28 wounded in church shooting in Karak
JERUSALEM -- Jordanian government spokesperson says 6 killed, 28 wounded in church shooting in Karak.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
Gunmen opened fire inside a church in Jordan on Friday, causing a number of deaths and injuries, the kingdom’s law enforcement agency said. Authorities didn’t immediately provide a death toll.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.
Security services were investigating the shooting, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said in a statement. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

title: Trump administration stopped sharing evidence in Good and Pretti killings, Minnesota officials say
summary: State officials say in court filings that the federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers
story: State officials say in court filings that the federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers

The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers, state officials said in recent court filings.

Minnesota officials sued President Donald Trump's administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings during Trump’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.
The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.

State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence.”

But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Minnesota told her on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with D.C.," according to the documents.

State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations."

In a reply filed Tuesday, attorneys for the Justice Department argued it's within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. They cited the department's rules for responding to record requests, known as the Touhy regulations, which apply only when formal legal proceedings are underway. The attorneys said there was no active court case when Minnesota made its requests.

Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, while she was leaving a Minneapolis protest on Jan. 7. Bystander video shows Good in the driver’s seat of an SUV, repeatedly honking the horn, when masked immigration officers order her to step out of the vehicle. She starts to pull forward, and an officer standing in front of the car fires at her windshield. The officer, now standing about an arm’s length from the open window on the driver's side, fires twice more, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense.

Good's death and that of Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was killed weeks later by a federal officer in Minneapolis, ignited nationwide protests against the Republican president's immigration enforcement efforts.
No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the fatal shootings.

Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings, and a gun taken from Pretti before he was shot.

title: Trump says he 'heard something about' Justice Department probe into longtime ally Corey Lewandowski
summary: President Donald Trump says he has heard about the Department of Justice investigating Corey Lewandowski
story: President Donald Trump says he has heard about the Department of Justice investigating Corey Lewandowski

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump told reporters that he had “heard something about” the Department of Justice investigating allegations that Corey Lewandowski profited off his past role as an adviser at the Department of Homeland Security, after media reports of an investigation surfaced Thursday.

Lewandowski, who worked at the agency as a special government employee during Kristi Noem's tenure as Homeland Security secretary, was longtime ally of Trump. The details of the allegations against Lewandowski aren't yet clear, though the president said Thursday after a report in The Wall Street Journal that he had heard of the probe.
The president notably didn't defend Lewandowski, who was his first campaign manager in 2016.

“I don't know exactly what it is,” Trump told reporters. “All I know is, I want my people to be honest. And if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted." He added, "I'll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that the probe was launched after a referral from the DHS inspector general, which included details about Lewandowski's time at the agency. Lewandowski was Noem’s lead adviser while at the department, where he appeared to play an outsized role even though his position was supposed to have a limit on days worked.

An attorney for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, wrote in a texted comment to The Associated Press that “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity.”
The Washington Sun reported this week that some open records requests from the department during Lewandowski’s time there were denied due to an ongoing criminal probe.

An investigation into a longtime Trump adviser would be a departure for the Justice Department, which has focused considerable efforts at investigating and attempting to prosecute longtime Trump political critics.
The Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the AP.

title: Plaintiffs in Trump arch project seek injunction to stop administration from beginning work Nov. 5
summary: Plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to stop the Trump administration from building a triumphal arch along the Potomac River are asking a federal judge to halt all construction plans, one day after the National Park Service signaled it would begin work Novem...
story: Plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to stop the Trump administration from building a triumphal arch along the Potomac River are asking a federal judge to halt all construction plans, one day after the National Park Service signaled it would begin work Novem...

WASHINGTON -- Plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to stop the Trump administration from building a triumphal arch along the Potomac River asked a federal judge on Thursday to halt all construction plans, one day after the National Park Service signaled it would begin work Nov. 5.

The plaintiffs — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — asked U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service “from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation.”

The NPS and the executive office of the president filed a notice Wednesday in the lawsuit saying they planned to possibly begin construction as early as Nov. 5, pending the approval of the construction by the National Capital Planning Commission. The commission is scheduled to meet that day to consider final approval of the site and building plans.

The government's notice said construction could begin once that approval was finished, the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published. “NPS may publish such notice as early as November 5, 2026, and construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026,” the notice said.

The arch has been one of Trump’s pet projects, one that he said might also include national security functions such as drones and snipers. Plans submitted to the NCPC by the Interior Department don’t include mention of the “military complex” he has said it would host, although the agency said the plan could accommodate such a feature. The structure is planned to be 250 feet tall (76 meters).

The plaintiffs' filing Thursday said notification “makes clear that the defendants have no intention of awaiting this court's decision on the cross-motions for summary judgment and have every intention of imminently beginning construction of the arch on Memorial Circle.”

Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by President Donald Trump, the plaintiffs sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

The Public Citizen Litigation Group, which is one of the legal groups representing the plaintiffs, cited several projects being pursued by the administration that had moved forward with work despite pending lawsuits.
Chutkan ordered the two sides to meet and file a briefing schedule by noon Friday.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that President Donald Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Just this week, plaintiffs in the East Potomac Park golf course case argued in a five-hour hearing that the Trump had made clear that construction plans were forthcoming, despite the pending litigation.

The lawsuit in federal court in Washington is one of two challenging construction of the arch. The Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit earlier this month opposing the construction of the Triumphal Arch, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against the planned monument.
That lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process.
The administration disputed that claim.

title: Agriculture secretary says agency is 'full-bore ahead' on Forest Service reorganization
summary: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins says the Trump administration remains “full-bore ahead” with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service after a judge blocked the changes last week
story: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins says the Trump administration remains “full-bore ahead” with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service after a judge blocked the changes last week

BILLINGS, Mont. -- Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday that the Trump administration remains “full-bore ahead” with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service and other agencies after a judge blocked the changes last week.

The administration wants to move Forest Service headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City, shutter 23 research stations, and close many regional offices and replace them with state offices. It's part of a broader realignment at the Agriculture Department that also would change programs for food and nutrition, rural development and other services.
For now the plan is stalled under court order. But that's already under appeal, and Rollins made clear Thursday that the administration hasn't given up.

“We are full-bore ahead in the reorganization,” Rollins said during a conference call with reporters following an announcement on fertilizer production. “We believe in it more today than we ever have — taking the USDA to our constituents, which is rural America, the Forest Service out West.”
Administration officials say the reorganization will trim costs and further concentrate resources in Western states that are home to nearly 90% of national forest lands.

Federal employee unions, environmental groups and local officials, including in California, Maryland and Washington state, are trying to quash the plan. They say the shuffling of employees is a ploy to achieve the administration's goal of deep cuts in the workforce.
U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria in California sided with those arguments in an Oct. 13 order halting the reorganization while a lawsuit from opponents works its way through the courts.

“If implemented, the planned reorganization activities will likely put thousands of USDA employees to the choice of relocating far from their current home — often to a different state — or losing their job,” Chhabria wrote. He said the administration “almost certainly” violated congressional restrictions on using money on the reorganization that was intended for other purposes.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has been eliminating layers of management as part of President Donald Trump’s push to slim the federal workforce and make it more efficient.

Trump also wants to take away one of the Forest Service's most prominent roles — fighting wildfires — and transfer responsibility to the new federal Wildland Fire Service. Congress so far has blocked that move.

With wildfires getting worse in recent decades due to climate change, battling them has consumed a greater share of the Forest Service budget. That's forced officials to look for cost savings elsewhere.

It's not clear how much the reorganization will actually save, said Chris Iverson, who spent almost three decades at the Forest Service before retiring from a leadership position during Trump's first term. Yet Iverson said the changes could result in the loss of personnel with extensive experience, including battling wildfires.

He added that the elimination of regional offices and creation of state offices could open the door to more influence by governors pushing the interests of the timber, oil and gas and grazing industries.
“It's just going to be a closer alignment of Forest Service leadership with state government priorities,” Iverson said.

Gov. Spencer Cox in Utah has described the Forest Service reorganization, including a new headquarters in Salt Lake City, as “a big win for Utah and the West.” GOP lawmakers said it would ensure agency officials get more local input.

The administration last month scaled back part of its plan and said 41 research facilities across the country that faced possible closure would remain open. Almost two dozen research stations still are slated to close.
The Forest Service workforce has been cut about 16% under Trump, from more than 39,000 employees to 33,000, according to government data.

During his first term, Trump moved the Bureau of Land Management to Colorado, citing many of the same reasons — including a desire to put top officials closer to the public lands they oversee. The Biden administration reversed course, moving BLM headquarters back to Washington, D.C., after two years.
The National Federation of Federal Employees union said a survey of Forest Service workers showed a large majority opposed the pending reorganization plan and most were unwilling to relocate.

title: Execution staff warned IV site might have 'blown' during Christa Pike's execution attempt
summary: A court document says Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution
story: A court document says Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution

Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or “blown,” before she was injected with pentobarbital, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.

The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.

After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.

title: Tom Skerritt, known for roles in "Alien," "Picket Fences," dies at 93
summary: Tom Skerritt died of natural causes, his family said in a statement.
story: Tom Skerritt, the actor known for his roles in "Alien," "Top Gun" and TV's "Picket Fences," has died, his publicist confirmed to CBS News on Thursday. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"We are heartbroken by his loss," the family said. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives."

Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for CBS' "Picket Fences," winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in "The Turning Point," Sally Field's husband in "Steel Magnolias" and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in "Contact."

"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.

Onstage, he was the narrator in "Our Town" at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's "A Time to Kill," in which The Associated Press wrote he "nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer."
Skerritt's early life
Skerritt grew up in a middle-class Detroit family, his father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child.
He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by a viewing of "Citizen Kane."

His performance in a Los Angeles theater production of "The Rainmaker" led to his first film role — a supporting role as a sergeant in the 1962 scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film "War Hunt." The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

Redford and Skerritt were vying for the same lead role, with the former winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, paid Skerritt back with compound interest in "A River Runs Through It," handing him the plum role of the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times was impressed by his "halting, thoughtful manner."

Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."
"Alien" and "Top Gun"

After "War Hunt," however, Skerritt still struggled for screen time, landing a small role in "M*A*S*H" and "Thieves Like Us" for Robert Altman, and doing a bit part as a motorcycle cop in "Harold and Maude" for Hal Ashby.

Things changed with "The Turning Point," which earned him a National Board of Review win. Then came "Alien," with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the ship Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct, hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea."

Things shifted again after that, including a memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark "Top Gun": "Gentlemen, you are the top 1% of all naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."

Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in "Picket Fences," a comedy created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.

Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, playing his doctor wife in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place with bizarre happenings, like having a robber leaving a trail of frogs or the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.

"It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'"

Also on the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's "Brothers and Sisters," Jimmy Ford on TNT's "Leverage" and he had the recurring character Evan Drake on "Cheers." He starred in the Hallmark movie "What the Deaf Man Heard," co-starring Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modeled for Guess jeans.
Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie "Divided by Hate."

"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."
He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

title: John Anderson, country music Hall of Famer, dies at 71
summary: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, died on Wednesday, his family said. He was 71 years old.
story: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, has died, his family said Wednesday. He was 71 years old.
"It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend," his family said in a statement on Instagram.

"To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives," they said. "To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special."
"His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever," they said.

Anderson's unmistakable voice helped make him a country music legend. And for some of Nashville's biggest names, he was required listening, with stars like Blake Shelton collaborating with him. Others, including Luke Combs and Ashley McBryde, recorded his songs for his tribute album, "Something Borrowed, Something New."
The Florida native arrived in Nashville as a teenager, playing clubs and working construction — even helping build the roof of the Grand Ole Opry.
But before long, he was the one raising it.
"Swingin'" became a no. 1 hit and the CMA Single of the Year in 1983.
A decade later, "Straight Tequila Night" and "Seminole Wind" brought Anderson's distinctive sound to another generation.
But years later, a mysterious life-threatening illness nearly silenced him, taking away his hearing and leaving him wondering whether he would ever make music again.
Anderson told CBS News in 2022 that the first part of the illness brought severe, terrible headaches, starting in 2016. Then, he said, his hair fell out and he lost his hearing "almost completely."
"They never really figured out just what it was," he said.
His return to music included the 2020 album "Years." Then, in 2024, came country music's highest honor: a place in its Hall of Fame.
"It's a long long road from Apaka, Florida, to standing right here on this stage, but I must say, behind all of that there was a lot of adventure, and I got to choose my own way," he said.
Anderson died just days after attending a Hall of Fame ceremony in Nashville on Sunday.

"I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony," country star McGraw wrote on social media. "He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off. I am completely heartbroken by his passing. There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his."

title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
summary: Christina Applegate said on her MeSsy podcast that her doctor recently revealed she did not have multiple sclerosis.
story: Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, more than five years after announcing she had been told she had the chronic condition.

Applegate, 54, shared the news in a double episode of her podcast MeSsy, where she and co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler discuss life with multiple sclerosis. Applegate had taken a break from the podcast in recent weeks. She said Tuesday she had taken that time to process the new information.

Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago," her doctor wanted to take her off an infusion treatment and see how her B cells reacted. The cell count didn't increase or decrease after the treatment stopped, which began "kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate said. Eventually, her doctor had surprising news: Applegate had never had multiple sclerosis at all.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said. "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."

Multiple sclerosis, or MS, is a disease where the body's immune system attacks the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from person to person, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, and there are multiple types of the disease. The condition has no known cause, and its progression is impossible to predict.

Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said on the podcast that almost one in five people who have been told they have multiple sclerosis "didn't actually have it." Misdiagnoses with the condition are "fairly common," she said, because there is no one test for it.
Applegate said at the time of her initial diagnosis, she underwent tests including a spinal tap and MRIs. Scans showed lesions on her brain, she said.
Applegate said that she continues to have debilitating symptoms that affect her daily life and mobility.

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. And that's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021, why did this happen?"
The investigation will begin next week, she said.

Applegate has previously described living with symptoms including numbness, an off-balance feeling, and a tingling sensation in the limbs. She said in a 2022 interview with The New York Times that she "can't walk without a cane."

In the same interview, she said she used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix hit "Dead To Me," and the show's script was adjusted to accommodate her symptoms. In 2023, Applegate said her symptoms might lead to her giving up acting on camera. She said Tuesday that she has physical therapy three times a week.
After she was officially diagnosed with the disease, she became an outspoken advocate for MS. On Tuesday, she said the misdiagnosis made her feel "like I let everybody down."
"It's very unnerving and it's really confusing for me," Applegate said.

title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Metropolitan Opera singer Martina Arroyo (Feb. 2, 1936-Oct. 13, 2026) was a sparkling talent acclaimed as an interpreter of Verdi and Mozart, starring as the heroine in productions of "Aida," "Don Carlo," "Il Trovatore," "Macbeth," and "Don Giovanni." She was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2013.

Arroyo was born in Harlem to a father raised in Puerto Rico and an African-American mother who gave her a love of culture and a pioneering spirit. Her first exposure to opera came via radio. "My parents used to listen to the Metropolitan Opera on Saturday afternoon," Arroyo told "CBS This Morning" in 2013. "And I couldn't see them and I couldn't care less what they looked like. I just liked the sound and making music."

She studied the arts as a child, and took voice lessons while teaching Italian in a Bronx public school and serving as a case worker in the city's welfare department. In 1958 she won a radio competition to audition for the Metropolitan Opera's training program. The soprano would go on to sing at Carnegie Hall, and in the 1960s performed on stages in Europe.

Her big break came in New York in 1965, when Met star Birgit Nilsson fell ill; Arroyo was called in at the last minute to perform Aida. At the end, there was a standing ovation — and everything changed. She became a Metropolitan Opera contract singer, and over 20 seasons starred in a run of 199 performances, including major Verdi and Mozart roles, as well as Puccini ("Madama Butterfly"), Ponchielli ("La Gioconda"), and Wagner, becoming the first Black woman to perform Elsa in "Lohengrin." She also sang in Berlin, Chicago, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, London, Paris, Prague, San Francisco, Vienna and Zurich.
A prolific recording artist, she also performed in recitals and oratorios, and appeared regularly on "The Tonight Show."

Arroyo gave her last opera performance in 1991, but she continued to give lectures and lead master classes around the world. She also established the Martina Arroyo Foundation in 2003 to aid artists at the beginning of their careers. In 2013 she spoke of the impact of teaching singers starting out: "Because I think that it all led to this. It's knowing that it doesn't end with you. It's going to go on, and you want it to go on even better than when you were working in that profession."

title: Theranos whistleblower calls Holmes "almost unrecognizable" in film
summary: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Elizabeth Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."
story: Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and one of the whistleblowers credited with exposing Elizabeth Holmes' now-infamous biotech company as a fraud, said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."

"The Elizabeth that I knew completely commanded a room, even if that room was full of secretaries of state, secretaries of defense, generals, senators. She would own a room," Shultz said Monday on "CBS Mornings." "She had so much confidence, and the woman that I saw onscreen looked, frankly, like a, a broken woman."
"It was almost unrecognizable," he added.

Shultz also said he believes Holmes misled Nathan Fielder, who directed the documentary alongside Lance Oppenheim, when at one point in the film she pulled out what she claimed was Theranos' blood-testing device.

"She brings out the Theranos device, and she lays it across the table and all of its components, so you know you can see everything," said Shultz. "But my problem was: that was not the device that I worked with 12 hours a day. That was not the device that we hid from regulators. That was not the device that failed quality controls. That was not the device that we used to knowingly give patients incorrect medical information, and she completely misled [Fielder] down this completely different rabbit hole."

Holmes never admitted wrongdoing in the wake of the Theranos scandal, a stance on which she held firm in the documentary, which brings viewers inside Holmes' San Diego rental property in 2023 just weeks before the start of her 11-year prison sentence. At the time, she was living with her partner, Billy Evans, who is also featured prominently in the documentary, and their two children.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of multiple counts of defrauding Theranos' investors, who, like the public, were led to believe that the company could conduct thorough clinical analyses on tiny blood samples pricked from a fingertip rather than drawn the traditional way. The technology was billed as revelatory for the field of diagnostics, increasing access to and costs of crucial, even life-saving, testing.

But Theranos turned out to be a sham — the technology couldn't do what it claimed. And Holmes, who had become a symbol of Silicon Valley's visionary potential, became the subject of widespread scrutiny as people wondered how she managed to deceive so many, and why she had gone to such great lengths to try to build a business on a false promise.

"She knows that she did something wrong," Shultz said on Monday. "She knows that she was lying, because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies."

Shultz was hired in 2013 as an intern at Theranos, where his grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz, served as a board member. Tyler left the company the following year and went on to serve as an informant for investigations into its dubious practices by The Wall Street Journal and various government regulatory agencies. He later participated in the 2016 HBO documentary "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley," which covered Theranos' downfall.
"You Can See Everything" premiered on Friday and earned $15 million at the box office in its opening weekend, the second-most profitable opening weekend ever for a documentary.
This story published first on CBS News at 10:50 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2026.

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: Medicare Advantage plans cut for 1 million seniors, insurers say
summary: Two of the largest private insurers are discontinuing some Medicare Advantage plans amid higher costs and a spike in utilization.
story: Two of the largest private health insurers in the U.S. are canceling some Medicare Advantage plans for seniors, CBS News has learned.

Humana and UnitedHealthcare each said they are discontinuing the plans beginning next year, ending healthcare coverage for a total of about 1 million people who are 65 or older. Healthcare Brew first reported the insurers' moves.
Humana's decision to exit the plan will affect roughly 600,000 enrollees, according to a company spokesperson.

"We regularly evaluate our Medicare offerings to ensure we can continue providing affordable, coordinated care and access to high-quality care. As previously disclosed, we anticipate plan exits for 2027 will impact approximately 600,000 members," Humana said in a statement to CBS News.
The company noted that most of its affected members will be offered an alternative plan.
UnitedHealthcare also confirmed that it is closing a Medicare Advantage plan for roughly 390,000 of its members, who will have access to another UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan.
The insurer said it is facing higher costs and increased plan usage, pressures that are affecting the whole healthcare industry.

title: AI could take your job. Here's how Congress wants to help workers.
summary: Sen. Ron Wyden on Friday introduced a bill that would double unemployment benefits to 52 weeks if the jobless rate jumps.
story: As artificial intelligence capabilities improve, many Americans are worried that the technology could one day put them out of work — a possibility more lawmakers in Washington are preparing for.

Members of Congress have recently introduced a series of bills to safeguard the nation's workforce against potential AI-related disruptions. Their proposals range in scope, with many geared toward creating training programs to support workers if their roles are eliminated.

On Friday, Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, joined the push to protect workers with "The Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act," a bill that would expand unemployment benefits during "high unemployment periods."
For instance, the bill would extend unemployment benefits for 52 weeks if the unemployment rate reaches 8.5%, double the current standard of up to 26 weeks.
The bill would also assist workers displaced by AI disruption by providing them with education and retraining for higher-paying jobs, Wyden's office said in a statement.

The raft of proposals comes amid warnings about the large-scale displacements AI could cause — some of them from the leaders of AI labs themselves. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and spike unemployment to 10% to 20% in the next one to five years.
Prominent tech leaders have also sounded the alarm bell. In a recent essay, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warned that AI could put millions of jobs at risk.

Those projections haven't materialized, with economists noting that AI hasn't yet created major workforce displacements. While there have been AI-related layoffs, most have been concentrated in the tech industry.

That hasn't done much to quell the concerns of Americans, nearly 80% of whom said it's extremely or very important to protect workers in the age of AI, according to a poll earlier this month from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
Here's a rundown of some of the proposals lawmakers have introduced to address those concerns.
Make AI Work for Americans Act

This bill, introduced last month by Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, would create three excise taxes on the AI industry, including a 5% tax on digital advertising revenue, an AI usage tax and a 50% excess profits tax.
Revenues generated by the tax would go into a fund that could be tapped to retrain displaced workers, among other options.
AI Tax and Work Protection Act

Democratic Reps. Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California introduced this bill in August. It proposes taxing artificial intelligence companies based on token usage, with the tax rate rising if the unemployment rate rises.
The money would be used to create jobs to offset AI layoffs, according to Rep. Casar's office.
AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act

Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat from Virginia, and Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, introduced this bill, which would enhance transparency about workforce disruptions. Introduced last year, it would mandate that major companies and federal agencies report AI-related layoffs to the Department of Labor, which would then share the data publicly.

Democratic Reps. Steven Horsford of Nevada and Sara Jacobs of California, along with James Moylan, who serves as the House's delegate for Guam, introduced a version of the bill in the House this July.

title: AI agents detected inside customer bank accounts, report says
summary: Banks have detected personal AI agent activity inside customers' accounts as experts warn about the risks of oversharing with AI.
story: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating within their customers' online accounts, according to a new Axios report.
Some of the biggest financial institutions in the U.S. say customers have given their personal AI agents, which are unvetted by banks, access to their financial accounts.

"In a lot of cases, this is just going to be customers giving their username or password to an AI agent that the bank hasn't had a chance to vet yet, that goes against the bank's terms of service," Madison Mills, senior AI reporter for Axios, told CBS News. "In other cases, in our reporting, we did find evidence that appeared to look like agents taking actions in customer accounts that were not authorized."
Examples of agent behavior that a user never approved include the AI calling a bank with a complaint without first consulting the account holder.
"So, really a nightmare of AI agent activity for banks," Mills said.

To be sure, these agents weren't going rogue or hacking customer accounts and depleting their funds, Mills said. They were largely following user instructions without the bank's permission to transact on behalf of a human account holder.
"In no way cyberattacks"

White House AI czar David Sacks responded to the Axios report, saying in a post on X that there's a clear distinction between personal AI agents that help manage users' bank accounts and hackers deploying AI for nefarious purposes.

"There's a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks," he said. "Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf."
Sacks added, "This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks."

He believes banks should support the use of such user-authorized AI agents, but that if banks want to limit their access, they could grant AI agents "read-only" permission, meaning they could view a user's spending and other bank activity but couldn't take autonomous actions.

Under such circumstances, an agent could view your purchases and opine on whether you're spending too much money eating out, for example. But it couldn't make a purchase on your behalf or take any other action.
"Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully," he said.
Mills noted that it's an industrywide problem facing dozens of financial institutions as they race to curb AI agents' access to customer accounts.
Banks taking action
Some banks said they're taking action to make their customers aware of the risks of sharing their credentials with AI.

"Customers should not give their username and passwords to anyone. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers to meet customers' needs while keeping their accounts safe," a Chase spokesperson told CBS News.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon expressed concern about AI agents taking actions in customers' accounts on the company's Oct. 13 earnings conference call.
"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said.
Charles Schwab's CEO earlier this month said the company has been blocking unauthorized agents, according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Morgan Stanley said it had not observed any unauthorized AI agent activity across its platforms.
Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment on the matter.

title: Trump says new fuel supply push will lower prices. Will it work?
summary: The Trump administration said using the DPA funding will increase refining output and lower fuel prices for Americans. Experts are skeptical.
story: President Trump on Thursday said his administration will invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production in the U.S., the latest effort from the administration to lower fuel prices.

The Defense Production Act, or DPA, is a Korean War-era law that allows the president to use loans, purchase commitments and other mechanisms to incentivize the production of critical materials and goods.
The announcement follows a meeting President Trump had with refiners to discuss immediate steps to bring more capacity online, a White House official told CBS News.

In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Energy said the DPA funding will increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day and lower fuel prices for Americans, who have been paying more than $4 a gallon on average for gas over the last three months.

The new plan to increase fuel production comes as polling shows a majority of Americans are pessimistic about the U.S. economy amid a growing affordability crunch. Crude oil prices have continued to climb, hitting their highest level this week since May.
On Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was $116 a barrel, up 2.6%, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was around $103 a barrel, up 3%.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline stood at $4.29 on Friday and $6.32 for diesel, according to AAA. Those prices represent a 40% and 74% jump from a year earlier, respectively.

Passed in 1950, the DPA was originally aimed at boosting supplies for national defense purposes. However, Congress has broadened its application to address natural hazards, terrorist attacks and other national emergencies.
Will the measure be effective?
Experts told CBS News that invoking the DPA is unlikely to do much to lower fuel prices.
"I don't think that's really going to have any impact," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News in an email.

There are some potential upsides: DPA funds could speed up some refining expansions, Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News. However, he said any short-term benefits are unlikely.
"There is no slack in U.S. refining, so production can't be added regardless of political will," Kloza said. He said it typically takes months and calendar quarters to bring units back to service.
The White House official said the DFA funds will help expand capacity and modernize existing infrastructure, which is much faster than building a new refinery.
The U.S. produces more fuel than it consumes. Oil prices, however, are set on the global market, where the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted shipments, pushing prices higher.

The U.S. produces around 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel oil, a category that includes diesel, per day but consumes only about 3.6 million barrels per day, experts have noted. The U.S. also produces 9.5 million barrels of gasoline per day, more than the 8.9 million consumed domestically.
The U.S. exports about 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day, Kloza, told CBS News.
A spokesperson for the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, a trade association that represents refiners, said it appreciated the Trump administration's focus on the importance of refineries.

"Our country's 128 operating refineries produce more fuel in the United States than we consume," the spokesperson said in an email. "They are running all-out to keep Americans supplied and the global economy moving despite major disruptions and actual fuel shortages in other parts of the world."
