title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: Trump announces $8 billion in diesel relief for U.S. farmers
summary: The USDA said farmers don't need crop insurance to qualify and can prepare to apply by creating a Login.gov account.
story: President Trump said his administration will provide $8 billion in aid to farmers hurt by record diesel prices.

"Tonight I'm also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new Harvest Fuel Relief program, providing our farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Mr. Trump said at a rally in Kansas Monday night.
"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers," he added.

Earlier this month, Mr. Trump also signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a move aimed at lowering costs for farmers and truckers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

Farmers have faced financial pressures from soaring diesel prices, which are used to run agricultural machinery. Diesel reached a record of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, although it's eased slightly since then, with average U.S. prices now at $6.32 a gallon, up from $3.62 a year ago, according to AAA data.

"This $8 billion investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation," U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.

Farmers would benefit more from a resolution in the U.S. war with Iran, which would likely result in lower energy prices, Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist at the nonpartisan Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and formerly a senior adviser in the Office of the Undersecretary for Rural Development at the Department of Agriculture, said in an email. Ending the Trump administration's tariffs would also help ease prices for farmers, he added.

"The president's economic aid to farmers ahead of the midterm elections follows a pattern dating back to his first term: He imposes policies that harm farmers, then spends taxpayer money to offset the damage his policies create," Ajilore said.

The USDA said the plan, called the Harvest Fuel Relief program, will pay farmers to cover part of their estimated losses for the 2026 crop year, using a standard formula. The calculation will use planted acreage reported to the Farm Service Agency, estimated production costs and crop yields and prices from the USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report.

The agency said it will announce payment rates for major commodity crops in November, with details for other eligible products to follow. Farmers won't need crop insurance to qualify and can prepare to apply by creating a Login.gov account linked to USDA.

The USDA estimates that net farm income will drop 2.6% this year as production costs rise 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to a September forecast by the agency.

title: Poll finds Democrats still boosted by voters' economic concerns
summary: President Trump is a key factor driving support and opposition; turnout looms large
story: Call it the "avoidance" election, with many on each side more motivated by trying to prevent or stop things than by what they'll gain.

Against a backdrop of continued concern about inflation and the economy, Democrats maintain their lead in a bid for a House majority. They're currently on pace for 229 seats in our CBS News House model estimate, which translates voters' congressional preferences into seats.
The potential range of outcomes could reach into the 230s in our model, but Republicans do still have a very narrow path to hold the majority, too.
While that Democratic lead has been durable over recent weeks, it hasn't expanded, either.
In other words, there isn't a growing wave, at least not as of today.
If anything, the still undecided or uncertain voters tend to profile as more Republican.
Whether they decide to show up is perhaps the key question of 2026.
Either way, voters describe a dynamic in which they're more motivated in opposition to things they think might happen. For instance:
More think gas prices will go up if Republicans win than if Democrats do.
(Though they don't think Democrats will make gas prices go down.)
Most voters don't think Democrats have a plan and won't make people financially better off, either...But more voters think they'll be worse off if Republicans win.
The president remains a central factor. It would be a high number voting either to support or oppose a president in a midterm if this sentiment holds through Election Day.
Most of the Democrats' voters are trying to oppose either President Trump or Republicans, even more than to help Democrats.
(Whether that rationale ultimately limits Democrats' gains or not is another key question.)
But he's motivating for most Republicans, especially MAGA.
Some of this lead is attributed to more Democrats saying they'll either definitely vote, or have already voted early.
But this is not over: The voters who describe themselves as only "probably" or "maybe" going to vote are more Republican. If they become motivated, this can all change.
So, what happens if either party wins?
Few voters think gas prices will go down no matter who wins.
But the GOP is now relatively more associated in voters' minds with rising gas prices: More think they'll go up if Republicans win than if Democrats do.
Most voters don't think they'll be better off financially, no matter who wins. That cynicism does permeate the electorate.
But as a choice, relatively more think they'll do better with Democrats.
Most voters think there will be more corruption in government if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
Both Democrats and Republicans — at about similar large majorities — see government corruption as a factor in their votes.
The Trump factor: A motivator for both sides, but more so for Democrats
Mr. Trump looms large over the midterms, particularly for Democrats. More than seven in 10 voting for Democrats say their vote for Congress is to oppose him.
Mr. Trump is also a factor for those backing Republicans. Most say their vote is to support him, but to a lesser extent than Democrats are voting to oppose him.
For most who are backing Democrats, their motivation is more about stopping Mr. Trump and GOP policies than advancing the Democrats' own policies.
Here's how prevalent opposition to either party is as a motivating force this year.
Neither Democrats nor Republicans are perceived by a majority of voters as having a clear plan, should either win control of Congress.
There are four in 10 voters supporting Democrats who don't believe the party has a clear plan, should they win. They say opposition to Mr. Trump is the main motivator for them.

Meanwhile, there are four in 10 voting Republican who say their vote isn't about the president. They're less likely to consider themselves MAGA, tend to just "somewhat," rather than "strongly," approve of Mr. Trump. But a big majority of them have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party – so they remain in the Republican camp.
Other issues
Many voters feel a win by the other side is a threat to their way of life. Democrats think a Republican win would be a threat to theirs.
MAGA Republicans in particular, more so than non-MAGA, think the Democrats would be a threat.
Although the issue ranks behind others as a factor in voters' decisions, Republicans lead Democrats among those who consider transgender issues a major factor in their vote.
Immigration

There are a third of voters who think the Democratic Party puts the interests of recent immigrants ahead of those of U.S. citizens, and voters who hold this view are backing Republicans in big numbers.
(Another third does think the Democratic Party prioritizes both groups, and these voters are supporting Democrats.)
Trump and finances
Americans' overall ratings of the economy continue to be negative, as they have been for years. They've even dipped a bit lower now, to where they were last spring.
And most likely voters feel the president's policies are making them financially worse off.
The economy and inflation remain top concerns. Those calling inflation a very important issue mostly back Democrats, as do those who feel prices have been difficult or a hardship.
Against that backdrop, voters voice broader concern about whose financial interests they think the president prioritizes.
More feel he prioritizes his own financial interests and those of his family over the financial interests of the people in the country. And those who hold this view are backing Democrats.
Republicans mostly feel Mr. Trump prioritizes the financial interests of people in the country over his own.
Trump on the trail: Is he helping or hurting?
The president's numerous appearances on the campaign trail may help to rally the base behind Republican candidates, but those events may not have as much impact with the rest of the party.
Most MAGA Republicans say that when they see Trump campaigning for political candidates, it makes them more likely to vote for Republicans.
For many non-MAGA Republicans, these campaign events do not do that.
The voting process
Most voters express at least some confidence in their own local and county elections administration to conduct the election process, including determining eligibility and correctly counting ballots.
In turn, most tend to voice confidence that their own vote will be recorded and counted accurately in this election.
On both of these measures, more Democrats than Republicans are very confident.
Republicans are far more likely to believe that illegal voting by non-citizens happens in federal elections.

This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a nationally representative sample of 2,355 U.S. adults interviewed between October 21-23, 2026. The sample was weighted to be representative of adults nationwide according to gender, age, race, and education, based on the U.S. Census American Community Survey and Current Population Survey, as well as 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error for the total sample is ±2.6 points, it is ± 2.9  points for the sample of registered voters, and  ± 3.0 points for likely voters.

The estimated numbers of Republican and Democratic seats come from a statistical model developed by CBS News and YouGov which includes data from this poll, past vote and other district-level characteristics, demographics and historical patterns. These estimates are subject to statistical error. We simulate many elections, with the error calibrated to include historical polling accuracy, to obtain a range of seat estimates. We report 95% confidence intervals from the simulations. These estimates describe which party is ahead today and may change as additional data are collected closer to the election.

title: In the Venezuelan stronghold of Doral, some voters discouraged by Trump's policies
summary: Doral, Florida, has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
story: Latinos voted in record numbers for President Trump in 2024, but polling shows that voting bloc is up for grabs in the midterms.
And one region that reflects that shift is Florida's Miami-Dade County, where Latinos and Hispanics make up more than 70% of the population.
In January, CBS News met Andrea Ramos and her husband in Doral, Florida, as they were celebrating and closely following the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Ramos, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Venezuela, told CBS News that she credited President Trump with Maduro's capture. Doral has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
"I had such big admiration for him," Ramos told CBS News about her sentiments for the president following Maduro's arrest and extradition to the U.S.
But about nine months later, her feelings have changed.
"I feel disappointed," Ramos said. "I feel, in a way, betrayed."
While disappointed with the economy, it is the Trump administration's immigration crackdown that has led Ramos to sour on Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
"Overall, I'm not feeling like the law is being respected," Ramos said.

According to a CBS News Battleground Tracker poll released earlier this month, 60% of Hispanic likely voters said they were likely backing congressional Democrats in the upcoming midterms, compared to 39% who said they were likely backing Republicans.
That marked a considerable shift from 2024 CBS News exit polls, which found that 51% of Hispanics voted for Democrats, compared to 46% who voted for Republicans.
In the same new poll, 59% of Hispanic likely voters found that the Trump administration was trying to deport more people than they had expected, compared to 51% of all likely voters.
Asked in the poll about the Trump administration's focus on deportation, 59% of Hispanic likely voters responded that it was too much, compared to 49% of all likely voters.

Stephanie Caro's family-owned coffee shop in Doral is among many local businesses that have seen a decrease in foot traffic and sales as masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have been photographed on the city's streets.
"I'd say there is a heightened sense of fear," Caro said.
Some local business owners have said they're concerned they'll have to close their doors.
"It really impacts the entire community," Caro said. "People are scared to leave their houses. They're changing their daily routines."
Doral voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, driven by Venezuelan Americans who fled Maduro's socialist regime.

But ICE has increasingly targeted asylum seekers who have pending cases and active work permits, and Mr. Trump's close relationship to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez has impacted his support in Doral.
When CBS News asked Doral's Republican Mayor Christi Fraga three times if she still supported Mr. Trump, Fraga refused to give a direct answer.
"There is a lot of things that I support, and there's also questions that I've raised," Fraga told CBS News.
Ramos remains undecided on who she will vote for in the upcoming midterms. On that question, Fraga also declined to advise her constituents to vote for Republicans.
Said Fraga, "Vote your conscience."

title: DOJ demands that some California counties set aside alleged noncitizen ballots
summary: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens.
story: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Trump's Justice Department, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted L.A. County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of more than 20,000 people who it alleges are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.
The Trump administration on Friday asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the L.A. County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They were given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.
"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.
The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including Social Security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

However, the California attorney general's office said the letters contained errors. For example, Mendocino County officials received a list of people who were not residents there, according to a court filing by the state.

Department of Justice spokeswoman Kiersten Pels emphasized in a statement on Saturday that the department is explicitly "not requesting a purge, cancellation of registrations, or any programmatic action."
Instead, Pels wrote, federal officials are asking for collaboration to "ensure the most secure election in California history."

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.
"All of this is simply meant to raise huge doubts about the integrity of this election," said John Tuteur, the registrar of voters for Napa County in California's wine country.

Tuteur said that two uniformed Department of Homeland Security officers delivered a letter to his office late on Friday afternoon. The letter included the names of 42 people whom the federal government accused of being noncitizens illegally registered to vote. There are roughly 86,000 people registered to vote across the county of over 130,000 people, Tuteur said. Approximately 11,000 people had already cast a mail-in ballot as of Friday.
Tuteur and other election officials who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday said they have already started to count ballots that have trickled in from the state's 23 million registered voters.
"We're not changing anything we're doing. We're proceeding with the election," he said.
He said his employees and his relatives were worried about what could come next.
"My family's upset, worried about what's going to happen to me," he said.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

"This is NOT A DRILL: Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said in a statement Friday. "Trump's DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They've admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere."

title: In Ohio rally, Obama blasts Ramaswamy, GOP over controversial Acton ad
summary: Former President Barack Obama took aim at gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton.
story: Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton. Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."

"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He campaigned in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in Midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.
Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Mr. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Mr. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint in the midterms' final days, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

"This is a disgrace," Mr. Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton says her mother "was not well" and her stepfather "was not a good person"

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

"I hope that everyone is seeing all the facts," Acton told CBS News ahead of the rally. "The facts are: I was removed from custody from my mom. She was not well. From even a very young age, my brother and I experienced a lot of abuse and neglect, even before my stepfather. But my stepfather was not a good person, and it got worse then. He was indicted in a grand jury. He was a fugitive, and they left together. And she obviously decided to leave with him. There's a lot out there of what has happened to her since, but I have not seen her since I was 12 years old in a courthouse. So this is a sad story."
Acton told CBS News that "we all know that that was a line crossed too far," adding that "no one running for office should endure something like this."
She went on: "But I can tell you, my childhood made me who I am. It made me stronger. You know, I'm not the only one who's gone through a thing or two in my childhood."
Appearing on stage before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."
Obama blasts White House for "chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence"

In Ohio, Obama also called out Mr. Trump's inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Mr. Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Mr. Trump's allies, he said.

"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in modern times, you get a chance to say enough is enough."

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama headed to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Mr. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

title: President Trump, first lady vote early in person in Florida

title: DOJ sues to block Alaska Senate certification if Sullivan loses
summary: The Trump administration is suing to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if GOP Sen. Daniel Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola because of the other Dan Sullivan who is on the ballot.
story: The Trump administration is suing to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if Republican Sen. Daniel Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola because of the other Dan Sullivan who is on the ballot.
Alaskans will choose their senator in a ranked-choice contest with four candidates on the ballot: Sen. Dan Sullivan, Peltola, Gerald Heikes, and a teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan.
The Justice Department argues that if Sen. Sullivan were to lose because of votes unintentionally cast for the Daniel J. Sullivan instead of the senator, the election should not be considered valid.
"The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X Saturday.

"This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska's governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead," Blanche wrote.

The government alleges that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name and party affiliation as the incumbent senator. It argues that he is potentially diverting votes and Peltola stands to benefit.

In its court filing Friday, the Justice Department argued that allowing Daniel J. Sullivan to be on the ballot "threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan" and said that some of his supporters "likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan."
Further, the senator's other supporters "likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola" and "might not rank Senator Sullivan at all."
Peltola's campaign spokesperson, Harry Child, told CBS News in a statement that the effort was "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."

"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," Child said.

A sample ballot included in the Justice Department's filing shows how the two Sullivans would be listed: Daniel J. Sullivan appears first, as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," with no party affiliation, while Sen. Sullivan appears next, as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent."

In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot, upholding a ruling from a lower court. The state courts reversed the decision by the state Division of Elections that Daniel J. Sullivan was ineligible because he was allegedly trying to "cause voter confusion."

Daniel J. Sullivan's lawyers argued the state "lacked any basis in Alaska law to exclude Mr. Sullivan from the ballot" and didn't have the power to look into his "private motivations." They said that state law doesn't give officials the power to keep qualified candidates off the ballot due to potential confusion.
If Sen. Sullivan loses in November but would have won had the other Sullivan's votes been counted for him, the Justice Department would ask for an investigation, according to its complaint.
A Justice Department spokesperson said that the DOJ filed the complaint "to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters."
The department says that Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy constitutes a violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which was enacted to make the voter registration process more accessible.

President Trump has criticized the dueling Sullivans' presence on the ballot, calling it "totally confusing" and "CHEATING" in a Truth Social post Wednesday, and writing: "It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM." He said his administration was "looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot."
Asked Friday about the Justice Department's lawsuit, Mr. Trump told reporters: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'do it.'"
Alaska's other senator, Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski, said the department "should never have filed this lawsuit."

"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski, a frequent Trump critic, wrote on X.

title: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA
summary: The CIA posted a video on X showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.
story: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with the CIA, the latest ploy in the growing efforts from the Trump administration to remove Cuba's communist regime from power.

"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio wrote Friday on X. "The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."

Shortly afterward, the CIA reposted Rubio's message and a similar call in Spanish for Cubans to work with the agency. A video was posted alongside the message showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.

A strict U.S. embargo and sanctions seeking to put pressure on Cuba's communist government have led to prices of basic goods skyrocketing and decreased access to medical care for its citizens. Cubans reported waiting in bread lines for hours and others reported lining up to see a doctor.
Last week, the U.S. government announced additional economic sanctions on Cuba's state-run bank, saying the institution had ties to Iran.

President Trump said on Friday during a campaign rally in South Florida that "we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran." He was referring to the U.S. Navy warships deployed near the Strait of Hormuz.

Mr. Trump added: "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Cuba's government has pushed back, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla responding Friday on X, saying: "We reject any threats stemming from U.S. ambitions toward Cuba."
Rodriguez Parrilla added: "Our shores are lined with beautiful beaches, but they are also rugged and inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile intentions and a desire for domination."

title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in a memo to Secretary of State Rubio that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," and the plots have "reached advanced stages."
story: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.

The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.

"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.

Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.

Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

title: Melania Trump secures "temporary ceasefire" in Ukrainian city
summary: First lady Melania Trump's office says she secured a localized ceasefire for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
story: First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons.

In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.

Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."

"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."

The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
The first lady added that she's secured an American media organization to document both Russian and Ukrainian teams. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, said it would be going.
White House communications director Steven Cheung called the announcement "amazing news."
"This is a major, positive step towards peace," Cheung said on X. "History will remember her tireless work to help those in need."
Last week, the Vatican said Pope Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the phone and "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky."
Melania Trump has worked to reunite 34 children so far with their families, after Russia forcibly removed children.

Although he said he would bring about an end to Russia's war with Ukraine on his first day back in office, peace has remained elusive for Mr. Trump. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, saying Ukraine should have a new leader and dismissing concerns about Russia's continued slaughter of Ukrainians.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this week. "They haven't been doing much."
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced backlash for calling Putin a "humanitarian" upon the release of American Stephen Hubbard.

title: Thune campaigns with Ashley Hinson as Senate GOP zeroes in on Iowa
summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigned with GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa on Friday in his latest effort to prop up Republican candidates on the campaign trail.
story: Sioux City, Iowa — Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigned with GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa on Friday in his latest effort to prop up Republican candidates on the campaign trail, emphasizing how the Hawkeye State, reliably red in recent elections, now may hold the key to control of the Senate.
"The majority in the United States Senate must run through the state of Iowa," Thune said.

Iowa is one of several states that entered the midterm conversation in recent months, with a number of Senate races appearing in play for Democrats despite being unthinkable at the start of the cycle. And in the final sprint to Election Day, Republicans are doing everything they can to hold the line.

Speaking at a roundtable event at a bar and grill alongside Hinson and a half dozen local workers, Thune warned that if Democrats win the majority, the next two years will be spent doing "nothing but investigations and impeachment trials and all that sort of thing." He said, "That's not a good place for the American people to be."
"There's a lot more to do. And we look forward to rolling up our sleeves and lacing them up and getting after it," Thune said. "But we've got to get through Nov. 3."

Hinson is facing off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for an open Senate seat. Democrats haven't won a U.S. Senate race in Iowa since 2008, but as affordability issues squeeze Iowans, with extra strain on farmers, polls have shown Hinson and Turek locked in a dead heat.

Hinson, a former local news anchor who's represented Iowa in the House since 2021, has emphasized the need for someone responsible at the wheel for Iowans, speaking to voters about being a minivan mom and joking that her experience parenting teenagers has prepared her to work with "unreasonable people" in Congress. And although she initially campaigned on her close proximity to the White House, she's pushed back in recent weeks over the unpopular war in Iran and high energy prices. But she still appeared alongside President Trump on Thursday at a rally just a few miles down the road.

Thune, who hails from neighboring South Dakota and did not attend the rally with the president, told reporters that he and Hinson had "a good full day" campaigning on Friday, including a visit to a local air base, where they heard about the need to complete a runway, along with the roundtable later on.
Speaking to reporters after the event, Thune called it "a great opportunity" to hear the issues on the "hearts and minds" of Iowa voters.
"And I think, like a lot of places, it's economic issues," he added.

At the event, local business leaders, including the head of a fertilizer distribution network and a restaurant owner, spoke of high prices, the availability of childcare, supply chain issues and housing and diesel costs. Hinson outlined a list of priorities, including making the no-tax-on-tips policy permanent, focusing on housing and lowering costs for farmers.
In recent weeks, Hinson has pushed for suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports from the United States and offering diesel relief to farmers and truckers.

Thune said as someone who represents a neighboring state, "we share a lot of common issues that we deal with — whether it's transportation or whether it's national security issues, water, a whole bunch of things that kind of bind us together."

Asked about the political environment, as the president and the Senate majority leader made visits to one of the state's reddest areas to boost her candidacy, Hinson told CBS News that she's "focused on all Iowa issues and driving down prices for everyone."
"She's going border to border," Thune chimed in.
Questioned about why the race has grown so competitive in Iowa more broadly, in a state that the president won by 13 points in 2024, Thune cited "economic and political headwinds" for GOP candidates.

The picture extends to other Midwestern states, like Nebraska and Kansas, where Republicans are locked in more-competitive-than-expected contests. With 53 Republicans in the Senate, Democrats would need to flip four seats, and defend a handful of others, to take control of the chamber. And while Democrats still acknowledge that nearly everything would need to go right for them to secure the majority, it's no longer an unthinkable scenario.
But at least in Iowa, Thune expressed confidence that Hinson will pull it off.

"You're talking about a midterm election, a non-presidential year, those are all factors that, you know, sort of weigh into what the overall environment is," Thune said. "But in spite of that, she's going to win."

title: Trump lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods in boon to Sen. Susan Collins
summary: President Trump on Friday slashed tariffs on a handful of Canadian products that are used widely by Maine's agricultural industry, a move cheered by GOP Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection battle.
story: President Trump on Friday slashed tariffs on a handful of Canadian products that are used widely by Maine's agricultural industry, a move cheered by Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection battle in the New England state.

The items that are no longer subject to 50% tariffs include corrugated boxes, crates, plastic sacks, packing machinery, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, according to a White House proclamation. Several new categories of Canadian products were slapped with 50% duties in exchange, including shampoo, vinyl flooring, coffins, carpets and window-unit air conditioners.

In a statement, Collins said the carveouts will protect Maine farmers, including wild blueberry producers who rely on "specialized harvesting boxes from Canada," and apple and potato farmers who also use Canadian products during the harvest.
The senator, who is seeking a sixth term in a blue-leaning state, said she asked top Trump administration officials for "tariff relief for these important products."

"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
Democrats have criticized the tariff exemptions and called them politically motivated.

"After attacking Canada and crushing the American people, I can't think of a more desperate admission of failed trade policy than temporarily lowering tariffs on select products to favor a political ally 11 days before an election," said Rep. Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee. "This stunt only proves further that Trump's trade strategy is not grounded in anything legitimate, but rather in naked politicization and manufactured chaos."

The products were previously included in the billions in Canadian imports that Mr. Trump hit with 50% tariffs in late August after envoys from the two countries failed to strike a trade deal. Canada retaliated with steep tariffs on some U.S. goods.

Mr. Trump has argued the tariffs on Canada are necessary in order to resolve what he views as unfair trade practices by Canada. But the prospect of a trade war with one of the U.S.'s top trading partners — including steep duties on Canadian goods — has drawn pushback from some Republicans in an election year dominated by cost-of-living concerns.
Collins has criticized the trade war — but emphasized that she has pushed for exemptions to help Maine, which borders Canada and is economically intertwined with the country.

"Canada is not China. It is our neighbor, our friend, our closest ally and our biggest trading partner," Collins said during a debate with Democratic opponent Troy Jackson earlier this month, adding that she has "also been working behind the scenes."
Collins pointed to previous tariff exemptions for road salt and pulp.

But Democrats have argued that the powerful senator hasn't done enough to press Mr. Trump to lift the tariffs entirely. During an early October debate, Jackson said: "What about everything else? I mean, we can't eat road salt."

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with lying about Hunter Biden laptop probe
summary: Two former FBI agents have each been charged with one count of lying to Congress about the investigation into Hunter Biden's laptop.
story: Washington — Two former senior FBI officials are facing criminal charges for allegedly making false statements to Congress during testimony in 2023 about the bureau's investigation involving Hunter Biden's laptop.

Nikki Floris, 46, a former intelligence analyst in charge in the bureau's Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, 56, the former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence Division, each appeared in court on Friday in Washington, D.C., where they were presented with a copy of a criminal complaint charging them with one count each of lying to Congress about their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election, specifically the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

A statement of facts prepared by the FBI and filed with the complaint alleges that Floris made false statements to Congress on July 19, 2023, and Benavides allegedly did the same that September. Their alleged false statements pertained to "their awareness of involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden," it said.

"The evidence further establishes probable cause to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of concealing [the Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with and communications about the Hunter Biden investigations and impeding the congressional investigation," it said.

The decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. to charge the pair in a criminal complaint stemming from three-year-old allegations is highly unusual, and both their defense attorneys and the magistrate judge who presided over Friday's hearing and unsealing raised questions about the decision.

"The alleged conduct happened years ago. The government has had the information about this for years," said Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides. He asked Zia Faruqui, the magistrate judge at Friday's hearing in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, to immediately schedule a preliminary hearing "as soon as humanly possible" to review whether there was adequate probable cause that a crime was committed.

The politically charged case was also unsealed just about two weeks before the midterm election — a fact that may raise questions by DOJ veterans about the timing of a case involving testimony to Congress that occurred more than three years ago.
Faruqui said he thought the manner in which the case was charged seemed "strange" and he rejected a request by prosecutors to delay the preliminary hearing for two weeks or more.
He ordered the parties to return at 11 a.m. on Tuesday.
"This is the Sword of Damocles hanging over their heads," he said. "This will follow them for the rest of their lives."
Former President Joe Biden's son Hunter has long been a target of President Trump and his allies.

Hunter Biden was extensively investigated by the FBI over his business dealings in Ukraine with the energy company Burisma, and the contents of his laptop after he left it at a repair shop in Delaware.

Former Attorney General Merrick Garland eventually appointed a special counsel to handle the investigations. Hunter Biden was tried and convicted on three felony gun charges. He pleaded guilty in a separate criminal case to three felony tax offenses and six misdemeanor tax offenses.
He was pardoned by his father shortly before his father left office, and was never charged with wrongdoing in connection with the allegations involving his overseas business dealings.
The charges
The criminal complaint unsealed on Friday said an FBI unit chief told investigators in October 2026 that Floris and Benavides both had oversight roles into the various Hunter Biden probes.

The complaint focused on an FBI counterintelligence operation by the Foreign Influence Task Force known as "Round River," which, it said, was focused on collecting "derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation."
Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election, it said.

"Witness accounts and contemporaneous documents from December 2019 through September 2021 show that Floris and Benavides knew about and were actively involved in the FBI's investigations of Hunter Biden. FITF hosted classified briefings for the agents and prosecutors on the Hunter Biden case in which Floris and Benavides  were active participants," the complaint said.

When Floris later testified to the House Judiciary Committee in July 2023, the complaint alleged she lied about her involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation and the role of the Foreign Influence Task Force.
In one exchange cited in the complaint, she was asked: "Did you have any involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation?" to which she responded, "I did not," the complaint said.
In another exchange cited, it said she was asked: "Was there ever a discussion at the FITF about Hunter Biden?"
"No. At least not with me," she responded, adding: "And again, there's a whole team below me, so whether or not conversations happened, I don't know, but I personally did not have any conversations."

In the September 2023 interview with Benavides before the House Judiciary Committee, the complaint said he told investigators he only learned some of the details about the investigation into the Hunter Biden laptop from Wikipedia when preparing for the hearing.
"When did you learn that there was an ongoing criminal investigation related to the laptop?" it says he was asked.
"The Wikipedia page," he said.
When pressed whether he had any knowledge about the matter during his time at the FBI, the complaint alleges he said, "No."
The complaint also cited a congressional staffer who was present for both interviews. That staffer told investigators the testimony from both officials appeared to be "materially untrue."
An FBI employee also later told investigators that he personally spoke with Benavides about the laptop and discussed reviewing its contents.

"Floris testified that she had no involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations. In reality, she was in frequent communication with the case team for over a year during which she both sent and received information about Hunter Biden," the complaint said.
"Benavides' testimony followed a similar pattern," it added.

The complaint and accompanying sworn statement also allege that Floris and Benavides were involved in reviewing materials to help prepare a script for a defensive brief, which aims to warn someone that he or she may have been the subject of foreign disinformation.

On Aug. 6, 2020, they provided two separate defensive briefings to Sen. Charles Grassley and Ron Johnson related to potential Russian disinformation, it said. It also alleged that Benavides and Floris were involved in reviewing and approving a Round River report that scrutinized informant intelligence related to the Hunter Biden investigations.
Floris' attorneys said in a statement that she has been falsely accused of a crime and raised concerns about the timing of the charges.

"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they said.

"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points. It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

During Friday's hearing, James Kirkpatrick, a special assistant U.S. attorney who came from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Western District of Missouri, appeared at the lectern and spoke for the Justice Department. He was accompanied by George Massucco, the criminal chief in the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C.

A spokesperson for Pirro's office said that Kirkpatrick does work in the criminal division there, though an internal Justice Department directory and his LinkedIn page still listed him as being in Kansas City.

At the hearing,  after the defendants' attorneys asked for a preliminary hearing as soon as Monday,  Kirkpatrick raised concerns about such rapid timing, saying the case agent is from out of town and that he would be out of town as well.
"You have charged this case," Faruqui retorted. "So you will be spending a lot of time in town."

Kirkpatrick's LinkedIn profile has since been taken down. A spokesperson for Pirro said that Cory Jacobs, the deputy chief of the criminal division, and John Borchert, the chief of the Fraud, Public Corruption and Civil Rights Section, are also working on the matter.
This is not the first time that the Justice Department has tapped prosecutors from other districts to help on controversial cases.

Last year, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia tapped prosecutors in the Eastern District of North Carolina to help with the prosecution of ex-FBI Director James Comey over lying to Congress.

That office also tapped an assistant U.S. attorney from the Eastern District of Missouri who mostly handled civil cases to work on the prosecution of New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was accused of bank fraud in connection with a mortgage.

In the Comey and James cases, prosecutors from out of town were brought in after people inside the office refused to participate due to concerns with the evidence, sources previously said. Both cases were dismissed, after a judge found the interim U.S. attorney who secured the indictments was unlawfully appointed.

title: Intel Democrats on how they'll react if Trump alleges election meddling
summary: The top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee says lawmakers have prepared for a range of situations ahead of the midterms, including that President Trump "is not going to accept the results."
story: The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees say they are preparing for the possibility that President Trump makes claims of foreign interference to challenge next month's midterm elections.

The lawmakers said recent intelligence assessments show no indication of foreign efforts to manipulate voting machinery or vote counts. But Mr. Trump and his allies have an established history of raising claims about voter fraud and election interference.

Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia and Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut said this week they have asked CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to be reachable by phone on Election Day, seeking direct access to the senior intelligence officials who could help verify, in real time, any claims of foreign interference made by the president or his administration.
"What we can demand is, what is the basis of this intelligence? What is the source of this intelligence?" Warner said.

"We're making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party," Himes told reporters on Wednesday. "There's a wide array of scenarios that we have war-gamed and trained for."

The lawmakers, who could become chairmen of their respective committees if Democrats win control of both chambers in November, said they are concerned Mr. Trump could cite fabricated or selectively presented intelligence to cast doubt on election results or justify extraordinary federal intervention, potentially including attempts to seize ballots or voting equipment.
Himes added, however, that recent meetings with career intelligence officials had given him confidence that analysts would resist pressure to manufacture evidence of foreign interference.

In a July prime-time address, Mr. Trump cited declassified intelligence about China's acquisition of American voter data to raise concerns about election security. The material he released did not show that Beijing had altered votes or election results, and it is not clear how much of the voter data acquired by China was publicly available, though the White House has said it included nonpublic data.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told CBS News that Clayton, since his confirmation in July, "has made it clear to the leadership of the House Intelligence Committee and Senate Select Committee on Intelligence that he is available to them 24/7 on any issue."
A CIA spokesperson said: "Director Ratcliffe is responsive to CIA's Oversight Committees and will continue to be available as appropriate."
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

The lawmakers' preparations come as the intelligence community continues to track foreign influence operations aimed at American voters, but to date has identified no evidence of plans to interfere with the mechanics of the election, Warner and Himes said.

The intelligence community distinguishes between foreign influence, which is aimed at swaying voters or undermining confidence in elections, and interference, which involves targeting the technical aspects of voting, including voting machines and registration systems.
"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference," Himes said, contrasting that assessment with a "pretty robust influence environment."
He said recent intelligence assessments had observed influence efforts underway by Russia, Iran and China, with a "grab bag" of other actors, including North Korea, weighing potential action.

Warner said Russia was pursuing operations this cycle "similar to prior occasions," including efforts targeting Democrats. Himes added that Russian campaigns "are also particularly focused in a bipartisan way on people and things that have been aggressive on Ukraine."
Iranian actors are "looking at disruption in Europe," Warner said, while Chinese operations have been more selective and aimed at local races.

Ahead of the 2024 election, U.S. intelligence officials assessed that Moscow favored Mr. Trump's candidacy, while Tehran favored his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris. Iranian operatives were also accused of targeting presidential campaigns through cyber operations, including the compromise of Mr. Trump's campaign.

The U.S. intelligence community also found that Russia tried to influence the 2020 election to support the Trump campaign, while Iran sought to denigrate the Trump campaign. Intelligence agencies found "no indications that any foreign actor attempted to alter any technical aspect of the voting process," including voter registration or vote-counting.

Warner and Himes said Congress has yet to receive several election-related intelligence assessments required by law, including reports due 120, 60 and 30 days before Election Day. The committees received a classified update this week, and the House panel expects another bipartisan briefing next week.
They blamed the overdue updates on the tenures of Clayton's predecessors at ODNI — Tulsi Gabbard and Bill Pulte, who held the role in an acting capacity.
"The previous two DNIs had zero interest in complying with the law here," Warner said, while acknowledging that Clayton had made an effort to address some of the deficiencies.

The lawmakers also expressed concern about what they described as a weakening of the federal government's capacity to detect and counter election threats, with reductions to the Foreign Malign Influence Center at ODNI, as well as a significant staffing reduction at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps state and local officials protect election infrastructure.

Himes warned that the loss of technical expertise could undermine the government's ability to detect foreign threats, even if career intelligence analysts remain committed to producing objective assessments.

"You can do a lot of work with loyal analysts at ODNI or at CIA," Himes said. "If you don't have the technical talent to identify technical — either collection or exploitation — you have a huge problem."

title: Alleged Chinese agent pleads not guilty in Los Angeles courtroom
summary: A Southern California realtor accused of being a Chinese foreign agent​ pleaded not guilty to the allegations in a Los Angeles federal courtroom Friday.
story: A Southern California realtor accused of being a Chinese foreign agent pleaded not guilty to the allegations in a Los Angeles federal courtroom Friday.
Wanying Zhang, 34, appeared in a white jumpsuit and shackles, speaking only to deny charges that she surveilled the Taiwanese president's son in a Seattle suburb in September 2025.

The plea puts the case on track for a trial that will require the Justice Department to lay out its evidence of the allegations she conspired with Chinese intelligence officials for what prosecutors called a spy mission.

She was arrested earlier this month at L.A. International Airport while attempting to board a flight to China. She has been charged with one count of acting in the U.S. as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang's husband, Edric Ding, had appeared in earlier court hearings. The couple have been realtors together at the same firm in Irvine, California.

But Ding did not appear at the short hearing on Friday. This is after prosecutors claimed in a recent court filing that Zhang was having an affair with a man who accompanied her on the alleged surveillance mission to Washington state last year. CBS has identified him as Fatai Miao, a construction entrepreneur who recently left Southern California on a one-way ticket to China.
Miao's son told CBS News he does not believe his father was working for the Chinese government, and Miao has not been charged with any crime.
The judge set a pretrial hearing for Nov. 12. The trial is scheduled to begin Nov. 30 at a federal courthouse in Santa Ana, California, and will last an estimated four days.
Both prosecutors and Zhang's attorney, Craig Harbaugh, declined to comment on Friday.
