title: Hero dad who stopped Oregon school shooter shares his story
summary: 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco shared his story with Oregon Public Broadcasting a week after the school shooting that killed three children and a teacher.
story: Kaylub Giamanco, the man praised as a hero for fatally shooting a gunman at a school in Bend, Oregon, last week, is speaking out for the first time about the moments leading up to the shooting and how he is grappling with the aftermath.

The 36-year-old carpenter, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School, told Oregon Public Broadcasting that it was happenstance that he was passing by the school at that moment. He said he had decided to go home for lunch that day instead of eating the food he had packed.

As he drove by the elementary school, he saw a "man in black" holding a long gun and shooting at a vehicle. At first, he thought it was a prank, but then the shooter threw the gun over the school fence before climbing it.

"That's when panic fled into my brain and that's when I opened my center console and said, 'No. No. No. No,'" Giamanco said in the interview. In the console of his truck was a .40-caliber handgun he rarely used.
He said he grabbed the weapon's magazine from another compartment, drove into the school parking lot and saw the shooter walk across school grounds.

"I just was in full panic, like, 'No, there's children, there's babies in there,'" he recalled. "I told my Siri to call 911." He said the dispatcher had questions for him, but he didn't stay on the call.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said.
He described trying to stay out of sight as he followed the gunman.

"I heard him fire two shots into the doors," Giamanco said. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do."

Giamanco said he crawled in through a broken window, staying on his knees until he reached the special education classroom. He said he saw a teacher struggling with the shooter. He said he swung the door open and fired.
"He (the shooter) was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else."

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek was among those who praised Giamanco's bravery, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Police Chief Mike Krantz also credited the teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to take his gun, which "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

Police later identified the shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. The attack killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded.
"I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all."
After police and first responders arrived at the school, Giamanco went back to his truck, emptied his weapon and called his wife and then his mother.

"She was just like, 'OK, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You're a hero. You saved lives.' And I was just like, 'I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all,'" he recalled of the conversation with his mom.
His mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in California, told CBS News Sacramento that her son "has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children."
A week later, Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting that when he goes to bed at night, he replays that day in his head and wonders if he could have stopped the shooter sooner.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams," he said.
"It was split-second decisions while gunfire was going off, while children were losing their lives."
He grew emotional when talking about the families who lost children.
"I want to apologize for not saving their babies," he said. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

In the days after the shooting, Giamanco sought to avoid the limelight, putting out a brief statement expressing gratitude to first responders and the community. However, he told Oregon Public Broadcasting he's now decided to share his story.

"I've always wanted to change the world, but I've felt small. I'm just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family," he said. "I feel like if I'm going to have a voice, then I'll be damned if I'm not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place."
He said he hopes to help raise funds for local schools to improve their safety.

title: Judge allows Jane Doe anonymity in Cornell sexual assault lawsuit
summary: Jane Doe can remain anonymous in her sexual assault lawsuit involving former members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity, a judge ruled.
story: A judge ruled Friday that Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit alleging sexual assault involving seven former members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity, can remain anonymous as the legal proceedings move forward.

Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond granted the anonymity protections, citing the highly publicized nature of the allegations, concerns about retaliation and threats and the potential harm that could result from publicly identifying the plaintiff.
In her ruling, the judge also suggested that the anonymity designation "should likewise be extended" to the defendants, adding that she would welcome such a filing.

The ruling requires court filings to conceal Jane Doe's identity and other sensitive personal information. However, defendants will be permitted to privately share identifying information when necessary to investigate the allegations and prepare their defense, subject to confidentiality protections.
Perry-Bond also encouraged broader privacy protections for defendants and witnesses involved in the case.
In her ruling, the judge warned that anyone who engages in cyberstalking, harassment or threats against Jane Doe, the defendants or their attorneys could face criminal prosecution.

The decision does not address the merits of the sexual assault allegations or determine whether any of the defendants are liable. Instead, it establishes privacy protections for those involved as the civil lawsuit proceeds.
In a civil lawsuit, Jane Doe alleged she was drugged, gang-raped and sexually assaulted by seven men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. All seven have denied the allegations.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with lying about Hunter Biden laptop probe
summary: Two former FBI agents have each been charged with one count of lying to Congress about the investigation into Hunter Biden's laptop.
story: Washington — Two former senior FBI officials are facing criminal charges for allegedly making false statements to Congress during testimony in 2023 about the bureau's investigation involving Hunter Biden's laptop.

Nikki Floris, 46, a former intelligence analyst in charge in the bureau's Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, 56, the former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence Division, each appeared in court on Friday in Washington, D.C., where they were presented with a copy of a criminal complaint charging them with one count each of lying to Congress about their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election, specifically the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

A statement of facts prepared by the FBI and filed with the complaint alleges that Floris made false statements to Congress on July 19, 2023, and Benavides allegedly did the same that September. Their alleged false statements pertained to "their awareness of involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden," it said.

"The evidence further establishes probable cause to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of concealing [the Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with and communications about the Hunter Biden investigations and impeding the congressional investigation," it said.

The decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. to charge the pair in a criminal complaint stemming from three-year-old allegations is highly unusual, and both their defense attorneys and the magistrate judge who presided over Friday's hearing and unsealing raised questions about the decision.

"The alleged conduct happened years ago. The government has had the information about this for years," said Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides. He asked Zia Faruqui, the magistrate judge at Friday's hearing in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, to immediately schedule a preliminary hearing "as soon as humanly possible" to review whether there was adequate probable cause that a crime was committed.

The politically charged case was also unsealed just about two weeks before the midterm election — a fact that may raise questions by DOJ veterans about the timing of a case involving testimony to Congress that occurred more than three years ago.
Faruqui said he thought the manner in which the case was charged seemed "strange" and he rejected a request by prosecutors to delay the preliminary hearing for two weeks or more.
He ordered the parties to return at 11 a.m. on Tuesday.
"This is the Sword of Damocles hanging over their heads," he said. "This will follow them for the rest of their lives."
Former President Joe Biden's son Hunter has long been a target of President Trump and his allies.

Hunter Biden was extensively investigated by the FBI over his business dealings in Ukraine with the energy company Burisma, and the contents of his laptop after he left it at a repair shop in Delaware.

Former Attorney General Merrick Garland eventually appointed a special counsel to handle the investigations. Hunter Biden was tried and convicted on three felony gun charges. He pleaded guilty in a separate criminal case to three felony tax offenses and six misdemeanor tax offenses.
He was pardoned by his father shortly before his father left office, and was never charged with wrongdoing in connection with the allegations involving his overseas business dealings.
The charges
The criminal complaint unsealed on Friday said an FBI unit chief told investigators in October 2026 that Floris and Benavides both had oversight roles into the various Hunter Biden probes.

The complaint focused on an FBI counterintelligence operation by the Foreign Influence Task Force known as "Round River," which, it said, was focused on collecting "derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation."
Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election, it said.

"Witness accounts and contemporaneous documents from December 2019 through September 2021 show that Floris and Benavides knew about and were actively involved in the FBI's investigations of Hunter Biden. FITF hosted classified briefings for the agents and prosecutors on the Hunter Biden case in which Floris and Benavides  were active participants," the complaint said.

When Floris later testified to the House Judiciary Committee in July 2023, the complaint alleged she lied about her involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation and the role of the Foreign Influence Task Force.
In one exchange cited in the complaint, she was asked: "Did you have any involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation?" to which she responded, "I did not," the complaint said.
In another exchange cited, it said she was asked: "Was there ever a discussion at the FITF about Hunter Biden?"
"No. At least not with me," she responded, adding: "And again, there's a whole team below me, so whether or not conversations happened, I don't know, but I personally did not have any conversations."

In the September 2023 interview with Benavides before the House Judiciary Committee, the complaint said he told investigators he only learned some of the details about the investigation into the Hunter Biden laptop from Wikipedia when preparing for the hearing.
"When did you learn that there was an ongoing criminal investigation related to the laptop?" it says he was asked.
"The Wikipedia page," he said.
When pressed whether he had any knowledge about the matter during his time at the FBI, the complaint alleges he said, "No."
The complaint also cited a congressional staffer who was present for both interviews. That staffer told investigators the testimony from both officials appeared to be "materially untrue."
An FBI employee also later told investigators that he personally spoke with Benavides about the laptop and discussed reviewing its contents.

"Floris testified that she had no involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations. In reality, she was in frequent communication with the case team for over a year during which she both sent and received information about Hunter Biden," the complaint said.
"Benavides' testimony followed a similar pattern," it added.

The complaint and accompanying sworn statement also allege that Floris and Benavides were involved in reviewing materials to help prepare a script for a defensive brief, which aims to warn someone that he or she may have been the subject of foreign disinformation.

On Aug. 6, 2020, they provided two separate defensive briefings to Sen. Charles Grassley and Ron Johnson related to potential Russian disinformation, it said. It also alleged that Benavides and Floris were involved in reviewing and approving a Round River report that scrutinized informant intelligence related to the Hunter Biden investigations.
Floris' attorneys said in a statement that she has been falsely accused of a crime and raised concerns about the timing of the charges.

"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they said.

"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points. It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

During Friday's hearing, James Kirkpatrick, a special assistant U.S. attorney who came from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Western District of Missouri, appeared at the lectern and spoke for the Justice Department. He was accompanied by George Massucco, the criminal chief in the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C.

A spokesperson for Pirro's office said that Kirkpatrick does work in the criminal division there, though an internal Justice Department directory and his LinkedIn page still listed him as being in Kansas City.

At the hearing,  after the defendants' attorneys asked for a preliminary hearing as soon as Monday,  Kirkpatrick raised concerns about such rapid timing, saying the case agent is from out of town and that he would be out of town as well.
"You have charged this case," Faruqui retorted. "So you will be spending a lot of time in town."

Kirkpatrick's LinkedIn profile has since been taken down. A spokesperson for Pirro said that Cory Jacobs, the deputy chief of the criminal division, and John Borchert, the chief of the Fraud, Public Corruption and Civil Rights Section, are also working on the matter.
This is not the first time that the Justice Department has tapped prosecutors from other districts to help on controversial cases.

Last year, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia tapped prosecutors in the Eastern District of North Carolina to help with the prosecution of ex-FBI Director James Comey over lying to Congress.

That office also tapped an assistant U.S. attorney from the Eastern District of Missouri who mostly handled civil cases to work on the prosecution of New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was accused of bank fraud in connection with a mortgage.

In the Comey and James cases, prosecutors from out of town were brought in after people inside the office refused to participate due to concerns with the evidence, sources previously said. Both cases were dismissed, after a judge found the interim U.S. attorney who secured the indictments was unlawfully appointed.

title: UFO files detail strange, silent triangular craft: "Acoustic silence"
summary: Federal agents encountered a large aircraft that zoomed across the sky from a standstill while making no noise or giving off any exhaust, according to new files.
story: Washington — Federal agents in the western U.S. this year encountered a large, triangular aircraft that zoomed through the sky from a standstill while making no noise or giving off any exhaust, according to new documents released by the Pentagon.

The agents' recollections were included in the Defense Department's latest release of files related to UFOs, or UAP, unidentified anomalous phenomena. Friday's disclosure was the seventh under an executive order that President Trump signed earlier this year mandating the release of sensitive UAP files. The latest batch included 28 PDF files.

The triangular craft is detailed in two documents: a memo from the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office describing investigators' debrief with the agents, and a signed statement the agents gave to the FBI.
The encounter occurred in June near an unspecified "national security site" in the western U.S.

The agents told investigators that they were alerted to the object by a third agent stationed nearby. They quickly repositioned themselves to get a better look, and spotted the craft above a ridgeline a few miles to the west, against the glow of the sky after sunset.

"We initiated a visual survey of the western horizon and almost immediately observed a substantial, nonreflective, dark black triangular object most resembling a delta wing drone," they said in their FBI statement. "We estimated the object's wingspan at approximately nine to fifteen feet, its depth at six to nine feet, and its thickness at one to two feet."
The FBI document included illustrations showing the scene and a representation of the craft.

The AARO report notes that the "unidentified craft was executing a slow, controlled, perfectly vertical ascent directly over the ridge line. The craft climbed approximately two to three hundred feet while maintaining a completely static orientation without tilting, swaying, or wobbling. The non-reflective, matte black exterior presented a continuous, featureless profile."
Investigators wrote that the "ascent occurred in absolute acoustic silence."

The agents told the FBI that when viewed through an infrared scope, the object "appeared hotter than ambient temperature with a completely consistent thermal signature across the entire airframe and no visible exhaust gases."
When the craft was 200 to 300 feet above the ridgeline, it "instantaneously" stopped moving and began hovering, staying perfectly still for about 20 seconds, the AARO debrief said.
The craft then sped off, reaching a velocity "compared to that [of] a military fighter jet." The agents lost sight of it within a few seconds.

"Absolute acoustic silence persisted throughout the high-velocity phase," the memo said. "No impact signature, smoke, dust, or physical disturbance was observed. A ground survey of the canyon drainage conducted the following morning located no wreckage, ground scarring, or vegetation damage."
The incident is similar to other encounters reported by federal agents in the western U.S., detailed in previous releases of UAP files.

In 2023, federal law enforcement agents at an undisclosed location reported seeing orange orbs that released smaller red orbs over a two-day period, according to files released in May. A later batch included the agents' own accounts, with one describing red lights that "accelerated instantly" and another comparing the orbs to "grapes being expelled from a basketball."
Another instance, detailed in August, involved an agent who recorded infrared video of two "black-hot" objects moving together at the same slow speed.

Regarding the June incident, the Pentagon noted that AARO said it "warrant[s] further investigation due to the close alignment of the phenomena's reported morphological features and kinematic profiles with those of other reported incidents in the western United States region."

title: ICE crackdown prompts some Texas Latinos to turn away from Trump
summary: "I regret my vote for Biden. Now I regret my vote for Trump," one man said. "What other options do we got?"
story: McAllen, Texas — Benny Melendez, the owner of a small construction company along this stretch of the U.S.-Mexico border, says he's been forced to take drastic measures to protect his immigrant workers.

"If I don't install fences, ICE is going to come into my property and take my workers away," Melendez said as he showed CBS News the fencing he's set up at one of the several construction sites he manages in South Texas.

Melendez says the fencing is designed to prevent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from arresting his workers, and to require them to have judicial warrants before entering his job sites.

Local officials say construction is one of the industries hardest hit by President Trump's sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration. Construction company owners like Melendez say they're struggling to find workers, with some having been detained by ICE and many scared of showing up to work and getting arrested. Building a home, he said, is now taking his team a year due to manpower issues — up from an average of four months before the Trump administration's crackdown began.
"We're blessed that we have two workers today," Melendez said.
The South Texas resident, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after supporting President Biden in 2020, said ICE operations have also made him rethink his vote.
"I regret my vote for Biden. Now I regret my vote for Trump," Melendez said. "What other options do we got? They're not working for us, neither party."

Melendez's disillusionment is emblematic of broader concerns among some Latino voters — including some who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 — who believe his mass deportation crackdown has gone too far. A recent CBS News poll found nearly 60% of Latinos believe the Trump administration has deported more people than they expected.

Democrats are hoping those concerns will help them in key races in the midterm elections in November, as they try to retake control of Congress. That bet will be put to the test in Texas, where Mr. Trump and Republicans saw huge gains among Latinos in 2024, especially in communities along the southern border directly affected by the migration crisis there under the Biden administration.

Democratic state representative James Talarico and Ken Paxton, Texas' Republican attorney general, are in a hotly contested race for an open Senate seat. In Texas' 15th congressional district, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, a Democrat, is hoping to unseat Republican Congresswoman Monica De La Cruz.

Javier Villalobos, the Republican mayor of McAllen, the largest city in that congressional district, warned that his party is now at risk of losing some of the gains it made in Latino border communities. He called concerns about ICE's crackdown the No. 1 issue among his constituents.

"Inflation, the economy, everything is important. But what hits you immediately, what hits personally is the crackdown, when you see the ICE agents, masked, and pulling people out of vehicles," Villalobos told CBS News. "It is not a good picture."

Villalobos noted that local residents supported efforts to bolster border security and deport violent criminals in the U.S. illegally. But he said many now see ICE's deportation campaign as "a crackdown on the Hispanic community," one he believes has instilled fear in his city, including among American citizens.

CBS News has reached out to the White House for a response. Trump administration officials have routinely defended ICE's enforcement efforts, noting the president ran on expanding deportations and cracking down on illegal immigration.

"I particularly don't care about midterms," White House border czar Tom Homan told CBS News earlier this month when asked about criticism of ICE by some Republicans. "My job as a border czar is to keep that border secure and enforce immigration law."

Jessica Vuittonet, a coffee shop owner in San Benito, roughly a 45-minute drive from McAllen, said she voted for Mr. Trump two years ago, mainly because of her religious views. But she says she now regrets that decision, citing cases of local residents getting detained by ICE.
"I know he was going to start deporting people but not innocent people — not hardworking people," she said.

title: Medicare Advantage plans cut for 1 million seniors, insurers say
summary: Two of the largest private insurers are discontinuing some Medicare Advantage plans amid higher costs and a spike in utilization.
story: Two of the largest private health insurers in the U.S. are canceling some Medicare Advantage plans for seniors, CBS News has learned.

Humana and UnitedHealthcare each said they are discontinuing the plans beginning next year, ending healthcare coverage for a total of about 1 million people who are 65 or older. Healthcare Brew first reported the insurers' moves.
Humana's decision to exit the plan will affect roughly 600,000 enrollees, according to a company spokesperson.

"We regularly evaluate our Medicare offerings to ensure we can continue providing affordable, coordinated care and access to high-quality care. As previously disclosed, we anticipate plan exits for 2027 will impact approximately 600,000 members," Humana said in a statement to CBS News.
The company noted that most of its affected members will be offered an alternative plan.
UnitedHealthcare also confirmed that it is closing a Medicare Advantage plan for roughly 390,000 of its members, who will have access to another UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan.
The insurer said it is facing higher costs and increased plan usage, pressures that are affecting the whole healthcare industry.

title: AI could take your job. Here's how Congress wants to help workers.
summary: Sen. Ron Wyden on Friday introduced a bill that would double unemployment benefits to 52 weeks if the jobless rate jumps.
story: As artificial intelligence capabilities improve, many Americans are worried that the technology could one day put them out of work — a possibility more lawmakers in Washington are preparing for.

Members of Congress have recently introduced a series of bills to safeguard the nation's workforce against potential AI-related disruptions. Their proposals range in scope, with many geared toward creating training programs to support workers if their roles are eliminated.

On Friday, Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, joined the push to protect workers with "The Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act," a bill that would expand unemployment benefits during "high unemployment periods."
For instance, the bill would extend unemployment benefits for 52 weeks if the unemployment rate reaches 8.5%, double the current standard of up to 26 weeks.
The bill would also assist workers displaced by AI disruption by providing them with education and retraining for higher-paying jobs, Wyden's office said in a statement.

The raft of proposals comes amid warnings about the large-scale displacements AI could cause — some of them from the leaders of AI labs themselves. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and spike unemployment to 10% to 20% in the next one to five years.
Prominent tech leaders have also sounded the alarm bell. In a recent essay, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warned that AI could put millions of jobs at risk.

Those projections haven't materialized, with economists noting that AI hasn't yet created major workforce displacements. While there have been AI-related layoffs, most have been concentrated in the tech industry.

That hasn't done much to quell the concerns of Americans, nearly 80% of whom said it's extremely or very important to protect workers in the age of AI, according to a poll earlier this month from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
Here's a rundown of some of the proposals lawmakers have introduced to address those concerns.
Make AI Work for Americans Act

This bill, introduced last month by Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, would create three excise taxes on the AI industry, including a 5% tax on digital advertising revenue, an AI usage tax and a 50% excess profits tax.
Revenues generated by the tax would go into a fund that could be tapped to retrain displaced workers, among other options.
AI Tax and Work Protection Act

Democratic Reps. Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California introduced this bill in August. It proposes taxing artificial intelligence companies based on token usage, with the tax rate rising if the unemployment rate rises.
The money would be used to create jobs to offset AI layoffs, according to Rep. Casar's office.
AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act

Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat from Virginia, and Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, introduced this bill, which would enhance transparency about workforce disruptions. Introduced last year, it would mandate that major companies and federal agencies report AI-related layoffs to the Department of Labor, which would then share the data publicly.

Democratic Reps. Steven Horsford of Nevada and Sara Jacobs of California, along with James Moylan, who serves as the House's delegate for Guam, introduced a version of the bill in the House this July.

title: AI agents detected inside customer bank accounts, report says
summary: Banks have detected personal AI agent activity inside customers' accounts as experts warn about the risks of oversharing with AI.
story: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating within their customers' online accounts, according to a new Axios report.
Some of the biggest financial institutions in the U.S. say customers have given their personal AI agents, which are unvetted by banks, access to their financial accounts.

"In a lot of cases, this is just going to be customers giving their username or password to an AI agent that the bank hasn't had a chance to vet yet, that goes against the bank's terms of service," Madison Mills, senior AI reporter for Axios, told CBS News. "In other cases, in our reporting, we did find evidence that appeared to look like agents taking actions in customer accounts that were not authorized."
Examples of agent behavior that a user never approved include the AI calling a bank with a complaint without first consulting the account holder.
"So, really a nightmare of AI agent activity for banks," Mills said.

To be sure, these agents weren't going rogue or hacking customer accounts and depleting their funds, Mills said. They were largely following user instructions without the bank's permission to transact on behalf of a human account holder.
"In no way cyberattacks"

White House AI czar David Sacks responded to the Axios report, saying in a post on X that there's a clear distinction between personal AI agents that help manage users' bank accounts and hackers deploying AI for nefarious purposes.

"There's a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks," he said. "Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf."
Sacks added, "This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks."

He believes banks should support the use of such user-authorized AI agents, but that if banks want to limit their access, they could grant AI agents "read-only" permission, meaning they could view a user's spending and other bank activity but couldn't take autonomous actions.

Under such circumstances, an agent could view your purchases and opine on whether you're spending too much money eating out, for example. But it couldn't make a purchase on your behalf or take any other action.
"Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully," he said.
Mills noted that it's an industrywide problem facing dozens of financial institutions as they race to curb AI agents' access to customer accounts.
Banks taking action
Some banks said they're taking action to make their customers aware of the risks of sharing their credentials with AI.

"Customers should not give their username and passwords to anyone. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers to meet customers' needs while keeping their accounts safe," a Chase spokesperson told CBS News.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon expressed concern about AI agents taking actions in customers' accounts on the company's Oct. 13 earnings conference call.
"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said.
Charles Schwab's CEO earlier this month said the company has been blocking unauthorized agents, according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Morgan Stanley said it had not observed any unauthorized AI agent activity across its platforms.
Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment on the matter.

title: Trump says new fuel supply push will lower prices. Will it work?
summary: The Trump administration said using the DPA funding will increase refining output and lower fuel prices for Americans. Experts are skeptical.
story: President Trump on Thursday said his administration will invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production in the U.S., the latest effort from the administration to lower fuel prices.

The Defense Production Act, or DPA, is a Korean War-era law that allows the president to use loans, purchase commitments and other mechanisms to incentivize the production of critical materials and goods.
The announcement follows a meeting President Trump had with refiners to discuss immediate steps to bring more capacity online, a White House official told CBS News.

In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Energy said the DPA funding will increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day and lower fuel prices for Americans, who have been paying more than $4 a gallon on average for gas over the last three months.

The new plan to increase fuel production comes as polling shows a majority of Americans are pessimistic about the U.S. economy amid a growing affordability crunch. Crude oil prices have continued to climb, hitting their highest level this week since May.
On Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was $116 a barrel, up 2.6%, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was around $103 a barrel, up 3%.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline stood at $4.29 on Friday and $6.32 for diesel, according to AAA. Those prices represent a 40% and 74% jump from a year earlier, respectively.

Passed in 1950, the DPA was originally aimed at boosting supplies for national defense purposes. However, Congress has broadened its application to address natural hazards, terrorist attacks and other national emergencies.
Will the measure be effective?
Experts told CBS News that invoking the DPA is unlikely to do much to lower fuel prices.
"I don't think that's really going to have any impact," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News in an email.

There are some potential upsides: DPA funds could speed up some refining expansions, Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News. However, he said any short-term benefits are unlikely.
"There is no slack in U.S. refining, so production can't be added regardless of political will," Kloza said. He said it typically takes months and calendar quarters to bring units back to service.
The White House official said the DFA funds will help expand capacity and modernize existing infrastructure, which is much faster than building a new refinery.
The U.S. produces more fuel than it consumes. Oil prices, however, are set on the global market, where the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted shipments, pushing prices higher.

The U.S. produces around 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel oil, a category that includes diesel, per day but consumes only about 3.6 million barrels per day, experts have noted. The U.S. also produces 9.5 million barrels of gasoline per day, more than the 8.9 million consumed domestically.
The U.S. exports about 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day, Kloza, told CBS News.
A spokesperson for the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, a trade association that represents refiners, said it appreciated the Trump administration's focus on the importance of refineries.

"Our country's 128 operating refineries produce more fuel in the United States than we consume," the spokesperson said in an email. "They are running all-out to keep Americans supplied and the global economy moving despite major disruptions and actual fuel shortages in other parts of the world."

title: Anthropic previews Claude Duet personal AI agent for subscribers
summary: Anthropic said Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for paying subscribers. Here's what it can do.
story: Anthropic has joined the race to develop AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of humans with Claude Duet, a new app it previewed this week.
The agent competes with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, rival developers' agents that are already popular with consumers.
Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for Claude U.S. Pro and Max subscribers, according to Anthropic.
What can Claude Duet do?
Claude Duet works as a "proactive agent" for human customers, taking autonomous actions to complete tasks assigned to it.

"It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said, noting that it was designed for professionals and small business owners "with more on their plates than they can track."
Anthropic said Claude Duet's utility lies in its superior judgment, describing it as smart enough to know what to prioritize and which tasks require a user's attention.

Each morning, Claude Duet sends its user a daily brief outlining the day's most important items. For the agent to have context, it must be connected to a person's apps, like their email accounts and calendars. Some security professionals have raised concerns about new AI agents' access to such information, warning users to limit how much they share.
"Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work," Anthropic said.
What about security issues?
Anthropic highlighted built-in security measures that it says make the app safe to use, noting that the agent never directly sees a person's passwords or sign-in tokens.

Claude Duet can also handle administrative tasks like scheduling meetings and creating financial or sales forecasts. It can build web apps, too, Anthropic said. It can draft job postings or make purchases on a business owner's behalf.
Anthropic researchers who have tested the app have used it to manage their to-do lists, build apps, schedule interviews and more.
How do you sign up?
Anthropic said people can sign up on the waitlist at its Claude Duet product page.
Invitations are issued in waves, and the product is only available in the U.S. during its research preview, the company said.
"We're adding people gradually, and you'll get an email when it's your turn," the company said.

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: Trump praises Ramaswamy ad as some GOP critics speak out
summary: "Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" President Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"
story: Washington — President Trump on Thursday praised the "very powerful ad" Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is running featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, after the ad drew pushback from some Republicans like Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine.
Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that he suggested Ramaswamy keep the ad up, saying the press is "trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good!"

The ad, which first circulated on social media on Monday and is now television, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar" and sought to undermine her credibility. Acton's campaign condemned the ad, and her brother, Philip Stearns, called it a "despicable low."

According to court documents provided by the campaign, Arthur's now-deceased husband was charged with raping Acton, which she said occurred when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial.

DeWine on Thursday said he thought the Ramaswamy campaign should take the ad down. "It's wrong to run this ad," the Ohio Republican told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down." DeWine did not rescind his endorsement.
But Vice President JD Vance and now Mr. Trump are defending the ad and using it to criticize Acton.

"Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse," Mr. Trump wrote in his social media post. "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad.' Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
In his post, Mr. Trump did not mention why Acton and her birth mother are estranged, or any of the family's backstory.

Shortly after his post, on the White House South Lawn, reporters told Mr. Trump the backstory — that Acton's mother stayed married to the man charged with raping her. CBS News senior White House reporter Weijia Jiang asked the president why anyone should listen to what the estranged mother has to say.

"Well I know nothing about it," the president responded. "All I know is the mother said very bad things about Acton, who I guess is running for governor against Vivek. And all I can say is Vivek is great. And I know one thing, if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story, that's for sure. So I don't know what it is, but I guess the mother said very bad things about the one who's running for governor. And I think you have to say that seriously."
"I'm defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it, you would love every inch of it," Mr. Trump added.
In his Truth Social post, the president specifically went after DeWine.

"Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party," Mr. Trump wrote. "He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up..."
Mr. Trump added he only wishes the "mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse."
"Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" Mr. Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"

Mr. Trump continued to defend the ad during a rally in Iowa late Thursday. He said he advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it," later adding: "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much.'"
Vance, too, defended the ad, saying Republicans who have criticized it should "stop whining."
Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, who is running for reelection, said he "would not have run that ad."
Outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina called the ad the "most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season."
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told a local ABC station he "probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."

Acton's brother said earlier this week it's "not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

title: Kim Jong Un visits China to open new bridge, reaffirm ties
summary: The North Korean leader used the trip to reaffirm ties with its powerful neighbor.
story: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and vowing to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor.

Kim's visit to China, the first in a year, is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a "new Cold War."
Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry and China's official Xinhua News Agency.
In Dandong, Kim visited a memorial marking China's support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War and met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China's Communist Party.

At the memorial, Kim said that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) will "firmly carry forward the invincible DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood all the time," according to the North's official Korean Central News Agency.

During their meeting, Kim reaffirmed a resolve to develop bilateral cooperation, while Wang conveyed Chinese President Xi Jinping's greetings and said Kim's visit to the memorial was "of great significance" in carrying forward the friendship between the two countries, KCNA said.
The two toured a car factory as well, before Wang accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to KCNA and Xinhua.

While returning home via the bridge, Kim said "the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries," KCNA reported.

Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. China, for its part, has sought to restore its unique influence over North Korea.
North Korea has sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.

title: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protesters and police clash
summary: While demonstrations throughout France were largely peaceful, police reported clashes with protesters Saturday evening.
story: Police made 1,314 arrests in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Sunday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.

Nuñez 53 officers were hurt in marches. He said on Saturday marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.

He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000.  An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.

Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week.

Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.
Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march

Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."

Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.

The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.

As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."
Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said.

The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.
Protesters march against far-right gathering

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.
French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.
Protesters and police clash in smaller cities

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.

A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.
Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city.
Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details.
In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured.

Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.

In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.
Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
More protests spread across Europe
Other protests took place across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italian police said in a statement that they carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement said. Police on Saturday also said they had arrested a 30-year-old man suspected of being the figure behind the "October 17 Movement," a group which had called for the protests.

Soldiers were deployed to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, ahead of fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Others remained defiantly open after a call by the city's mayor Giuseppe Sala not to "panic."

"We want to give the message that we are not scared by these kids," said Alessandro Buhne, 30, who works at the Philipp Plein menswear shop. "Tourists are scared of this situation so we want to give the signal that you are safe if you enter our store."

Italy Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.
In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Some protesters briefly broke into the Colosseum, officials said.
Police "managed to isolate and contain the violent fringes, with balance and professionalism," Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
"In Italy there can be no room for those who delude themselves that they can act with impunity," he said.

Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.
In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.
Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
summary: Police said firefighting efforts were hampered due to local conditions.
story: A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.
There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."
The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

title: Elon Musk says SpaceX throttled Ukraine Starlink speeds over drone strikes
summary: SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink internet service has become the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations.
story: Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
Musk admits he was behind Starlink's speed restriction

Before Musk's confirmation, questions persisted last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.
President Trump had said he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. On Tuesday, CBS News reported that Musk was behind the disruption.
In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defenses since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Mr. Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."
Zelenskyy on Saturday thanked Americans and "all our partners, who took all this seriously and are really helping us."

title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
summary: A gunman opened fire from his car in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
story: A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and injured at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.

"These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents. "There is no place for this in France."

Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims. They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.

"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, the Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties. Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated.
Rabeh said the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.

A police source told the Agence France-Presse news agency that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time. Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window. His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X that the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised." Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
Suspect had booby-trapped apartment, investigators say
The suspect has been partly identified as Kevin T. He is 39 years old. The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office said Saturday that his detention has been extended.
Investigators said the suspect had booby-trapped his apartment with gas bottles and electrical wires connected to a timer. He also had tear gas grenades in his car, officials said.
A source close to the investigation told the AFP that a copy of Adolf Hitler's "Mein Kampf" was found in the suspect's apartment. A Bible and Quran were also found, the source said.

The prosecutor's office said Saturday that "three additional individuals" from the suspect's "family and circle of friends" were placed in police custody on Friday evening and overnight. The office did not say why those individuals were placed in custody.

The AFP reported later Saturday that four members of the suspect's family and circle of friends were arrested and were being questioned by investigators. A source close to the case told AFP that the suspect's parents were among those under arrest.

The office also said the suspect's criminal record includes four prior convictions, all of which had been legally expunged. The office did not say what those convictions were for or when they occurred.
Deceased victim identified as MMA fighter
The deceased victim was identified as Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old man of African origin. He was an up-and-coming mixed martial arts fighter.

Hundreds of people rallied Saturday at the spot where he was killed, as other protests swept across France. The demonstrators held placards that called for "justice" and led a moment of silence honoring Wangi.
"It could have been anyone. He opened fire on Blacks, Arabs. He knew the majority of the population here in Trappes is Muslim," a local shopkeeper of North African origin told AFP.

Wangi's family said the shooter was known to authorities, and demanded to know whether he had been properly monitored before the incident. In a statement released by the family's lawyer, they called for an investigation into potential failures on the part of the authorities and "to exhaustively establish the path that led to (the shooter's) radicalisation."
Multiple injured, including 12-year-old girl
Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.
A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the AFP.
The injured victims have not been identified. Rabeh said that one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."
France on edge after street violence and protests

The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, took to the streets again Saturday across the country.

French police have maintained a large presence to maintain order. Dozens of arrests were reported, and some groups were tear-gassed. Resources including elite police units, helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons have been deployed.

In the city of Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration group. Some placards seen at the march referenced the shooting in Trappes.

"Racism kills. The far right kills," a lawmaker from the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, Mathilde Panot, said at the rally near the spot of the shooting. Demonstrators also protested against Macron's policies and called on him to resign.
Le Pen called for a "relentless" investigation and said it was "despicable" if racism was the shooter's motive.

title: German man arrested for allegedly driving U.S. teen to die by suicide
summary: The 18-year-old German was arrested in Hamburg on Thursday, accused of being the indirect perpetrator of murder and grievous bodily harm, prosecutors say.
story: German police, acting on an FBI tip-off, arrested an alleged online sadist accused of driving a 14-year-old U.S. girl to hang herself, prosecutors said Friday.
The 18-year-old German was arrested in Hamburg on Thursday, accused of being the indirect perpetrator of murder and grievous bodily harm.

FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O'Malley said in a statement that their office worked with the Fort Wayne Police Department to provide information to the German police to help advance the arrest. The Fort Wayne Police Department said in a statement that its Homicide Unit identified a suspect who contributed to the juvenile's death.

"Anyone who targets or exploits a child should understand this: There is no safe haven from justice. It doesn't matter where you live or where you try to hide. The FBI will work with our partners around the world to find you and hold you accountable," O'Malley said.
The suspect was linked to an online group called "Nefarious Maniac Kult" or "NMK," part of a global network known by the labels "764" or "COM," the Hamburg public prosecutor's office said.

From September 2024 to September 2025, the FBI has seen a 300% increase in nihilistic violent extremism cases — many involving the 764 group, said FBI Director Kash Patel. The group 764 lacks a specific ideology, but members openly encourage self-harm and violence and encourage victims to produce videos documenting acts of self-harm or child sexual abuse material.

Between September and October, the suspect, then aged 17, allegedly "exerted influence" via the social network Discord over the girl from Indiana state whom prosecutors described as "psychologically fragile".

The suspect allegedly pressured the girl to cut herself and write the letters "NMK" on a wall in her own blood, and had her send him video recordings of these acts. A few days later, she hanged herself in her bedroom, prosecutors said.
The suspect allegedly sought a video recording of her death, hoping to gain status within the group or to secure entry into it.
