title: Larry the Cable Guy takes aim at corporations that considered his Southern brand ‘too controversial’

story: Larry the Cable Guy and Nebraska legend Eric Crouch join the ‘Big Noon Kickoff’ to preview Nebraska-Indiana, discuss the Cornhuskers' ceiling, Crouch's 2001 Heisman season and more.
Larry the Cable Guy says corporate America has a double standard when it comes to choosing which entertainers are too controversial for advertising campaigns.

The comedian went on a tirade against DirecTV, suggesting the satellite TV provider missed an obvious advertising opportunity — "Larry the Cable Guy has switched to DirecTV" — because of concerns about his image.

During an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," Larry recalled seeing a DirecTV commercial with an actor "back in the day" and said, "The first thing I thought was, 'Why don't they get me? Larry the Cable Guy is switching to DirecTV.’"
JEFF FOXWORTHY REVEALS HOW 'REDNECK' INSULT INSPIRED DECADES OF COMEDY

Larry the Cable Guy criticized what he sees as a double standard in corporate advertising, arguing that brands embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)

The comedian agreed, saying, "It would have been huge!"
Larry said he believed the company's concern was that his Southern accent and edgy humor might appeal to only one slice of America and make him too controversial for a national advertising campaign.

"At the time, ‘Well, Larry the Cable Guy is only really for one part of the country, you know, ’cause of the Southern accent, sometimes he says things that are a little controversial,'" he explained of the general sentiment then.

"There's a lot of hypocrisy in corporate, who they get and who they don't get. Look, I've had a good career. I ain't worried about it. But I'm just saying that DirecTV pissed me off."

title: Kate Gosselin says her kids know who she ‘truly’ is as son Collin levels abuse allegations
summary: Kate Gosselin responded to a fan on TikTok, saying her kids know who she "truly" is after Collin Gosselin's abuse allegations and memoir release.
story: ‘In the Shadow of Eight’ author tells Fox News Digital he's willing to hear from estranged mom Kate Gosselin but insists she must own up to her alleged treatment of him during his childhood.
Kate Gosselin says her children know who she "truly" is amid abuse allegations made by her son Collin.
The 51-year-old former reality star took to TikTok Thursday to celebrate her boyfriend Steve Neild’s birthday and got support from her fans in the comments section.

"Happy Birthday Steve ! Strength isn’t just about enduring—it’s about loving deeply enough to do what is right even when it costs you," one TikTok user wrote in the comments section. "Look at the beautiful life and happily ever after You have found now that You made sacrifices that no Mama should have had to make alone.
"When people attack You, it might sting for a moment, but it can never shake who You are. It only confirms that You stood your ground and remained true through it all. God is guiding You two."
‘JON & KATE PLUS 8’ STAR COLLIN GOSSELIN ACCUSES MOM OF TRYING TO ‘BURY’ HIM TO ‘PROTECT HER REPUTATION’
Kate received support from fans in the comments section of her latest TikTok. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)
KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR

"I know what it feels like to have to fight to have a relationship with your siblings. I don’t have one with my siblings, and I know how much that hurts. title: ‘80s pop star Taylor Dayne celebrates 4 years cancer-free after frightening diagnosis with no symptoms
summary: Taylor Dayne opens up about her colon cancer journey, urging women to advocate for colonoscopies earlier as she prepares for her Las Vegas residency.
story: ‘Tell It to My Heart’ singer Taylor Dayne says she's been cancer-free for four years after battling Stage 2 colon cancer. Dayne is gearing up for her first Las Vegas residency. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Taylor Dayne has plenty of reasons to celebrate.
The pop star, known for the '80s hit "Tell It to My Heart," has been keeping busy gearing up for her first Las Vegas residency at Harrah's Las Vegas.
The Grammy-nominated artist, who announced in 2022 that she'd privately battled Stage 2 colon cancer, said she's been given the all-clear and is ready to party with her fans.
TAYLOR DAYNE RECALLS FINDING FAME WITH ‘80S HIT ‘TELL IT TO MY HEART’: ‘I WAS PRAYING TO GET SIGNED'
Taylor Dayne is launching a Las Vegas residency beginning Nov. 24, 2026, at Harrah's Las Vegas titled "Tell It to My Heart" after her hit song. (Sequoia Emmanuelle Photography)

"I've been cancer-free for four years now," she told Fox News Digital with a smile. "I've been on the path of being very ardent about taking care of my health and being on top of my colonoscopies. There are no guarantees in life, but especially as women, we need to advocate for our health and be on top of our checkups.

"I was already on top of my colonoscopies when I was told I had a lot of polyps," the singer said. "It was through a routine checkup that they found a very aggressive polyp. This is how quickly these things can escalate and really take a turn. But my mindset was, 'What do I do right now?' I was very much in action mode."

Taylor Dayne performs onstage during the 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame induction ceremony at the New York Marriott Marquis June 11, 2026, in New York City. Dayne was diagnosed with colon cancer four years ago and survived it. (Getty Images for Songwriters Hall Of Fame)
Dayne, who didn't experience any symptoms before her diagnosis, stressed that routine screenings are essential.

Taylor Dayne attends the 28th annual Angel Ball at Cipriani Wall Street on Oct. 19, 2026, in New York. The pop star is "all clean" four years after her colon cancer diagnosis. (Variety via Getty Images)

"I was 50 years old, and they said, 'Now's the time to go in for this,'" Dayne, 64, said. "It's not like that anymore, because of our food, our diets, what we're exposed to daily. You really have to think about your timeline earlier than we've ever done. And we have such high-paced lifestyles. Most people are busy working, busy being parents, busy just being out there juggling. We can't put our health on the sidelines."

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that adults at average risk begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45, down from the previous recommendation of 50. People at increased risk, including some with a family history of colorectal cancer, may need to begin screening earlier.
Taylor Dayne circa 1990 (Getty Images)

"I thought it was a male-dominated disease, like prostate cancer," she said. "I was like, 'Colon?' It wasn't really resonating with me, and it certainly wasn't resonating with anyone in my family. I learned from my experience: Be your own warrior, be your champion. And that's what I did. It started with me asking, 'Why do I keep developing polyps?' You have to be your own champion, your own voice in getting the information you need, the plan you need."
Taylor Dayne is embarking on her first Las Vegas residency in her career. (Sequoia Emmanuelle Photography)
Dayne said her experience also taught her the importance of speaking up early. She noted that advocating for oneself can be harder when seriously ill.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Taylor Dayne told Fox News Digital she didn't experience any symptoms before her diagnosis four years ago. (Getty Images)

"When you're that ill, there's very little that the person can do," she explained. "Your advocate is usually your partner, your spouse, your best friend. But, oftentimes, it's just yourself. It made me realize a lot of things. And I'm so grateful, ever grateful. For me, it turned on a lightbulb, a desire to live, a desire to really push through things. And it's brought a lot of love to my heart because I've met so many people I otherwise wouldn't have met because we have so much in common now. Survivors."
Singer Taylor Dayne and her children attend the premiere of Battlefield America at AMC Universal City Walk in Universal City, Calif., May 23, 2012. (Getty Images)
Dayne's renewed focus on her health is also tied to her desire to be present for her children.

"Your kids don't think of you as having a career," she said. "They don't think about your fame, your awards, the guest house. All they want is for their needs to be met. You're just mom to them. I became a very different touring artist then. And touring was the largest component of my career. But I was a single parent. I raised them. I was then the mother bird who needed to always come back to her nest."
Taylor Dayne and son Levi Dayne attend the Big Game Kick-Off event hosted by Merging Vets and Players at Academy LA in Los Angeles Feb. 9, 2022. (Getty Images)
Dayne follows a no-nonsense health regimen that helps her look and feel her best as she prepares for her Las Vegas residency.
Taylor Dayne performs onstage at the 28th annual Angel Ball held at Cipriani Wall Street Oct. 19, 2026, in New York. (Variety via Getty Images)

"I'm very religious with my morning ritual, whatever my morning looks like, because my morning could be one o'clock in the afternoon, and it could be five in the morning," she said. "I do my peptides. I do my collagen. I do my bone broth. I do copper for my skin. I want to be optimal. That takes stretching, Pilates, yoga, daily exercise. You have to take care of yourself spiritually, emotionally, mentally.

Taylor Dayne and Kelly Clarkson appear on "The Kelly Clarkson Show." Dayne told Fox News Digital she follows a no-nonsense health regiment to help her look and feel her best. (Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"It's a real juggle," Dayne continued. "But the first moment you have in the morning, the first two minutes you have, should be centering yourself. And then I do my tinctures. I also like to have a big ol' smoothie. I usually have just liquids in the morning. I also love soursop, especially when I travel. I have to have a healthy lifestyle to meet the demands of what it takes to be physically on stage every night."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Taylor Dayne attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame 55th Annual Induction and Awards Gala at the Marriott Marquis Hotel in New York City on June 11, 2026. (WireImage)
Long before her health battle, Dayne experienced another life-changing moment of realizing just how quickly "Tell It to My Heart" had made her a star.

"I was in Munich preparing to make an appearance and I said, 'What are all these people doing outside? Why is their hair crimped? Why do they have red lips? Oh my God, they look like me,'" Dayne recalled.
Taylor Dayne performs on BR German TV show "200th Formel Eins" in Munich, Germany, in March 1988. (Redferns)

"It's not overnight stardom because I spent 15, 16, 17 in every club conceivable in New York in the '80s," she said. "But when you have a single like that, the next thing you know, you're on 'Top of the Pops.' I just knew my life would never be the same. I had no idea people would love my music so much, that they would want to look like me. Here we are, 39 years later.
Taylor Dayne (left) and Debbie Gibson (right) attend the 16th annual American Music Awards in Los Angeles. (FilmMagic, Inc)
"I never said, 'This is going to last forever,'" she said, reflecting on her fame. "How could you ever know? It was a moment. I was young, I was 22, 23. You just want to catch the wind."
Nearly four decades into her career, Dayne sees her upcoming Las Vegas residency as a victory lap.

Taylor Dayne poses for portraits on the red carpet during the 68th Grammy Awards pre-Grammy gala at the Beverly Hilton on Jan. 31, 2026, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"This is the cherry on top and recognizing that after three decades in this business, my music is still the soundtrack of so many people's lives," she said. "I am honored. My health, my wellness, my family, I am grateful for it all."

title: Bob Saget's widow, Kelly Rizzo, says his sudden death changed how she loves new boyfriend
summary: Kelly Rizzo shares the last text Bob Saget ever sent her and how Breckin Meyer has embraced his memory as their relationship grows stronger.
story: Kelly Rizzo, the host of ‘Comfort Food with Kelly Rizzo,’ shares how losing Bob Saget changed her approach to relationships, what she's learned from dating again and how her podcast helps others navigate grief.
Kelly Rizzo isn't sweating the small stuff when it comes to love.

Nearly five years after the sudden death of her husband, Bob Saget, Rizzo is approaching relationships differently. The 47-year-old told Fox News Digital she and her boyfriend, Breckin Meyer, have never had a fight in more than three years together, an outlook shaped by the sudden loss of her husband.
Rizzo hosts the podcast "Comfort Food with Kelly Rizzo," during which she sits down with celebrity guests and friends to discuss grief, coping and family.
SANDRA BULLOCK SAYS BRYAN RANDALL WAS ILL FOR 'HALF OF OUR RELATIONSHIP' AS SHE OPENS UP ABOUT HIS DEATH

Kelly Rizzo and Breckin Meyer attend Cool Comedy Hot Cuisine Benefiting The Scleroderma Research Foundation at Fairmont Century Plaza Oct. 29, 2024, in Los Angeles. Rizzo and Meyer have been dating since February 2024. (2024 Getty Images)

"It's been over three years, and I don't want to jinx it, but we have never had a fight," Rizzo told Fox News Digital. "We've never been in a fight. And I think, at least from my end, it's because I don't ever want to have a day where we're fighting and, God forbid, something happens, or where we're fighting, and he feels upset or sad because I never want to hurt his feelings.
"I just don't do a lot of the things that maybe I would have done in the past or if I was a little bit more immature," she said. "That's really what this dating journey has taught me about myself."
Kelly Rizzo and Breckin Meyer attend the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards at Dolby Theatre in Hollywood March 26, 2026. (WireImage)

Rizzo met Saget on social media in 2015, and they married three years later. On Jan. 9, 2022, the "Full House" star died at age 65 from accidental head trauma. Rizzo later found love again with Meyer, an actor. The couple made their public debut at Steven Tyler's annual Grammy Awards viewing party in February 2024, according to People magazine.
WATCH: KELLY RIZZO SHARES HOW BOB SAGET'S DEATH CHANGED HER DATING LIFE

"I've learned that it's so important to appreciate every single minute that you have with somebody because you don't know how much time you're going to get with them," Rizzo said. "You don't know how much time you're here on this Earth. So, I'm so much better today at not sweating the small stuff.
In "Comfort Food," Kelly Rizzo discusses grief, adult bullying, romance scams and more with celebrity guests and friends. (Ben Cope)

"I don't pick little fights," she continued. "You know, let's test him to see how much he loves me. I just don't do any of that anymore. I think a level of maturity also comes with my age and just having been in relationships in the past. But because I lost Bob so suddenly and so quickly, I know what a gift every single day is."
Rizzo said she learned the importance of expressing love from Saget during their marriage.
Season 2 of Kelly Rizzo's "Comfort Food" podcast launched earlier this year. (Courtesy of Kelly Rizzo)

"He always said, 'I love you. Tell everyone you love them,'" Rizzo said. "He was hugging people constantly. He was telling people ‘I love you.’ He never left a conversation without saying 'I love you' or leaving anything on the table. Everyone knew how he felt about them after every conversation or after every visit. And that was such a big lesson he taught people, even to this day. Even after almost five years."
Rizzo said opening her heart to someone new brought feelings of guilt, which she discussed on her podcast.

Bob Saget and Kelly Rizzo attend the "Untitled: Dave Chappelle Documentary" premiere during the 2021 Tribeca Festival at Radio City Music Hall on June 19, 2021, in New York City. Saget died in 2022 at age 65. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival)

"I was always so concerned, like, 'If people know that I love Breckin now, are they going to think I love Bob less?'" she said. "What I've learned is that it's just absolutely not true. ... You can have 100% of love for the person you lost and still have 100% of your love for the person in your life now. And having the new person does not take away the love from the person before, from the person who passed away, because they can live together and coexist so beautifully and so simultaneously."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Kelly Rizzo told Fox News Digital Breckin Meyer is one of the few people "Bob would be OK" with. (Getty Images)

"My love for Bob today, it's a little different than it was when he was here, but it's not any less," Rizzo said. "So, I think that's a big misconception. People are worried that if they move forward, it means that either they're going to somehow forget the person who passed away, or that people will think that they love the person less."

Rizzo previously said she sought the blessing of Saget's daughters, with whom she remains close. Saget had three daughters — Aubrey, 39, Lara, 37, and Jennifer, 33 — with his former wife, Sherri Kramer.
Kelly Rizzo and Bob Saget were married for just over three years before his sudden death. (JC Olivera/WireImage)

"It's truly the biggest gift I could ever have dreamed of, because they're such angels," she said of her relationship with her stepdaughters. "We've just still been a family. I talked to Aubrey today for an hour, and every conversation ends with 'I love you.' I'm going to see her tomorrow with my new step-granddaughter. It's just the biggest gift. I can't imagine doing this without them. And I don't want to put words in their mouth, but they've said the same.

Lara Saget and Kelly Rizzo attend Cool Comedy Hot Cuisine benefiting the Scleroderma Research Foundation at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles on Oct. 29, 2024. Bob Saget shared three daughters with his former wife, Sherri Kramer. (Getty Images)

title: Former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano thought she was 'going to die' after freak shooting accident
summary: Christy Carlson Romano reveals birdshot remains lodged a millimeter from critical structures near her eye after a clay pigeon shooting accident in Texas.
story: ‘Even Stevens’ and ‘Kim Possible’ star Christy Carlson Romano describes how a terrifying shooting accident nearly cost her an eye. The actress has written a memoir, ‘Once Upon a Trainwreck.’
Christy Carlson Romano is hoping to preserve her vision after a clay pigeon shooting accident in 2025 left birdshot lodged near her eye, putting her at risk of blindness.

"I was peppered with birdshot at about 250 feet away, and I was struck in a fat pocket under my eye and also in my forehead," Romano told Fox News Digital. "I still have birdshot behind my eye about a millimeter away from anything critical. And if it were to move, I would go blind. So, we're hoping that doesn't happen."
The former Disney child star opens up about navigating childhood fame and toxic relationships in her memoir, "Once Upon a Trainwreck."
She also recounts being struck by birdshot during the outing in Texas.
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

In 2025, Christy Carlson Romano was shot in the face by stray birdshot at a clay pigeon shooting range in Texas. She wrote about the experience in her new memoir, "Once Upon a Trainwreck: The Fall and Rise of a Child Star." (Andrew Toth/Getty Images)

"I, at one point, thought that I was going to die," the "Even Stevens" and "Kim Possible" star shared. " And when you have children, you can't help but start to see the world completely differently after an accident like that."
Romano's husband, Brendan Rooney, was celebrating his birthday when the couple decided to go clay pigeon shooting.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Once Upon a Trainwreck: The Fall and Rise of a Child Star" by Christy Carlson Romano is available now. (S&S/Simon Element)

"In Texas, it's quite common for people to be able to do these sorts of things," Romano said. "And I said, 'Well, you're a former Marine. You're going to enjoy this. Let's go do this.' And unfortunately, there was another part of our party that didn't choose to be responsible with their firearm and fired too closely in my direction."
WATCH: DISNEY STAR CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RECALLS TERRIFYING SHOOTING
Clay pigeon shooting is an outdoor sport in which circular clay targets are launched into the air for shooters to hit with shotguns that fire small pellets.
Christy Carlson Romano has been married to Brendan Rooney, a military veteran, since 2013. (Getty Images)
In her memoir, Romano wrote that she collapsed in front of the group and thought, "Am I dead? ... Oh God — my girls."
Romano wrote that her vision blurred as a "dark liquid" appeared to spread across her contact lenses.
Christy Carlson Romano still has birdshot behind her eye and forehead. (Courtesy of Christy Carlson Romano)
As Rooney and the unidentified shooter, whom Romano described as remorseful, rushed to her aid, she wrote that she looked "up at my husband of over 10 years. It's been a good run, right?"
"The Texas sky is big and beautiful today," she wrote. "Cicadas haven't quite woken up from their long winter's nap this February, and it's not too hot or humid. It's a beautiful day to die."
Christy Carlson Romano has two daughters with her husband, Brendan Rooney. (Getty Images)
Romano wrote that she became increasingly lightheaded as Rooney urged her not to fall asleep.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Christy Carlson Romano's eye was swollen with blood. (Courtesy of Christy Carlson Romano)
Romano recalled the drive to the hospital in her memoir, writing, "I try to break the tension as we fly down an empty freeway, going well over the speed limit — 112 miles per hour, to be exact."
"My oculoplastic surgeon had said that, usually, he's taking people's eyes out, kids, because they've been shot with a Nerf gun," Romano told Fox News Digital.

"It just so happened to hit the right fat pocket right under the eye. And I really almost survived through a miracle because I think there was any amount of outcomes when it came to having birdshot striking my skull and my face."
Christy Carlson Romano, seen here today, told Fox News Digital she had a "miraculous" recovery. (Matt Oliviera)
Romano wrote, "I'd have a scar and two pieces of birdshot permanently in my head, but I'd live. That's all that mattered."
She said doctors determined that removing the fragments would be too risky, so they were left in place.
Christy Carlson Romano previously opened up to her fans about the accident on social media. (Instagram.com/thechristycarlsonromano)

Romano's oculoplastic surgeon, Dr. Sean Paul, previously explained that the birdshot entered beneath her eye and became lodged in bone farther back, narrowly missing her eyeball, optic nerve and eye muscles by about a millimeter. Paul said she also suffered a subconjunctival hemorrhage, or bleeding beneath the membrane covering the white of the eye, but the pellet did not penetrate the eyeball.
Romano described her recovery as "pretty miraculous." She also thanked the medical staff at St. David's South Austin Medical Center in Austin, Texas, for their care.
Christy Carlson Romano starred as Ren Stevens, and Shia LaBeouf starred as Louis Stevens on Disney Channel's "Even Stevens." (Disney Channel via Getty Images)
"The biggest lesson that I took away from that experience was that life is short, and you need to be really attuned to what it is that you want out of life," Romano explained.

"And you need to have a good life. I'd lived such a chaotic lifestyle up until I became a mom that I think it really had me start to reflect even more with the book and exactly how I lived my life up until then. I think that's what gave me the impetus to write my letters to my daughters in the book."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Christy Carlson Romano told Fox News Digital she's grateful to be alive for her daughters. (Instagram.com/thechristycarlsonromano/)

Romano said she was compelled to write her memoir because "after turning 40, I experienced a lot of health scares." In February 2026, the "Vulnerable" podcast host revealed on Instagram that she had received a positive result from a cancer screening.

Romano and Rooney underwent cancer screenings because of her family's history of the disease. Both of her parents had cancer. Her mother survived, but her father died from the disease. Her maternal grandmother also died of lung cancer. Rooney's screening result was negative.

Christy Carlson Romano and husband Brendan Rooney attend Day 2 of the Chiller Theater Expo at the Sheraton Parsippany Hotel April 25, 2015, in Parsippany, N.J. They are raising their children in Texas. (WireImage)
Surviving the shooting and facing the possibility of losing her vision have given Romano a renewed sense of purpose, she said.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Christy Carlson Romano at the FOX Winter Press Day Nov. 18, 2024, in Los Angeles. (JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images)

"My life today is one that's really focused on personal growth," she said. "I think that my faith has become very big to me, and I have been praying just to really understand my calling and my purpose.

"And I really believe that if the book could help people feel a little less alone, that it would have been worth all of my vulnerability and all of my sharing. And I'm hoping the right people find it."

Christy Carlson Romano of "Kim Possible" and "Even Stevens" speaks at the Disney+ Pavilion at Disney's D23 Expo 2019 in Anaheim, Calif. (Getty Images for Disney+)

title: Rebecca Gayheart watched Eric Dane fight for time with daughters during ‘heartbreaking’ final months
summary: Rebecca Gayheart reveals the devastating moment she learned Eric Dane had ALS and how their two daughters navigated his final months together.
story: Actor Eric Dane, known for 'Grey's Anatomy,' died at 53 after battling ALS. Fox News' Dr. Marc Siegel details the disease's symptoms, rapid progression, ongoing research efforts and environmental factors.
As Eric Dane faced the final moments of his life, his family fought to hold on to every precious moment.

Rebecca Gayheart, who remained close to Dane after they separated in 2018, opened up about his final months battling amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the toll it took on their two daughters and how she's keeping his memory alive.
Dane died Feb. 19, less than a year after publicly revealing his ALS diagnosis.

"We tried to be present through all of our fear and frustration and uncertainty," Gayheart told People of the family's last months together. "It was truly an exhausting and heartbreaking experience, but it also showed us his extraordinary strength every day, and that was really wonderful for the girls and myself to witness."

Eric Dane died Feb. 19, less than a year after publicly revealing his diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). (John Shearer/WireImage)

While Gayheart tried to remain strong for Dane as they searched for answers about his worsening symptoms ahead of his diagnosis, she admitted nothing could have prepared her for the news that he had ALS.

"I went into my closet and closed the door," she told the outlet. "I was always telling him, ‘You’re going to be okay, we’re going to figure this out.’ But that day was like a punch in the gut. It took my breath away."
As Gayheart and Dane struggled to come to terms with the diagnosis themselves, they faced another challenge: explaining the news to their two young daughters.
"They had so many questions, it still felt like it wasn’t real," she said. "And their father let them know that he wanted to try to spend as much time as possible with them."

Dane began seeing symptoms of ALS in early 2024.

"I’m eating sushi with my kids, and suddenly I can’t work the chopsticks with my right hand," he wrote in his memoir, according to People. "My hand tingles, and then my fingers feel numb. Some kind of weird nerve thing, I think. I shake it off. I’m probably texting too much. Three weeks later, it happens again, only worse. I can’t grip the chopsticks at all."
The emotional impact of Dane's diagnosis was something the actor also addressed in his own words.

"[Rebecca and I] were married for 14 years, grew apart, filed for divorce, but never got around to signing the papers. We’ve since stayed close, co-parenting, going on vacations as a family, spending time together, and now we talk every day," Dane wrote. "I say to Rebecca on the phone, ‘It’s what we feared.’"

Gayheart and Dane married in Las Vegas on Oct. 29, 2004, and welcomed two daughters, Billie, born in March 2010, and Georgia, born in December 2011. The two shared a love story that lasted more than two decades, despite years of separation.
After his death, Gayheart revealed the moments she misses the most now that Dane is gone.

"After the kids downloaded me on their day, I’d call him and be like, ‘Oh my God, there’s a boy that likes Georgia.’ Or when Billie got her driver’s license, I wanted to call him so badly because that was something he was really excited about," she told People.

story: Pierce Brosnan credited his wife Keely and himself for giving their children a "simple life" to keep them grounded.

The 73-year-old actor spoke with Fox News Digital at the premiere of his son Paris' new film, "Seniors," about Paris' acting career and how he's warned his sons about how "tough" the entertainment industry is.

"No, it's a very tough business, it is a very capricious business at times, but Paris has the strength and the stamina, he has a talent there, he's got a charisma, and he's got good sense and intuition, he really has a talent there that will need to be nurtured and worked on," he said. The "Die Another Day" star shares two sons with his wife, Keely Shaye Smith — Dylan, 29, and Paris, 25 — and welcomed Sean, 43, with his late first wife, Cassandra Harris. SCOTT EASTWOOD CREDITS HIS FAMOUS FATHER'S WORK ETHIC FOR MAKING HIM AWARE OF 'BULLS---' IN THE FILM INDUSTRY

title: Country star Jimmie Allen says he’s the ‘victim’ after $1.8M judgment in sexual assault lawsuit
summary: Jimmie Allen claims he is the "victim" and reveals the dark mental health spiral that followed two sexual assault lawsuits and a default judgment.
story: Country star Jimmie Allen tells Fox News Digital he forgives the women who accused him of sexual assault while maintaining the allegations against him are false.
Jimmie Allen is maintaining his innocence and insisting he is the "victim" after a federal judge ordered the country star to pay nearly $1.8 million to a woman who accused him of sexual assault.

The 41-year-old singer faced two separate civil sexual assault and abuse lawsuits from two women in 2023. During an interview with Fox News Digital, Allen spoke candidly about the allegations that derailed his career, maintaining that his sexual encounters with both women who sued him were consensual while acknowledging that he was unfaithful to his then-wife, Alexis Gale.

When asked what he would say to his accusers today, Allen said he has forgiven both women but admitted that he struggled with being unable to publicly defend himself without being accused of blaming alleged victims.
JIMMIE ALLEN PUBLICLY APOLOGIZES TO ESTRANGED WIFE FOR ‘HUMILIATING HER’ WITH ‘AFFAIR’ AFTER SEX ABUSE LAWSUIT

"I wanted to just get on social media and call them liars and things like that," Allen said. "But it was interesting when I thought about it, someone said, 'No, well, you'll be a victim blamer and stuff like that.'"

"But I was like, 'I'm the victim here,'" he continued. "So they can say this about me, these horrible things about me and try to ruin and destroy everything that I worked my butt off for. But I can't say that they're lying."
Jimmie Allen is maintaining his innocence after he was ordered to pay nearly $1.8 million to a woman who accused him of sexual assault. (Rolling Stone via Getty Images)

In May 2023, the first woman, Jane Doe 1, who worked as the country singer's day-to-day manager, filed a lawsuit against Allen, in which she accused him of raping her in 2021 and subsequently sexually harassing her over the next 18 months.
JARED LETO RESPONDS TO SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS MADE BY MULTIPLE WOMEN IN EXPLOSIVE DOCUMENTARY

The second woman sued Allen in June 2023, accusing the "Big In A Small Town" singer of sexually assaulting her while she visited him at a Las Vegas hotel in the summer of 2022 while he was in Sin City for a bowling tournament. Jane Doe 2 claimed Allen had also recorded the encounter without her permission.

Allen denied both women's allegations and filed counterclaims against them in July 2023, accusing his former manager of defamation and other claims and accusing Jane Doe 2 of unlawfully taking his cellphone following their encounter.
In August 2025, Allen was found liable by default rather than following a trial in which a jury weighed the competing accounts.
The following June, a federal judge ordered Allen to pay Jane Doe 2 $1,790,541 in compensatory and punitive damages.
WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS HE'S THE ‘VICTIM’ AFTER SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS UPENDED HIS LIFE
KATY PERRY UNDER POLICE INVESTIGATION OVER RUBY ROSE'S SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen said that he does not intend to simply accept the judgment.

"I'm pursuing options because I – me as a man and as a father and as the son and brother of real sexual assault victims – I cannot in good conscience do that," he said. "And that's why I feel like as a man and as a father, it is my job to fight it and find and chase whatever other options I can."
Allen did not specify what legal action he intended to pursue. Fox News Digital reached out to his current attorney, Ted Anastasiou, for comment.

The default ruling followed a series of missed deadlines and court orders. According to court records, Allen and his touring company failed to meet discovery requirements, attend court-ordered mediation and obtain new counsel within deadlines set by the court.

Allen claimed that much of the breakdown was due to his former attorney, Alandis Brassel, becoming seriously ill while representing him. The singer told Fox News Digital that Brassel was a solo practitioner and claimed that he had difficulty reaching his lawyer while he was sick.
"I'm not in contact with the court. He is," Allen recalled. "So during that time, we missed a deadline."
Allen said Brassel later informed the court about his illness but claimed the judge "didn't care."
"So the judge dropped my countersuit, and they awarded Jane Doe 2 default judgment because I missed the deadline," he said.
The singer said that he was the "victim." (Wyatt/ACMA2021/Getty Images for ACM)
However, court records detail multiple missed deadlines and failures to comply with court orders.
The Grammy Award nominee acknowledged that there was at least one deadline during that period of time that he believed he could have met himself.
"I have no problem taking responsibility," Allen said. "I could have, you know, maybe done more. Absolutely."

"The other ones, I should have been more, I guess, involved with the court, but I've never been in a situation like this," he continued. "I didn't know even how to connect with the court. I didn't know if I could speak to the court without my lawyer because he was the one that was handling it."

Anastasiou later became Allen's legal representation. After the default ruling, Anastasiou similarly blamed Allen's "prior counsel's repeated failures to comply with discovery obligations and court orders" and said his client intended to seek to set aside the judgment.

"This ruling was not based on the merits of the allegations. Mr. Allen has consistently and unequivocally maintained his innocence, and he firmly denies these accusations," Anastasiou told People magazine in August 2025.

"As with earlier accusations brought on the same baseless grounds, this case is equally meritless," he continued. "The default judgment reflects the shortcomings of prior representation, not any wrongdoing by Mr. Allen. It is well-established that a client should not be penalized for the failures of their attorney, and Mr. Allen should not be deprived of his right to a fair defense."
Fox News Digital was unable to reach Brassel for comment.
WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS HE'S ‘PURSUING OPTIONS’ TO FIGHT $1.8M SEXUAL ASSAULT
According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe 2 met Allen on a flight to Nashville in May 2022 and the two remained in contact over the following months before meeting in Las Vegas.
FORMER MIT SCIENTIST WINS $6M DEFAMATION VERDICT AGAINST COLLEAGUE WHO ACCUSED HIM OF SEXUAL MISCONDUCT

Jane Doe 2 alleged that she willingly joined Allen in his hotel room and initially consented to having sex with him, but repeatedly told the singer that she was not on birth control and did not want him to ejaculate inside her. According to the complaint, Allen agreed but later disregarded her requests to stop and instead ejaculated inside her.

She also alleged that Allen secretly recorded their sexual encounter without her knowledge or consent. According to the lawsuit, Allen had asked her to remain on the hotel room's balcony after they arrived while he went inside, which she believed was because he was planning a surprise. Jane Doe 2 alleged that Allen instead used the opportunity to position his cellphone to later record them.

Jane Doe 2 alleged that after Allen fell asleep, she discovered the phone recording them, stopped the recording and deleted the video. According to the complaint, she was unable to permanently delete the footage without Allen's passcode and took the phone with her when she left the hotel room before later turning it over to police.
Allen was sued by two women for sexual assault and abuse in 2023. (Terry Wyatt/Getty Images)
EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M

Allen disputed Jane Doe 2's account, maintaining that their encounter was consensual and that she knew she was being recorded. He said that they were together on the balcony when he explicitly told her he wanted to record and asked permission. While speaking with Fox News Digital, he described their alleged conversation regarding the recording.

"She said, ‘You were recording us without my permission.’ I said, 'Oh, no, no.' I said, 'We were on the balcony.' And I have all this in texts that we were on the balcony. I told you, 'I'm recording, is it OK?' And I don't ever hide my camera, ever. Ever. It's not my thing,'" he told Fox News Digital.
Allen has maintained since 2023 that Jane Doe consented to the recording.
The singer claimed to Fox News Digital that the recording depicts him "passing out."
"In the video, you can see me passing out," he claimed. "You can see me black out, like pass out."

Allen further claimed the recording shows Jane Doe 2 continuing to engage in sexual activity with him after he passed out, later getting dressed, returning to bed and rubbing his back before approaching the camera and turning it off.
WATCH HERE: JIMMIE ALLEN SAYS SEXUAL ASSAULT LAWSUIT ‘LITERALLY SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER DOCTOR'S DIRE WARNING
Elizabeth Fegan, an attorney who represented both Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2, blasted Allen's claims in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Mr. Allen's attempt to portray himself as the victim is as outrageous as it is offensive to the women who have come forward to report his sexual misconduct," Fegan said. "Two women have accused Mr. Allen of sexual abuse. Rather than accepting responsibility for his actions, he has repeatedly denied their accounts, sought to discredit them, and now attempts to rewrite the facts through the media, all while evading his financial obligations to the women who sought justice through the courts."

"Let there be no ambiguity: Jane Doe 2 never consented to being recorded," she continued. "Mr. Allen's continued insistence otherwise does not change her account or the Court's findings. Nor do his self-serving descriptions of selected portions of the recording establish consent to its creation. His attempt to shift attention to her behavior is yet another effort to blame the woman whose rights he violated."
JIMMIE ALLEN WELCOMES THIRD CHILD WITH ESTRANGED WIFE AMID SPLIT, SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS

"The real victim here is the woman whose privacy, bodily autonomy, and trust were violated and who has endured years of trauma and litigation seeking accountability," Fegan added. "Mr. Allen has had ample opportunity to tell his story in court. He chose not to do so. He should stop attacking the women who came forward and start taking responsibility for his conduct."
The default ruling followed a series of missed deadlines and court orders. (Fox News Photo/Joshua Comins)
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen also addressed the allegations made by his former day-to-day manager, whose 2023 lawsuit first thrust the country singer into the scandal.

Jane Doe 1, who worked as Allen's day-to-day manager, accused the singer of repeatedly sexually harassing and assaulting her over an approximately 18-month period while she was employed by his management company.

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe 1 alleged that Allen first sexually assaulted her in March 2021 after a work trip to Los Angeles, where he was filming an appearance on "American Idol." She claimed that after having several drinks at a business dinner, she woke up naked in her hotel room with Allen beside her and had no memory of what happened after dinner. According to the complaint, she was bleeding and in pain and Allen insisted that she take Plan B.

Jane Doe 1 alleged that Allen continued to sexually harass and assault her afterward, including by touching her without her consent and forcing her to engage in sexual acts despite her objections. She claimed she repeatedly told Allen "no," pushed him away and tried to avoid being alone with him, but feared that resisting him could jeopardize her career because she was responsible for managing him.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen vehemently denied Jane Doe 1's allegations but acknowledged that the two had a sexual relationship, which he characterized as a consensual affair that continued on and off for approximately a year and a half.
"What I want people to understand about those allegations is one, they're not true," he claimed.

"I had an affair off and on for like a year and a half with my day-to-day manager," Allen said. "And it started, then we would cut it off, and it would start, and then we will cut it off. And it slowly became one of the things where I was like, I know what I was doing was wrong, but I was afraid to end it because I didn't really know exactly how to end without one, hurting her, right, and without hurting myself. Because it's one of those things where it's like you spend so much time, go, go, go, go, go on the road. And, you know, we were around each other a lot. We were adults that made a decision."
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen accepted responsibility for having the extramarital relationship but denied Jane Doe 1's characterization of it as sexual abuse.
Allen and his ex-wife Alexis Gale divorced in 2024. (Chris Polk/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)
"If I would have never cheated on my wife, I wouldn't have been in that situation anyway," he said. "And that's the part that I take accountability for."

Allen and his former manager reached a settlement in 2024 in which they agreed to dismiss their respective claims against each other. Jane Doe 1's attorney said at the time that she continued to stand by her sexual assault allegations against Allen and had agreed to settle to avoid reliving the alleged abuse at trial.
While Allen maintained he never sexually assaulted either woman, he told Fox News Digital he does not consider himself blameless for the circumstances that led to the scandal.

"Did I cheat on my wife? Yes. Did I apologize to my wife? Yes. Did I owe my wife an apology? Absolutely," he said. "And I'm not going to put the blame on my life on those two individuals. Yes, they might've fabricated a story, but I still slept with them and I put myself in that position."
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Allen recalled the impact that the allegations had on his personal and professional life.
The singer said that he would tell his accusers that they "made life really hard for my kids."

Allen and Gale, who share daughters Naomi and Zara and son Cohen, initially separated and filed for divorce in April 2023, shortly before the first sexual assault lawsuit was filed against the singer. They simultaneously announced that Gale was pregnant with their third child, Cohen.
In a May 2023 Instagram post, Allen apologized to Gale for having an affair and acknowledged that his choices brought shame and humiliation to his family.

Gale gave birth to Cohen in September 2023 and the following month, Allen's representative said the divorce had not been completed and that the couple had decided to "work on things" and were still together.
The former couple's divorce was ultimately finalized in October 2024.
The former couple share three children. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for CMT)
Allen told Fox News Digital that the "hardest conversation" that he had was with Gale. He admitted that he failed to even warn his then-wife before the first lawsuit became public.
"I handled that completely wrong," Allen said.

Allen said the fallout also affected his oldest son, Aadyn, whom he shares with a previous partner. He recalled struggling to explain why some of his son's friends stopped speaking to him or inviting him to parties after the allegations against his father became public.
The singer also recalled how his thriving career collapsed amid the scandal and worried about how he would continue providing for his children.
"Everything I've worked for is just gone," he said. "Record label gone, management gone, bookings gone, PR gone, endorsement deals gone."
He said that his mounting fears sent him into an increasingly dark place and eventually led him to contemplate taking his own life.
"Two years ago, I was riding around my truck at like three in the morning and I had my gun in my lap and I was trying to decide, do I want to live or not?" he told Fox News Digital.
Allen said he eventually sought help, turning to therapy and spending time in rehabilitation as he worked to get his mental health back on track.

He recalled that his struggles had begun well before the allegations became public. As Allen's career took off, the singer said he began taking pills to stay awake and others to keep himself in a good mood while trying to meet the demands of touring, his record label, radio, his family and fans.
Allen said that by 2021 and 2022, he felt like he was on a "train" going "a thousand miles an hour," knowing he needed to get off but unsure how.

"I would say in 2023, when that lawsuit came out, I felt like that was God derailing the train," he said. "One, it hurt because of what was being said about me. But at the same time, it literally saved my life."
"My doctor said if I had kept going, I'd have been dead in six months," Allen continued.
Allen told Fox News Digital that getting help also forced him to reconsider his relationship with music, which he admitted he had grown to hate at the height of his struggles.
However, Allen said that as he worked to rebuild his life, he also began rediscovering the love of music that he had lost.
Allen recalled how his career collapsed following the allegations. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for dcp)
Allen told Fox News Digital that while some relationships disappeared amid the controversy, he was surprised by the support he received from others in the entertainment industry.

"Dolly Parton being one of them," he said. "She called me, and she told me she loves me. She said, ‘Jimmie, I know who you are.’ She said, ‘Try to just keep yourself surrounded by people that love you.’"
Allen recalled Jelly Roll, Darius Rucker, Kathie Lee Gifford and Kid Rock were among others who reached out to him.

Kid Rock's support eventually extended beyond words of encouragement. The "Freedom Was a Highway" singer recently collaborated with Kid Rock on his Christian album "Halfway to Jesus," marking another step in Allen's return to recording music.
Allen recalled Kid Rock telling him, "'As Christians, we're quick to ask for forgiveness but don't want to give it.'"

He recently collaborated with Kid Rock and is working on several projects of his own. (Getty Images)

The musician is also working on several projects of his own, including Christian and gospel music as well as country and R&B material. He said his approach to his career has changed dramatically from the relentless pursuit of success that he described before the allegations surfaced.
"It's not about winning Grammys or CMAs or number one records," he said. "It's about doing what I love."
When asked whether he believes Nashville is ready to give him another chance, Allen explained being accepted back into the country music establishment was not his priority.

title: 'Goldbergs’ star Jeff Garlin says he planned to take his own life amid turbulent final days on sitcom
summary: Jeff Garlin reveals he planned to take his own life after his turbulent exit from "The Goldbergs," detailing the crisis that led him to seek help.
story: Jeff Garlin told Adam Corolla last week that he hasn't worked an acting job in nearly three years, as the pair discussed Hollywood jobs moving out of the state.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Jeff Garlin reached his breaking point after a tumultuous chapter on "The Goldbergs."

The comedian, who exited the hit ABC sitcom in 2021 amid allegations of misconduct on set, opened up about his mental health crisis, his struggles with bipolar disorder and the treatment that helped him rebuild his life.
Garlin revealed he had planned to take his own life and even told a loved one the exact time he intended to die during his appearance on SiriusXM's "Where Everybody Knows Your Name."
"The last scene I ever filmed was me with Tim Meadows, Dave Koechner, and Troy Gentile, who played my son. And it essentially was a Pizza Hut commercial. No one told me," he said.
JULIA LOUIS-DREYFUS REVEALS ‘TONS’ OF FRICTION BEHIND THE SCENES OF ‘SEINFELD’

Jeff Garlin revealed he planned to take his own life after experiencing a severe mental health crisis and nervous breakdown following turmoil surrounding "The Goldbergs." (Tony Rivetti/Walt Disney Television via Getty Images)

Garlin said he confronted the production team after learning the scene doubled as a pizza advertisement without his knowledge. When producers explained that the money would help hire another writer, he questioned why the corporation behind the show couldn't cover the expense itself.
The actor refused to participate in the promotional scene and instead insisted that producers film his character leaving before the pizza appeared.
"I left, and I knew I'd never come back to that set again," he said.
But walking away from the set didn't mark the end of Garlin's troubles.

Garlin said a producer later visited his home and asked what it would take to convince him to return to the show. Although he had no desire to go back, the comedian demanded a substantial raise and a reduced schedule of just one workday per week. To his surprise, producers agreed.

Jeff Garlin exited "The Goldbergs" in 2021 amid allegations of misconduct on set. He recalled clashing with producers over a promotional pizza scene and later facing resentment from castmates over his favorable work arrangement. (Bob D'Amico/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
However, Garlin admitted the arrangement came at a cost.

"And so I had resentment from my castmates, not as much the crew, but there was great resentment from some of them," he admitted. "I didn't know it at the time, though. I was naive. I didn't know they knew anything about my anything."
As tensions surrounding the sitcom mounted, the comedian said he struggled with a devastating mental health crisis that pushed him to the brink and prompted a desperate message to a loved one.

"I had a nervous breakdown, and I was going to commit suicide," he recalled. "I reached out to Susie and I said, 'I hate when people don't reach out, but at noon today I will be dead. I'm letting you know I will be dead.'"

Jeff Garlin credited loved ones with intervening during his darkest moments. After telling a loved one the exact time he planned to die, friends and family stepped in to help him seek treatment. (Rick Rowell/ABC via Getty Images)

"And she called [ex-wife] Marla, and she called [girlfriend] Sari, and my friend Brad Morris," Garlin explained. "My girlfriend and my ex-wife called him. He's one of my best friends. He watched me while they were looking for a place for me to go."

Garlin said he traveled to Cincinnati in the dead of winter to seek treatment, where he underwent dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). He credited the treatment with helping him overcome his suicidal thoughts and regain enough stability to move forward with his life.
"I went to Cincinnati because I was serious," he explained. "I'm not going to some rehab in Beverly Hills. F--- that, man."

Garlin said he continued rebuilding his life through Alcoholics Anonymous, dialectical behavior therapy, regular counseling, boxing, physical fitness and creative projects that helped support his mental health and overall well-being.
"And I'm just now, this is from five years ago, whatever," he explained. "I'm just now feeling really good. Just now. Maybe the book coming out, but around now, really."

title: Catholic alcohol consumption drops to record low as Americans rethink moderate drinking habits
summary: Catholic adults now report drinking rates near the levels of Protestants as shifting health views and social habits reshape moderate drinking in America.
story: Josh Gowin explains how research has shifted the understanding of alcohol's health risks, including its association with reduced brain volume, as drinking habits and social norms continue to change.

A historic shift in American drinking habits shows Catholic alcohol consumption reaching record lows, though scientific experts caution against attributing the drop strictly to religious or cultural changes.
The share of Catholic adults in the United States who report drinking alcohol has fallen to 55%, according to a Gallup report authored by analyst Frank Newport.
That marks a decline from the 2002–2004 period, when 79% of Catholics reported consuming alcoholic beverages. Over that same timeframe, self-reported Protestant drinking rates remained flat at 54%.
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
"Drinking has dropped significantly within both the group of those who have no religious identity and, in particular, among Catholics," Newport wrote in the analysis.
However, experts urged caution when drawing sweeping conclusions from subgroup survey data.

Dr. Joshua Gowin, an associate professor in the Department of Radiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus who studies alcohol's effects on the brain, noted that self-reported polling figures can fluctuate based on sampling.
Historically, Catholics were far more likely to drink than Protestants, but a sharp drop in Catholic drinking has completely eliminated that long-standing gap. (iStock)
"There's definitely a general pattern of alcohol use decreasing across groups," Gowin told Fox News Digital.
"As far as the subgroups go, it wasn't clear or necessarily compelling to me that one group was showing a broad trend that wasn't reflected in the other groups," he went on.
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
"It seemed like really only one data point showed that effect ... which made me a little skeptical that this is a broader phenomenon versus a single survey sample."
Despite methodological limitations in tracking specific religious subgroups, researchers agree that broader social and health trends are driving a shift in overall drinking habits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Gallup findings indicate that a majority of Americans now view moderate drinking — defined as one or two drinks per day — as bad for their health.
In the latest polling, 52% of Catholics said moderate alcohol consumption is bad for health, alongside 56% of adults with no religious affiliation and 48% of Protestants.
Perceptions surrounding alcohol health risks have changed, with a majority across all religious demographics now viewing moderate drinking (one to two drinks daily) as bad for their health. (iStock)
Gowin noted that this public shift reflects decades of neuroscience and medical research.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Twenty years ago, there was still kind of a push and pull between some benefits of alcohol and then some things that even then we knew were potentially harmful," he said.
"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."
"Over time, we've gotten a lot more clarity on the things that are bad for our health ... the balance has just shifted more in favor of the evidence for negative health effects."
Gowin pointed out that large-scale neuroimaging studies now consistently link higher alcohol consumption to reduced brain volume, reinforcing public health warnings.
The report’s author cautioned that the drop may reflect normal survey variation rather than a long-term cultural shift. (iStock)
Researchers also attribute shifting consumption patterns to broader societal changes, including shifts in social behavior and loneliness.
Much of America's alcohol consumption has historically occurred in group settings, and changes in how people gather socially may be influencing drinking habits, they believe.

At the same time, experts caution that a drop in general social drinking does not mean severe alcohol problems have dissolved.

"One of the things that is a bit of a contradiction ... is that although the overall prevalence among all adults is down for the number of drinkers, there is actually a larger number of alcohol-related deaths in the past few years," Gowin noted.

"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."

title: Jalen Hurts puts spotlight on blood thinners: 5 mistakes that could put patients at risk
summary: Jalen Hurts' blood clot diagnosis puts blood thinners in the spotlight. Experts reveal five critical mistakes patients on anticoagulants must avoid.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'America's Newsroom' to break down Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary emboli.
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of blood clots in both lungs has put blood thinners in the spotlight.
Hurts is receiving treatment with the medication and is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, according to the NFL.
Even young, physically active people can develop dangerous blood clots, especially when risk factors such as an injury, long travel or recent surgery combine.
"Being in shape lowers your risk, but it doesn’t make you immune," said Dr. Joseph V. Lombardi, chief physician executive at AtlantiCare.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY
Hurts’ case also highlights the precautions patients taking blood thinners may need to follow.
Jalen Hurts is taking blood thinners to treat blood clots in his lungs, a treatment that can raise the risk of serious bleeding after an injury. (Mitchell Leff/Getty Images)

The medication can help prevent dangerous clots from growing or forming but can also make it harder for the body to stop bleeding after an injury, a concern for athletes playing high-contact sports or anyone who falls or gets hurt.

"Taking [blood thinners] consistently, understanding potential interactions and recognizing warning signs can greatly reduce the risk of complications," Dr. Yazan Abou-Ismail, a hematologist and thrombosis expert at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital.
STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT KEY TEST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD, EXPERT WARNS
Here are five mistakes patients should avoid:
Patients taking blood thinners should check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding new medications or supplements, experts say. (iStock)
1. Stopping treatment without medical guidance

While some patients only need blood thinners for a limited time, others may need them long term. When a clot has a clear cause, such as an injury, treatment often lasts about three months, Lombardi told Fox News Digital.

The duration depends on factors including the reason for treatment and whether a patient has had previous clots, Abou-Ismail added. Stopping too soon can raise the risk of another clot, while continuing longer than prescribed may increase bleeding risk.
SILENT INFLAMMATION COULD BE DAMAGING YOUR BODY — AND 5 HABITS MAY HELP KEEP IT IN CHECK
Patients should not stop or extend treatment without speaking with a doctor.
2. Skipping or doubling doses
Treatment with blood thinners varies, so patients should ask a healthcare team about doses, side effects and safe activities. (Getty Images)
Missing doses repeatedly can weaken a medication's protection against clots, Abou-Ismail said, but what to do after a missed dose depends on the specific drug.
Patients should follow the instructions for the prescription or call a pharmacist or doctor, not automatically take an extra dose to make up for a missed one.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
3. Adding medications or supplements without checking

Aspirin and NSAIDs, including ibuprofen, can increase bleeding risk when taken with blood thinners, Abou-Ismail said. Some prescription drugs and supplements, including fish oil and turmeric, can also affect bleeding or medication levels.
Patients should ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything new even if it is sold over the counter.
4. Brushing off signs of serious bleeding
Blood thinners can help prevent clots from growing, but they may also make bleeding harder to stop, doctors say. (Jeffrey Sauger/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Some bruising or minor bleeding may occur, but persistent nosebleeds, blood in the urine or unexplained increases in bruising warrant a call to a health care provider, Abou-Ismail said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Uncontrolled bleeding, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, a sudden severe headache or new confusion, vision changes or trouble speaking require urgent care.
After a significant head injury, patients should seek medical evaluation, even if they initially feel fine, experts note.
5. Taking part in high-risk activities
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
A hard hit or fall can lead to serious bleeding in patients taking a blood thinner, which is why Hurts cannot play football during treatment.
Patients taking blood thinners may be able to continue exercising, but doctors advise avoiding contact sports and checking with their care team about activity risks. (iStock)
Patients should ask a doctor which activities are safe for them. Some may be able to continue exercising, but contact sports and other activities with a high risk of injury warrant extra caution.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Blood thinners do not dissolve an existing clot, Lombardi cautioned. They help prevent it from growing while the body clears it over time. The right treatment and precautions vary, so patients should contact their care team with questions about doses, side effects or activity.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis after 5 years of treatment exposes alarming medical reality
summary: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis highlights how brain lesions and common symptoms can mislead doctors, with nearly one in five referrals wrong.
story: Richard Ransohoff, M.D., a Boston-based neurologist who sits on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation, spoke with Fox News Digital about why multiple sclerosis misdiagnoses are common.

Christina Applegate’s recent revelation that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis is raising questions about how the disease can be confused with other conditions even after years of treatment.
The actress, 54, shared the news during an Oct. 20 episode of her podcast, "MeSsy," alongside co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler, saying she was in a complete "state of shock."

Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in 2021 after experiencing debilitating symptoms and undergoing extensive testing, including brain and spinal MRIs and a spinal tap. She said doctors found dozens of lesions on her brain.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE SAYS SHE WAS MISDIAGNOSED WITH MS AND IS NOW 'BACK AT SQUARE ONE'
After years of treatment, her doctor decided to stop her regular infusions and monitor her B cells.

"And my B cells didn't change. They didn't go higher. They didn't go lower. They didn't change, and she had never seen that. So, I guess that began kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate shared.
Christina Applegate’s recent revelation that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis is raising questions about how the disease can be confused with other conditions. (AFP via Getty Images)
After additional brain scans, the doctor entered Applegate’s room and said, "Congratulations, you don't have MS."
The actress did not consider this to be good news, however.
"Because you don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden [you’re] better," she said. "I haven't gotten better. … If anything, I've gotten worse in some ways."
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS
Applegate noted that she has "every symptom" of someone with MS, adding that there are many conditions that mirror the disease.
"There is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS."

She recalled that her MRIs clearly showed around 30 lesions but said her neurologist identified a different feature, which she described as a "string," that led to the conclusion that she did not have MS.
"So, I'm back at square one [and] don't know what's going on with me."
Why MS can be misdiagnosed
Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor of neurology at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, said during a follow-up "MeSsy" podcast episode that misdiagnosis of MS is "fairly common."

In a study of patients referred to MS clinics at UCLA and Cedars-Sinai, Kaisey, who has not treated Applegate, said she found that nearly one in five who arrived with an MS diagnosis ultimately did not have the disease.
BRAIN TUMOR FOUND DURING PREVENTIVE SCAN PUTS FULL-BODY MRIS BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT
"Some [had been diagnosed] for decades," she said. "And a majority of them were on medication to treat their MS."
The primary challenge, according to the doctor, is that there is no single test for MS.
"It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says, yes, you have it, no, you don't," Kaisey said.
Instead, Kaisey said, "It's a list of criteria, some of which remain a little bit subjective."
New clues on brain scans
Most misdiagnosed patients did have some type of white matter spots, or lesions, on their MRI scans, Kaisey noted, but they had a different cause that was not MS.
Newer imaging techniques may help doctors distinguish MS lesions from white matter spots caused by other conditions.
Most misdiagnosed patients did have some type of white matter spots, or lesions, on their MRI scans, Kaisey noted, but they had a different cause that was not MS. (iStock)

Kaisey pointed to the "central vein sign," an MRI finding that looks for small blood vessels running through the center of lesions, which is a characteristic associated with MS. The sign was incorporated into updated MS diagnostic criteria to help doctors determine whether white matter lesions are consistent with the disease.

Richard Ransohoff, M.D., a Boston-based neurologist who sits on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation, called the central vein sign "a real step forward" in distinguishing MS lesions from other abnormalities.
"Things are getting better, and even in the time that Ms. Applegate has been having her symptoms and her evaluation, things have gotten better," said Ransohoff, who also has not treated the actress.
SELMA BLAIR'S LAWYER CITES MISSED MEDICATION, HEAD INJURY AFTER IN-FLIGHT ARREST: WHAT DOCTORS SAY
Many of the symptoms of MS, such as tingling or numbness in the feet, fatigue and brain fog, are common in other conditions, according to both neurologists.

"To distinguish MS from its mimics can be challenging, and doctors, even with the best intentions … can sometimes still get it wrong," Kaisey said. "To diagnose MS, we need a symptom that's kind of very specific to MS, and we also need the MRI that looks like MS."
Despite the potential for diagnostic uncertainty, doctors emphasized that the outlook for people who do have MS has improved dramatically. (iStock)

Kaisey said she has found that being "undiagnosed" with MS can be even harder than receiving the initial diagnosis, particularly when the disease has become intertwined with someone's identity, family and community.
"So, to suddenly take that away, I think it’s earth-shattering. It's life-changing in a huge way."
EARLY PARKINSON’S SYMPTOMS MISDIAGNOSED FOR YEARS, TERRY CREWS’ WIFE REVEALS
The neurologist emphasized that patients should feel comfortable asking questions and getting a second opinion.
"Don't be afraid to do that, especially if something inside is telling you that you need to dig a little deeper," she advised.
MS-mimicking conditions
Ransohoff reiterated that MS misdiagnoses are common.
"It’s a tough diagnosis, and there is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS," he told Fox News Digital.
The neurologist said even after a diagnosis, doctors should "keep an open mind" and be willing to reconsider.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If things start going differently from your expectations, if the person begins to have symptoms that really don't fit in with MS or they don't respond to treatment, then you really start to put on your thinking cap and say, ‘What else could this be?’
"It requires the ultimate in humility as a physician. You simply have to say there are certain things we know and certain things we don't know."
Christina Applegate attends the 28th Annual Critics Choice Awards at Fairmont Century Plaza Jan. 15, 2023, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images for Critics Choice Association)
Classic early MS symptoms tend to appear relatively quickly, persist for weeks and then recede, according to Ransohoff.

Anything producing a similar pattern can potentially mimic the disease. Some of those conditions may include certain strokes in younger people, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disease (a rare autoimmune disease of the central nervous system), MOG antibody disease (a rare autoimmune inflammatory disorder), lupus and migraine, he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
A migraine is one of the most common alternative diagnoses, both neurologists agreed.
Kaisey noted a migraine can also produce MRI abnormalities in the form of white spots, although they are usually smaller and in a different shape and location.
"Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go."
"If you're not looking closely at the MRI or you don't know exactly what to look for, you can confuse the two," she said.
In some cases, reversing an MS diagnosis can actually provide a concrete alternative diagnosis and better targeted treatment, but that did not happen in Applegate’s case, Ransohoff noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"You have to have tremendous sympathy for her suffering in that context, because even when treatment is not going as well as you would like, it's better to know what you're dealing with," he said.
"Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go."
Specialized care

To prevent misdiagnosis, Ransohoff recommends that everyone who receives a multiple sclerosis diagnosis is seen by a specialist at a specialty MS center who has developed pattern recognition after many occurrences of seeing the disease.
The neurologist noted that MS treatment has advanced dramatically over the course of his career, growing from virtually no options to more than 20 medications today.
Neurologists recommend that everyone who receives a multiple sclerosis diagnosis is seen by a specialist at a specialty MS center. (iStock)
"You want to work with someone who has experience with all those medicines, with all the various patterns that MS can show, because every person's MS is different," he said.
If a treatment isn’t helping or is causing significant side effects, an MS specialist can reassess the approach and help identify a more appropriate medication, Ransohoff added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor emphasized that the outlook for people who do have MS has improved dramatically.

"The person who's diagnosed with MS today is totally different from 40 years ago when I got started," the neurologist said. "If the diagnosis is correct and the treatment is correct, then they should do pretty well with their MS."
