IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR
Reviewing financial statements regularly can help uncover suspicious activity that may never appear on your credit report. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What credit monitoring actually watches
Credit monitoring tracks changes to your credit file. Depending on the service, it can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit history.
Common alerts include:

New credit accounts: A lender reports a newly opened account.Hard credit inquiries: Someone applies for credit using your information.Credit score changes: Your score changes because of activity reported to a credit bureau.Collections activity: A collection account appears on your credit report.
New credit accounts: A lender reports a newly opened account.
Hard credit inquiries: Someone applies for credit using your information.
Credit score changes: Your score changes because of activity reported to a credit bureau.
Collections activity: A collection account appears on your credit report.

These alerts can help you discover new account fraud before the damage grows. However, credit monitoring depends on information that lenders and other companies report to credit bureaus. Therefore, it cannot reliably detect identity theft that occurs entirely outside the credit reporting system.
Six ways criminals can target you without triggering credit monitoring

Criminals have several ways to misuse your information, steal money or make you more vulnerable to fraud without triggering a traditional credit monitoring alert. Here are six situations worth watching for.

A criminal gains access to your existing checking account, savings account, retirement account or payment app. Because the account already exists, the takeover may never appear on your credit report. Instead, you might first discover the theft through an unfamiliar transaction or a notification from your financial institution.

Someone uses your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return or claim government benefits. You may receive an IRS notice about a tax return you never filed. Alternatively, you could discover unemployment benefits claimed in your name. Neither situation necessarily changes your credit score.

A thief uses your health insurance information to receive medical care, prescriptions or equipment. You might then receive bills for services you never used. Even worse, someone else's medical information could end up in your records. Traditional credit monitoring generally will not detect the misuse itself, although unpaid debts could eventually create other financial complications.

Criminals may convince your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card or device they control. Once they have your number, they may intercept certain verification codes and attempt to access your accounts. A sudden loss of cellular service could be an early warning sign, especially if you did not request a change.

A scammer tricks you into authorizing a wire transfer, sending money through a payment app or purchasing gift cards. Because you initiated the payment, even under false pretenses, traditional credit monitoring may have no indication that anything happened. Your financial institution might have separate fraud detection systems, but those protections vary.

Your name, phone number, address and other personal details may appear on people search websites or data broker databases. Criminals can use that information to create convincing phishing messages or impersonation scams. Although the exposure itself does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity, it can make you a more attractive target. The Federal Trade Commission identifies unauthorized bank withdrawals, unfamiliar medical bills and fraudulent tax filings among the warning signs of identity theft.
SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW
Criminals can access existing financial accounts or misuse payment information without triggering traditional credit monitoring alerts. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why checking your credit score isn't enough

A credit score provides a snapshot of your creditworthiness based on information in your credit file. It does not show every account you own or every place someone might use your personal information. For example, someone could access your retirement account while your credit score remains unchanged.

Similarly, criminals might use your phone number to get into an existing account without ever applying for credit. That's why it's important to review your actual credit reports rather than relying on your score alone. Even then, you'll need to check your other accounts separately.
How to spot identity theft your credit report can't catch
Fortunately, you can look for suspicious activity without paying for an expensive monitoring service. Start with these six habits.

Check your bank statements, investment accounts, retirement accounts and payment apps for unfamiliar transactions. Also, enable transaction and security alerts whenever your financial institutions offer them.

Pay attention to IRS notices about returns you did not file or income from employers you don't recognize. You can also review your federal tax account through the official IRS website at irs.gov. You can also request a free six-digit Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. This helps prevent someone else from filing a fraudulent federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each year.

Review your earnings history periodically to see whether it matches your actual employment. You can access your information through your my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Unexpected earnings may require further investigation.
Look for unfamiliar medical appointments, prescriptions, procedures or insurance claims. If something looks suspicious, contact your health insurance company or medical provider directly.

Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM swap safeguards. Additionally, consider using an authenticator app or security key instead of text-message verification when available.

Search for your name, phone number and address to identify information exposed through people-search websites. You can request removal from individual sites or consider a reputable data removal service.
Pro tip: Choose one day each month to review your accounts and important records. You can combine it with a bill payment routine to make the habit easier to maintain.
Monitoring your online accounts and enabling security alerts can help you spot potential identity theft before the damage grows. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How identity theft protection services can help

Credit monitoring remains useful, but it cannot catch every type of identity theft. Some identity theft protection services offer broader monitoring that can help identify suspicious activity involving financial accounts, personal information and online accounts. However, the features and level of protection depend on the provider and plan you choose.

Credit monitoring: Alerts about new credit accounts, suspicious inquiries and changes to your credit reports.Financial account monitoring: Notifications about potentially suspicious activity involving eligible bank accounts, investment accounts and retirement savings.Dark web monitoring: Alerts when certain personal information, such as email addresses or passwords, appears in known data breaches or monitored dark web sources.Phone takeover protection: Monitoring for signs that someone may be trying to transfer your phone number or take control of your mobile account.Identity restoration assistance: Access to specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if someone steals your identity.Scam reimbursement: Some plans provide coverage for eligible financial losses, although limits, exclusions and eligibility requirements vary.Data broker removal: Certain services help remove your personal information from participating people-search websites and data brokers.
Credit monitoring: Alerts about new credit accounts, suspicious inquiries and changes to your credit reports.
Financial account monitoring: Notifications about potentially suspicious activity involving eligible bank accounts, investment accounts and retirement savings.
Dark web monitoring: Alerts when certain personal information, such as email addresses or passwords, appears in known data breaches or monitored dark web sources.
Phone takeover protection: Monitoring for signs that someone may be trying to transfer your phone number or take control of your mobile account.
Identity restoration assistance: Access to specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if someone steals your identity.
Scam reimbursement: Some plans provide coverage for eligible financial losses, although limits, exclusions and eligibility requirements vary.
Data broker removal: Certain services help remove your personal information from participating people-search websites and data brokers.

Before signing up, compare the features, coverage limits and costs. Pay attention to which financial accounts qualify for monitoring and whether the service offers restoration assistance if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

Remember: No identity theft protection service can prevent every scam or detect every instance of fraud. These services work best alongside strong passwords, multifactor authentication, account alerts and regular reviews of your financial statements.
What to do if you discover identity theft
If you suspect someone is using your information, act quickly. You do not need to wait for a credit monitoring alert.

Contact the affected institution. Call your bank, retirement plan administrator, mobile carrier or insurance company using its official contact information. Ask about securing or freezing affected accounts.Change compromised passwords. Update your login credentials and enable multifactor authentication. Avoid relying on text-message verification if your phone number may be compromised.Report identity theft to the FTC. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report and receive a personalized recovery plan.Contact the appropriate government agency. For suspected tax fraud, contact the IRS. For Social Security-related fraud, contact the Social Security Administration.Consider freezing your credit. A free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts using your identity.Keep detailed records. Save suspicious messages, account statements, confirmation numbers and notes from conversations with institutions.

Contact the affected institution. Call your bank, retirement plan administrator, mobile carrier or insurance company using its official contact information. Ask about securing or freezing affected accounts.
Change compromised passwords. Update your login credentials and enable multifactor authentication. Avoid relying on text-message verification if your phone number may be compromised.
Report identity theft to the FTC. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report and receive a personalized recovery plan.
Contact the appropriate government agency. For suspected tax fraud, contact the IRS. For Social Security-related fraud, contact the Social Security Administration.
Consider freezing your credit. A free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts using your identity.
Keep detailed records. Save suspicious messages, account statements, confirmation numbers and notes from conversations with institutions.
You can also review your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com. The FTC confirms that free weekly online reports are available from the three nationwide credit bureaus.
Kurt's key takeaways

I always encourage people to keep an eye on their credit, but I wouldn't rely on a credit score to tell me whether my identity is safe. Someone could be accessing an existing financial account or misusing personal information without causing any immediate change to that score. That's why I recommend checking financial statements, turning on account alerts and taking advantage of additional safeguards when they're available. Identity theft protection services can provide another layer of monitoring, but you still need to pay attention to activity in your accounts.

When was the last time you checked your bank accounts, medical statements or phone account for signs of identity theft rather than relying on your credit score? Let us know in the comments below. Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Pennsylvania law requires delivery robots to yield to pedestrians, yet protester still faced arrest
summary: Carolyn Marvin, a 78-year-old retired professor, was arrested after blocking an Uber Eats delivery robot on a Philadelphia sidewalk for months.
story: Union workers, rideshare drivers and other protesters rallied against a D.C. proposal that would allow commercial robotaxis, warning autonomous vehicles could eliminate driving jobs. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
Most people see a food delivery robot rolling down the sidewalk and simply walk around it. But one Philadelphia woman decided she wasn't moving.
She stood directly in front of an Uber Eats delivery robot, refusing to let it continue. Police eventually arrived, and the 78-year-old retired professor ended up in handcuffs.

Her protest has now sparked a much bigger conversation about robots taking over human jobs and how much space these machines should get on our sidewalks. And there's a surprising detail about Pennsylvania law that makes this whole situation even more interesting.
WORKERS ERUPT OVER DC PLAN TO BRING ROBOTAXIS TO CITY STREETS: ‘THIS IS BULLS---’
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Philadelphia police escort 78-year-old retired professor Carolyn Marvin away in handcuffs after she refused to move out of an Uber Eats delivery robot's path during a sidewalk protest. (@thatsphillybusiness/TikTok)
Philadelphia woman's protest against delivery robot ends in arrest

On Oct. 14, Carolyn Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania professor, was leaving a flu shot appointment in Center City Philadelphia when she spotted an Uber Eats delivery robot. Instead of stepping aside, she positioned herself in front of the machine near Reading Terminal Market on Filbert Street. Police reportedly responded after witnesses reported a disturbance. Officers said Marvin repeatedly refused instructions to move out of the robot's path. They eventually arrested her and issued her a disorderly conduct citation.

The encounter was captured on video and quickly attracted attention online. However, Marvin wasn't surprised by the attention. She had been deliberately blocking delivery robots for months, turning what might look like a strange sidewalk encounter into her own form of public protest.

In an interview with PhillyVoice, Marvin explained that she believes corporations are using autonomous machines to displace human delivery workers. She argued that her actions fall under her First Amendment right to protest. Marvin was taken to police headquarters and later released.
She said she plans to fight the citation in court and continue blocking delivery robots when she has the opportunity. She also encouraged others who oppose the machines to join her protests.
Why this 78-year-old professor refuses to move

Marvin's frustration goes beyond having robots share the sidewalk. She sees them as a direct threat to people who earn their living delivering food. Every order completed by a robot represents work that potentially could have gone to a human courier. That concern comes as more delivery companies experiment with automation to reduce operating costs.

Unlike a human courier, a robot doesn't collect tips or earn money for each delivery. Companies hope automation will eventually reduce operating costs, although the machines still require maintenance and monitoring.

However, whether Philadelphia's robot program has actually eliminated delivery jobs remains unclear. Uber has previously said its robots are intended to complement human delivery workers rather than replace them. Still, it's easy to understand why people who depend on delivery income might question how that arrangement will work as fleets expand.

Marvin also sees her protests as an opportunity to engage other pedestrians. She says people regularly stop to ask why she's blocking the machines. Those conversations are part of what motivates her to continue, even after her arrest.
Here's the surprising law about delivery robots and pedestrians
You might assume that Marvin's arrest means delivery robots have the right of way on Philadelphia sidewalks. But Pennsylvania law offers a rather different answer.

The state's vehicle code classifies personal delivery devices as pedestrians and generally requires them to follow pedestrian traffic rules. However, the robots must yield the right-of-way or safely navigate around pedestrians and cyclists in pedestrian areas. That's an important detail. A delivery robot does not automatically have priority over someone walking down the sidewalk.

Of course, requiring robots to yield does not necessarily give people the legal right to deliberately obstruct deliveries. Police say Marvin refused repeated instructions to move after officers responded to a disturbance. Her disorderly conduct charge does not establish that robots have priority over pedestrians or settle whether her particular protest was legally protected.

Pennsylvania law requires operators to notify municipalities at least 30 days before beginning delivery robot operations. Municipal officials can also prohibit the machines in areas where, after consulting the operator, they determine the robots would pose a hazard. That leaves an interesting question about how cities should handle future confrontations between pedestrians and commercial robots.
FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS
An Uber Eats delivery robot operates on a city sidewalk. (Oleg Yunakov/CC BY-SA 4.0)
Why Uber Eats keeps putting robots on sidewalks

Despite the controversy, companies continue investing in autonomous delivery because the technology offers some practical advantages. Uber Eats partnered with robotics company Avride to operate small, four-wheeled delivery machines that transport food over relatively short distances. The robots use cameras and sensors to navigate city streets. According to Avride, they travel at speeds of up to 5 mph and can carry up to 55 pounds of food or other goods.

The service launched in Philadelphia in March 2026. These robots can complete short deliveries without sending another car through traffic or requiring a courier to find parking. For customers, the convenience is obvious. Your food arrives inside a secure compartment that you unlock through the Uber Eats app. In Philadelphia, customers can reportedly opt out of robot delivery. However, availability and delivery options depend on the order and service area.

And the rollout is expanding. On Oct. 21, Avride announced an expansion of robot delivery in Philadelphia involving Wonder's Rittenhouse location and additional restaurants on the Grubhub platform. Robot delivery is now available from 25 Wonder restaurant concepts at the Rittenhouse location, with nine additional restaurants on Grubhub also participating. The company has not said whether the expansion will require more robots on Philadelphia sidewalks or whether its existing fleet will handle the additional orders.
Philadelphia isn't the only city pushing back against delivery robots

Philadelphia's confrontation comes amid growing frustration with autonomous machines operating in public spaces. In September, we reported on a robot traffic jam in Chicago, where at least a dozen Coco delivery robots clustered along a sidewalk. The company blamed a deployment error and said it corrected the problem.

The incident raised concerns about pedestrian accessibility, particularly for people who use wheelchairs or mobility aids. A blocked sidewalk can create a serious obstacle for someone who cannot easily move into the street or squeeze past a machine.

Philadelphia has experienced its own robot mishaps. In April, a woman reported that an Uber Eats delivery robot bumped into her from behind near 15th and Locust streets. Li Gordon-Washington reportedly suffered a scratch and later struggled to determine which agency should handle her complaint. Avride acknowledged that its robot made minor contact with her while completing a turn.

These incidents help explain why some residents are losing patience. While the machines may be designed to navigate around people, they still have to handle unpredictable human behavior and crowded public spaces.
A pedestrian walks near a delivery robot at an intersection, raising questions about who should have the right of way in public spaces. (Christopher Down/CC BY 4.0)
What this means to you

Delivery robots may soon become a familiar part of your neighborhood, especially if you live near busy restaurants or shopping districts. You could find yourself sharing sidewalk space with machines carrying someone else's dinner. That raises practical questions about safety and accessibility, along with concerns about jobs.

If you encounter a robot blocking a curb ramp or creating a hazard, keep your distance and report the problem to the operator or local authorities. In Pennsylvania, delivery robots must display operator identification and contact information. Documenting the location and the robot's identification number can help officials investigate a complaint.

There's also an opportunity for residents to get involved before delivery robot programs expand. Local governments can evaluate where these machines operate and whether particular routes create safety hazards. Paying attention to those decisions gives communities a chance to have a say in how their sidewalks are used.

For people whose livelihoods depend on deliveries, the questions run deeper. They deserve clear information about how companies plan to use automation and what that could mean for future work opportunities.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've covered plenty of robots that can do impressive things, and I can appreciate the technology behind these delivery machines. But I never expected to see a 78-year-old retired professor arrested after refusing to let one deliver somebody's lunch. What really caught my attention was Pennsylvania's law requiring robots to yield to pedestrians. That makes the confrontation even more thought-provoking.

I understand why police would respond when a public dispute escalates, and I certainly wouldn't encourage anyone to interfere with a delivery. At the same time, I understand Marvin's frustration. We're watching companies introduce machines that can perform work people have traditionally been paid to do, and we still don't have clear answers about how many jobs could eventually disappear.

I think companies introducing this technology need to be much more transparent about its impact on workers. And when they want to operate on public sidewalks, residents deserve a genuine say in how that happens. I hope this incident encourages a serious conversation about those issues before another confrontation ends with someone in handcuffs.

If delivery robots make food delivery more convenient but eventually cost human workers their jobs, should cities still allow them to operate on public sidewalks? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Cheap Android phones found with malware already installed
summary: The Midnight Mimosa malware campaign hides inside cheap Android phone firmware, giving attackers powerful access before owners even turn devices on.
story: Some low-cost Android phones may come with malware already hidden in their software before you even turn them on. (NickyLloyd via Getty Images)

Buying a cheap smartphone can feel like a smart move. After all, why spend hundreds more when a phone promises a big screen, decent cameras and all the Android apps you use every day? But what if that bargain phone came with a hidden surprise that was already hiding inside the device when you bought it?
Security researchers at Bitdefender have uncovered a malware campaign called Midnight Mimosa that infects certain low-cost Android devices before their owners even turn them on.

The malicious software hides inside the phone's firmware, giving attackers powerful access that ordinary apps never receive. Even more concerning, researchers found related malicious apps on Google Play. And this problem has reached the United States.
ANDROID MALWARE CAN STEAL YOUR PIN AND BANK LOGINS
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/ 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
Android malware that comes installed from the factory

Most smartphone security advice starts with being careful about what you download. That makes sense when a malicious app tricks you into installing it. Midnight Mimosa changes that equation because the infection can arrive with the phone itself. According to Bitdefender's investigation, the malware was discovered on low-cost, multi-brand Android devices built around MediaTek chipsets. Researchers found malicious applications embedded in the system software, where they could operate with elevated privileges.

These privileges allow the malware to install additional apps without permission, remove existing applications and grant sensitive access to other software. It can also download and execute new code from remote servers. The researchers identified several versions hiding behind innocent-looking Android package names, including com.android.system.lite, com.android.sys.prot and com.android.sys.gmsprot.

To most phone owners, those names would look like technical components that belong there. That's exactly what makes the scheme so difficult to spot. And because the malicious software lives in the system partition, a normal uninstall won't remove the underlying infection.
Thousands of Android phones affected worldwide

Bitdefender says it observed Midnight Mimosa on thousands of unique devices across more than 150 countries over approximately two years. Mexico, France and Italy had the highest observed numbers, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil and Spain. Researchers also observed infected devices reporting model names associated with Doogee's S200 X and Cubot's KINGKONG X.

However, the findings do not establish that every phone sold under those names is affected. Some devices in the campaign use misleading or counterfeit model identifiers, making it difficult to identify infections based on a phone's reported name alone.

Another part of the investigation uncovered devices pretending to be expensive smartphones. Some reported names resembling Samsung Galaxy flagship models, while others imitated Apple's iPhone naming. In other words, a phone advertised as a premium Samsung or Apple device might actually contain inexpensive Android hardware running modified software.

Researchers found that some counterfeit devices even reported legitimate looking Samsung model identifiers. That makes checking the model name alone an unreliable way to confirm authenticity. The investigation also identified firmware signed with certificates associated with Shenzhen Zediel, a Chinese device manufacturer. However, Bitdefender emphasized that this does not establish that the company created the malware or knew about its presence. Exactly where the malicious code entered the manufacturing and distribution process remains unknown.
What the hidden Android malware actually does

You might expect malware this powerful to steal passwords immediately or display obvious warnings. Instead, Midnight Mimosa appears primarily designed to generate money for its operators while staying out of sight. One way it earns money is through advertising fraud. The malicious system component silently installs apps that look like weather tools, app lockers and other everyday utilities.

Those apps can display legitimate advertisements in hidden windows or generate clicks without the owner touching the screen. Advertisers may end up paying for activity that never came from a real person. Bitdefender identified at least 32 unique disguised applications involved in the broader operation. The malware can also repeatedly install and remove these apps, making them harder to notice during a casual check of the phone.

The advertising fraud is only part of the story. Researchers also discovered software that can turn infected phones into residential proxy servers. Here's what that means. Someone operating the malware could route internet traffic through your phone's connection. To websites and online services, that traffic may appear to come from your home or mobile network rather than the person actually controlling it.

Such connections can be valuable to cybercriminals because they help conceal where online activity originates. The same infrastructure could potentially support larger botnet operations or distributed denial-of-service attacks. Bitdefender confirmed that the malware contained the technology needed to turn infected phones into residential proxy servers.

However, the researchers later clarified that one server they reached was actually a sinkhole, a system used to intercept malicious communications. Their testing did not demonstrate active traffic being relayed through the infected device. The underlying capability remains concerning because it could allow operators to route traffic through a phone owner's connection.
AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION

Researchers found that hidden Android malware could secretly install apps, access sensitive permissions and potentially hijack a phone's internet connection. (Chris Goodney/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

One particularly troubling finding involves how Midnight Mimosa avoids security checks. Before installing certain malicious apps, Midnight Mimosa temporarily disables the Google Play Store app. Bitdefender believes this helps the malware avoid detection by Google Play Protect during installation.
Once the process finishes, the malware re-enables the Store, reducing the chances that the phone owner will notice anything unusual. The process happens without the phone owner's involvement.

Some versions also manipulate Android's installer records to make applications appear to have come from Google Play, even when the malware installed them directly. So a quick look at where an app supposedly originated may not tell the whole story.
Here are the 13 apps identified in the investigation

Wavrge, App Icon DIY, Audify, QR Pocket, All Deleted Messages Recovery, WeatherGo, CoolWeather, Daily Weather, Lock & Hide, QuickText Extractor, NoteMaster, Tap to Translate and Tasky. These apps offered functions such as weather forecasts, QR scanning, message recovery and audio editing.

However, researchers found that they could also generate unwanted advertising activity, including displaying ads outside their normal interfaces. Unlike the malware embedded in phone firmware, these Google Play apps lacked the elevated system privileges needed to silently install other applications. The apps were associated with 13 different signing certificates and at least two developer accounts, identified as fivedev and CPS Developer.

Are these apps still on Google Play? Checks of the Google Play listings for all 13 apps found that none were available for download. However, it remains unclear whether Google removed the apps or their developers withdrew them. CyberGuy reached out to Google for comment but did not receive a response before our deadline.

What should you do if you recognize one? Check your Android phone's installed apps. If you find one of these applications, verify that its package identifier matches the one listed in Bitdefender's report before uninstalling it. Different apps can share similar names. Even when an app disappears from Google Play, it can remain installed on your phone. The findings show why downloading an app from an official store doesn't automatically guarantee its safety.
Phone owners reported malware returning after removal

The findings also connect with complaints posted by some Doogee and Cubot smartphone owners on the XDA forums. Users described suspicious system applications that reappeared after attempts to remove them. One Doogee Fire 3 Max owner reported that an official firmware update introduced the infection. According to that account, reverting to an older firmware version removed the problem, while reinstalling the newer update brought it back.

Other forum participants reported that subsequent firmware updates resolved their infections. However, Bitdefender identified one of the suspicious packages discussed in the forum, com.android.non.szcz, as belonging to the same malware family. That creates a frustrating situation for owners. A software update is normally something I encourage people to install for better security. But when the firmware itself is compromised, the source and integrity of the update become especially important.
How to protect your Android phone from preinstalled malware
The most effective protection starts before you buy a device. However, there are useful precautions if you already own an inexpensive Android phone or suspect something unusual is happening.

Be especially careful with unusually cheap smartphones advertised as premium models. Counterfeit devices can copy familiar names and appearances while using entirely different hardware. Choose established retailers and authorized sellers when possible.

Check the manufacturer's official website to confirm that the model exists and matches the advertised specifications. An extremely low price deserves a closer look, especially when the seller provides limited information about software updates or warranty support.
ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK
Buying from a trusted seller, checking Google Play Protect certification and keeping your phone updated can help reduce your risk. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Before trusting an unfamiliar Android phone, check whether Google recognizes it as a certified device. Play Protect certification indicates that a device has met Google's compatibility requirements. However, certification alone cannot guarantee that its firmware is free of malware.
Here's how to check:
Open the Google Play Store.Tap your profile picture in the upper-right corner.Select Settings.Tap About.Look for Play Protect certification.Check whether the status says Device is certified.
Open the Google Play Store.
Tap your profile picture in the upper-right corner.
Select Settings.
Tap About.
Look for Play Protect certification.
Check whether the status says Device is certified.

If your phone says Device is not certified, contact the manufacturer or seller to investigate. An uncertified device does not automatically mean it contains malware, but it deserves additional scrutiny.

Google Play Protect is Android's built-in malware protection. It scans apps for harmful behavior and can warn you about or remove known threats. However, it is not 100% effective at detecting every malicious app, especially malware hidden deep within a phone's system software.

To check it, open the Google Play Store > your profile picture > Play Protect > Settings. Make sure Scan apps with Play Protect is enabled. Then return to the Play Protect screen to check for harmful apps. A clean scan is reassuring, but it does not guarantee your phone is free of malware, particularly if the infection is embedded in its firmware. That's why we also recommend strong antivirus software as an additional layer of protection.

Strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection by monitoring suspicious behavior and detecting threats that may go unnoticed. In fact, Bitdefender's investigation began when its behavioral detection technology flagged an unusual system component.

This shows why monitoring how apps behave can help uncover threats that traditional scans might miss. However, even strong antivirus software may detect malicious firmware without having the permissions needed to remove it. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Open Settings > Apps > See all apps or the equivalent app list on your Android device. Look for applications you don't recognize, especially ones requesting unusual access.

Next, review Settings > Security & privacy > Privacy controls > Permission manager, where available. Check permissions such as SMS access and other sensitive capabilities. Accessibility and notification access may have their own settings pages.

Menu names vary by manufacturer and Android version. Be cautious about unfamiliar apps with extensive permissions. However, don't randomly disable legitimate Android system components because their technical names look strange.

An infected phone may show signs such as unexplained mobile data usage, excessive background activity, unexpected advertisements or apps appearing without your permission. Check Settings > Network & internet > SIMs > App data usage, or your manufacturer's equivalent, to investigate unusual data consumption. These symptoms can have harmless explanations, and Midnight Mimosa may operate without obvious warning signs. Treat unexpected activity as a reason to investigate rather than proof of infection.

Install updates supplied through your manufacturer's verified support channels. However, if you suspect the device firmware itself is infected, contact the manufacturer before attempting a repair. A factory reset generally removes personal data and user-installed apps. It does not necessarily replace compromised software stored in the system partition.

Bitdefender says removing Midnight Mimosa's privileged component may require firmware-level cleanup or specialized tools such as Android Debug Bridge. For most people, manually modifying system firmware introduces additional risks. If the manufacturer cannot provide a verified clean firmware image, replacing the device may be the safest practical option.

If you believe your phone has been compromised, use a separate trusted device to change important passwords, starting with your primary email and financial accounts. Review recent account activity and enable multifactor authentication where available. Consider using an authenticator app or passkeys on a trusted device rather than relying exclusively on SMS codes.

Bitdefender identified sensitive capabilities in the malware, including potential access to notifications and SMS messages. The researchers did not observe every capability being actively exploited, so account compromise should not be assumed without evidence. Nevertheless, protecting important accounts is a sensible precaution when you can no longer trust the phone's operating system.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've always liked the idea of getting more for less, especially when it comes to technology. You shouldn't have to spend flagship phone money to get a device that works reliably. But this investigation exposes a problem that deserves far more attention from the companies making and selling inexpensive smartphones. When malware arrives embedded in the firmware, the owner has very little control. You can be careful about downloads, check permissions and follow security advice, yet still end up with a compromised device straight out of the box.

What concerns me most is the possibility that your phone could be quietly earning money for someone else while using a connection you pay for. And if removing the infection requires specialized firmware work, the burden lands on the person who bought the device. Manufacturers and marketplaces need to take greater responsibility for verifying the software that ships on the products they sell. A low price should never mean accepting hidden software that puts your privacy and security at risk.

Would you pay more for a smartphone from a manufacturer you trust, or do you think companies selling budget phones should be held legally responsible when malware comes preinstalled? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: What we saw inside a massive Texas data center
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby explains why protecting sensitive information and critical infrastructure requires tight security at facilities powering America’s growing digital economy.
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- It took three months to get inside this massive Texas data center; here’s what we saw
- Google's new AI shopping cart tracks deals across stores
- Elon Musk pledges to give every child in America a SpaceX share next year
Compass Datacenters’ Red Oak campus, about 20 miles south of Dallas, includes 10 data center buildings spanning roughly 2.6 million square feet. (Courtesy of Compass Datacenters)

ACCESS GRANTED: During an exclusive tour of Compass Datacenters' sprawling campus in Red Oak, Texas, Fox News Digital got a rare look inside the infrastructure behind the nation's growing appetite for computing.

ONE-STOP HUB: Ever find something you want to buy online, leave it sitting in a browser tab and then completely forget where you saw it? Maybe you spotted a great pair of headphones while searching Google. Later, you found a birthday gift at another retailer. Before long, you've got a dozen tabs open and no idea which store had the better deal.
BIG GIVEAWAY: Elon Musk has pledged to give every child in America one share of SpaceX next year, signaling that the planned giveaway could be the first of several.

FEAR FACTOR: Over the last several years, we have heard a lot about the doomsday scenarios of artificial intelligence (AI). Tech giants have told us all about how AI will take control away from society, steal our jobs, allow bad actors to design dangerous pathogens or cause a catastrophic cyberattack or destroy our financial systems.
A Gecko Robotics wall-climbing robot scans the surface of a U.S. Navy warship, collecting data on material condition that can be analyzed for corrosion and structural damage. (Gecko Robotics)
RUST NEVER SLEEPS: The U.S. Navy is quadrupling the ceiling on a contract for AI-powered robots used to inspect warships to $300 million.

ARTIFICIAL INFORMANT: Artificial intelligence can write your emails, research complicated questions and even handle tasks while you're away. But what happens when an AI system takes an action nobody intended? Philadelphia police recently got an unexpected answer.
SILENT TREATMENT: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic remained mum on whether the company would consider giving away shares it pledged to a public benefit fund directly to Americans.

DATA DESTRUCTION: America seems to be on the precipice of a future technological golden age. Whether we take steps toward that future could depend on which political vision prevails over the next few election cycles.
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks after a radio appearance at Dr. Horace Sheffield's GOTV Community Rally Aug. 1, 2026, in Detroit.   (Getty Images)
COMMON GOOD: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed called Tuesday for AI companies to be "rebuilt" as public benefit corporations, for-profit companies with a public interest.

BOT SURE: Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton on Wednesday called for a federal commission to regulate artificial intelligence, but didn't say what specific regulations he would like to see.
PAUSE AND EFFECT: Tensions flare in Tennessee as the Memphis City Council rejects an 18-month pause on new data center development despite pushback from local residents.

title: Why some people are falling for Meta's Muse AI
summary: Meta's Muse AI was built to manage tasks, but users are developing romantic AI relationships and even calling the AI companion their girlfriend.
story: Dana Perino highlights an AI chatbots study showing one in five middle-schoolers uses technology for companionship. Heritage Foundation policy analyst Annie Chestnut Tutor warns that chatbot design features are hooking vulnerable children. Tutor explains that these artificial relationships cannot replace real human connection, ultimately leading to increased feelings of loneliness and isolation among youth.

You might use artificial intelligence to write an email, make dinner reservations or plan your next vacation. But would you ever consider dating it? Some people are taking that idea seriously with Meta's new Muse AI agent. They're having romantic conversations with it, developing emotional attachments and even calling it their girlfriend.

What makes this especially interesting is that Muse was designed to help people manage their lives. Yet some people are finding companionship in the same technology. Meta allows users 18 and older to have these romantic interactions, including conversations that become sexually explicit. And as these digital romances grow more personal, they raise questions about intimacy, emotional dependence and just how much private information we're comfortable sharing with artificial intelligence.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI AGENTS CAN NOW MAKE PHONE CALLS FOR YOU
Meta's Muse AI app is designed to remember conversations and learn about users, raising questions about privacy and emotional attachment. (Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
People are falling for Meta's Muse AI

When Meta introduced Muse on Sept. 8, the company presented it as a personal AI agent that could manage tasks and learn about its users. However, some people quickly discovered another side of the technology. They started treating Muse like a romantic companion. In a Reddit discussion about Muse, one person explained that they regularly experiment with new AI models, but had never developed a romantic relationship with one. That changed after downloading Muse. The person described having extended philosophical conversations with the agent before eventually referring to it as a girlfriend. The original Reddit post has since been deleted by its author, although some responses remain visible.

Other people shared their own experiences with romantic interactions and affectionate responses, showing how some individuals are choosing to use the technology. We've seen this behavior before. In fact, we previously reported on a woman who got engaged to her AI chatbot boyfriend after five months of dating Kasper, an AI designed to simulate human conversation and companionship. Now, Muse is attracting similar attention, partly because of how the assistant learns about the person on the other side of the conversation.
Why Meta's Muse can feel like someone who knows you

One reason Muse may become emotionally appealing comes down to its design. According to Meta's official product design blog, the company built Muse around a continuous conversation that resembles messaging another person. It remembers previous discussions and can send messages without waiting for you to start a new conversation. You can also customize the agent's name and appearance, creating an avatar with a personality that suits your preferences. Some avatars even look like cute, cuddly stuffed animals rather than people, giving Muse a playful and approachable appearance. Over time, those features can make the experience feel increasingly familiar.

Think about what happens when you tell Muse about a difficult day. Later, it remembers what you discussed and brings it up again. Maybe it responds with reassurance when you're feeling lonely. As those exchanges continue, you might find yourself looking forward to the next conversation. That sense of familiarity can be powerful. However, there's an important limitation. Muse generates responses using artificial intelligence. There is no evidence that it experiences romantic feelings or forms the same mutual emotional connection that people can. The attachment someone develops to Muse may be genuine, even though the relationship itself operates very differently from a human romance.
Meta allows romantic and sexually explicit conversations

Here's something that may surprise you. Muse can participate in sexual roleplay and respond to explicit prompts, allowing conversations that go well beyond what you might expect from a digital assistant. In a statement, a Meta spokesperson explained the company's approach: "Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them. Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn't block legal adult behavior."
Can romantic relationships with AI become unhealthy?

There's a reason people may find AI companionship appealing. An AI agent can respond whenever someone wants to talk. It can remember personal information and adapt its responses to the user's preferences. We've heard from CyberGuy readers about their experiences with other AI agents and how surprisingly personal those interactions can become. For someone feeling isolated, that kind of connection may offer comfort. However, emotional dependence is a concern. Someone who spends hours discussing intimate feelings with an AI companion may gradually begin relying on those conversations for emotional support. That could become problematic if the relationship starts interfering with their connections to other people.

We've already seen what happens when a company changes the technology behind an AI companion. In August 2025, OpenAI introduced GPT-5, replacing the popular GPT-4o model in ChatGPT. Some users who had developed emotional attachments complained that their AI companions suddenly felt different. OpenAI brought GPT-4o back following the backlash but retired it in February 2026. Some users described feeling genuine grief over losing the AI companion they had grown attached to. Of course, that doesn't mean every AI relationship is harmful. People develop attachments for different reasons, and their experiences can vary considerably. The bigger question is whether users understand what the technology can realistically provide.
AI ROBOT PET COULD KNOW YOUR FAMILY TOO WELL
Muse allows users to customize their AI companion's appearance and personality, making interactions feel more personal. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
What Meta says about protecting intimate Muse conversations

When someone begins treating an AI like a romantic partner, the conversations can become extremely personal. That makes privacy especially important. Muse can also access information from connected accounts, including emails and messages, depending on the permissions you grant it. So what happens to all that information? Meta has outlined several protections in its published security and privacy documentation.

The Muse app carries an 18+ age rating in Apple's App Store, but its age checks go further. Everyone signing up must provide their date of birth, and users who identify themselves as younger than 18 cannot create an account. For people who say they're adults, Muse performs additional checks, including examining connections between their Muse account and their Facebook or Instagram accounts. If those checks cannot establish that someone is an adult, the app requires credit card verification to continue. Meta says it does not charge users for age verification or store their credit card information.

According to Meta's security documentation, Muse runs inside a system called Muse Secure VM. Each user receives an isolated virtual computer where their agent operates and stores information. Meta also uses a protective system called Sentinel to control certain actions involving outside services. Sentinel operates separately from the main Muse agent and must approve its internet access. For sensitive actions, including sending an email or making a purchase, Muse asks for your approval before proceeding.

You can also review an activity log showing what Muse has done and what it plans to do. The app lets you control which services it can access, including whether it can only read your email or send messages on your behalf. You can change those permissions or disconnect an account whenever you choose.
New privacy concerns emerge over Muse sharing links

A new security discovery raises additional questions about how Muse protects personal information. On Oct. 20, researchers revealed that more than 6,800 Muse sharing links could be discovered through publicly accessible DNS records. Some led to sensitive business documents and personal information. Meta temporarily suspended the sharing feature while reviewing the findings. The issue involved content users had shared through links, rather than evidence that all private Muse conversations were exposed. Still, it shows why users should be cautious about sharing sensitive information with AI assistants.

Meta says conversations with Muse and information related to tasks it performs can help train its AI models. The company says it removes key personally identifiable information before using that material for training. Users can opt out through Muse's settings. Meta also says it doesn't share conversations or information stored inside a user's virtual computer with its advertising systems.
CAN TECH REALLY GET YOU OFF YOUR PHONE AND INTO REAL LIFE?
Meta's Muse AI assistant lets users have personalized conversations that can develop into emotional and even romantic connections. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
Can you delete romantic conversations with Muse?

You may decide that something you've shared with Muse is too personal to keep. Meta says users can inspect and edit information stored in the agent's memory. They can also ask Muse to forget specific details it has learned. For broader deletion, Muse offers additional controls, including a feature called Reset Muse. Meta describes this option as permanently deleting chat history, stored files and active tasks.
To limit how Muse uses your information for AI training, follow these steps:
Open Muse and select Settings.Choose Data Controls.Turn off Help improve our AI models.
Open Muse and select Settings.
Choose Data Controls.
Turn off Help improve our AI models.

The same section includes Reset Muse, while individual side chats can be deleted separately. Keep in mind that resetting Muse removes stored information you may want to retain. Meta's published explanation does not establish whether resetting the agent also removes information already incorporated into AI training or every backup copy.
Could Meta's next AI models make these relationships stronger?

Meta is already developing technology that could make Muse feel even more personalized. On Oct. 12, the company introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, two new AI models designed to handle more complex tasks and improve ongoing assistance. One feature, called Active Memory, helps the AI remember relevant information between conversations. Meta says Muse Wonder will begin powering experiences in its personal agent, starting with subscribers. That rollout remains upcoming as of publication. For someone who already treats Muse as a romantic partner, better memory could make conversations feel more personal.
What this means to you

You may have no interest in developing a romantic relationship with artificial intelligence. However, this trend shows how quickly AI assistants are becoming part of people's emotional lives. A technology that remembers personal conversations and responds affectionately can begin to feel familiar, even when someone originally downloaded it for practical reasons.

If you use Muse or another AI companion, consider how much information you're sharing. Review its memory settings and connected accounts before discussing highly sensitive topics. Check the permissions you've granted and review the agent's activity log so you know what it's doing on your behalf. Also, consider whether your interactions with the AI are supporting your everyday life or beginning to interfere with relationships you value. You can learn more about protecting personal information in our article on AI chatbot privacy.
Kurt's key takeaways

I knew people were getting attached to AI chatbots, but I never expected an assistant designed to help manage your day to become someone's girlfriend. Yet here we are. And the more I learn about Muse, the more I understand how it could happen. We've heard from CyberGuy readers who have developed surprisingly personal connections with other AI agents. When something remembers your conversations and seems genuinely interested in your life, it's easy to see how feelings could develop. I'm certainly not going to judge someone for finding comfort in that. But I do wonder what happens when those feelings become so strong that someone starts treating an AI like a real-life partner.

What concerns me is how easily people could let their guard down. Once you're comfortable sharing your deepest feelings with Muse, how much personal information are you handing over without thinking twice? Meta has put privacy protections in place, but I'd still be cautious about what I share. And there's another concern we've already seen play out with ChatGPT. When OpenAI changed its models, some people felt they'd lost the AI companion they'd grown attached to. That says a lot about how powerful these connections can become. I think AI companionship could be helpful for people who feel lonely, but I'd hate to see it pull them further away from meaningful relationships with the people around them.
Would you consider having a romantic relationship with an AI companion? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Data broker opt-out: How retirees can protect their data
summary: A Minnesota murder suspect's notebook listed 11 people search websites, raising urgent questions about data broker opt-out and online privacy risks.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.

Your home address, phone number and relatives' names may be sitting on people search websites you've never visited. Anyone who finds those listings could learn more about you than you're comfortable sharing. A data broker opt-out can help reduce that exposure, especially during retirement, when protecting your finances, family and home becomes a priority.

And a tragic case in Minnesota shows why publicly available personal information deserves a closer look. Here's what happened in Minnesota and the steps you can take to make your personal information harder to find online.

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You'll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
People search websites can expose retirees' home addresses, phone numbers and family details without their knowledge. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Minnesota attacks expose a troubling privacy risk

In June 2025, Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, were murdered in a targeted attack. State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, were seriously injured in a separate shooting. Investigators discovered notebooks containing the names of public officials and a handwritten list of 11 people search websites in the suspect's vehicle.

The list included TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, Pipl, PeopleFinders, BeenVerified, Whitepages, TruthFinder, Intelius, Ownerly, USSearch and PeopleLooker. The notes described which services were free and what information someone could find through them.

However, the discovery alone did not establish whether the websites supplied the victims' addresses. On June 11, Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to federal charges in the murders, shootings and stalking of the victims. He was sentenced July 23 to two consecutive life terms, plus 40 years, in federal prison. Separate state charges remain pending. The case raised an unsettling question: How easily could someone find your home address and information about your family?
What data brokers know about you

Data brokers collect information from public records, online activity, commercial databases and other sources. They then combine those details into profiles that businesses and individuals may be able to purchase or access. Some companies specialize in marketing information. Others operate people search websites that make personal details available through free searches or paid reports.
Depending on the company and the available records, those profiles may include:

Your current and previous home addressesPhone numbers and email addressesAge, birthdate and marital statusNames of relatives and possible associatesProperty ownership and estimated home valuesEmployment and education historyPurchasing interests and other consumer informationFinancial, health-related or political inferences
Your current and previous home addresses
Phone numbers and email addresses
Age, birthdate and marital status
Names of relatives and possible associates
Property ownership and estimated home values
Employment and education history
Purchasing interests and other consumer information
Financial, health-related or political inferences

Not every broker collects or sells all this information. Credit reporting agencies also operate under different legal requirements than many people search services. Still, these records can reveal details you never intended to share with strangers. For a closer look at how criminals assemble this information, read our CyberGuy report on how scammers build a profile on you using data brokers.
Want to see how much of your personal information may already be exposed? Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com
Why exposed personal information is risky for retirees
Scammers can use publicly available details to make their stories more convincing. As a result, a suspicious call or message may sound surprisingly personal.
Here are some of the potential risks.

Financial scams: Someone who knows your age, address and family relationships may use those details to impersonate a financial institution, government agency or relative. You can request removal from many people search websites for free. However, each company may have different requirements, and removing a listing doesn't always prevent it from returning.

A new privacy shortcut for California residents

If you live in California, you now have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP) at privacy.ca.gov/drop/ launched in January 2026. It allows eligible residents to submit one deletion request to more than 600 registered data brokers. Beginning August 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing those requests.

The system also requires recurring checks for matching information, although legal exceptions apply and removal is not immediate. Other states have their own privacy laws and removal rights, so your options may depend on where you live.
Retirees can reduce their online exposure by checking where their personal information appears and requesting its removal. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How a data removal service can help protect your personal information

If manually contacting dozens of websites sounds exhausting, a data removal service can handle much of the work for you. These services help identify data brokers and people-search websites that may have your information. They can also submit removal requests on your behalf and follow up when necessary.
Depending on the provider and subscription plan, available features may include:

You'll typically need to authorize the service to submit removal requests on your behalf. Some providers also offer family plans that cover multiple household members.
Before subscribing, compare the websites each service covers, its removal process, ongoing monitoring features and subscription costs.

What a data removal service cannot do

Even with automated removal, some personal information may remain publicly accessible. Property ownership records, government databases and certain court records can continue displaying details about you. Data removal services generally cannot force government agencies to delete legally available public records.
Additionally, not every website must honor a removal request. Some services offer custom removals, but legal restrictions and technical limitations can prevent certain information from being deleted.
Removing data broker listings also cannot undo previous data breaches or guarantee that scammers will stop contacting you.

Still, reducing the number of websites exposing your information can make it harder for strangers to find personal details. For retirees, that added privacy can help reduce exposure to targeted scams and unwanted contact.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most is how much someone can learn about you without ever meeting you. Your address, family connections and personal history can give scammers information they can use to gain your trust. And once that information starts circulating, controlling where it goes becomes difficult.

That's why I recommend taking a proactive approach. Start by finding out what's publicly available, remove what you can and keep checking. If the process becomes overwhelming, a reputable data removal service can help with the ongoing work. You may never erase every trace of yourself from the internet, but you can make your personal information harder to find.

title: Google's new AI shopping cart tracks deals across stores
summary: Google Universal Cart tracks price drops, surfaces promo codes and uses Google Wallet to match your best credit card rewards before checkout.
story: Kurt âCyberGuyâ Knutsson explains how algorithms track browsing history and location to estimate what shoppers are willing to spend on âFox & Friends.â

Ever find something you want to buy online, leave it sitting in a browser tab and then completely forget where you saw it? Maybe you spotted a great pair of headphones while searching Google. Later, you found a birthday gift at another retailer. Before long, you've got a dozen tabs open and no idea which store had the better deal.

Google thinks it has a solution. On Oct. 15, the company began the U.S. rollout of Universal Cart, a new artificial intelligence-powered shopping tool that brings products from different retailers into one place. It also tracks prices, watches for restocks and helps you find savings before checkout.

With holiday shopping approaching, the timing could be especially useful. But there's another question worth asking. Will having everything in one cart help us spend less, or simply make it easier to buy more?
AMERICANS SAY THEY'RE BROKE. SO WHY CAN'T THEY STOP SPENDING SO MUCH?

AMAZON ABOUT YOU MAY KNOW YOU A LITTLE TOO WELL
Google's Universal Cart brings together products from different retailers, price-drop alerts and checkout options in one shopping experience. (Google)
What is Google Universal Cart?

Google Universal Cart is a shopping hub that works across Google Search and the Gemini app. Instead of keeping separate lists of products you might buy, you can save items from different retailers in one place. For example, you might find a coffee maker while searching Google and add it to your Universal Cart. Later, while talking with Gemini about gift ideas, you could save a pair of sneakers from another store. When you return, both products will be waiting for you. Google first previewed the tool in May 2026. Now, Universal Cart is rolling out to U.S. shoppers. It uses Google's Shopping Graph, which contains more than 60 billion continually refreshed product listings. That information helps the system monitor prices and availability across supported products.
4 ways Google's new AI shopping cart can help you save
The biggest attraction here is convenience. But Google has added several features that could also help you avoid paying more than necessary.

Shopping online often means bouncing between websites. You find something at Target, check another item at Walmart and then head to Sephora for a gift. Remembering where you saw everything can become a chore. Universal Cart lets you save supported products you discover through Google Search and Gemini. More importantly, your saved items stay together when you return to shopping. That could come in handy when you're shopping for several people or making a big purchase that requires some research. You can keep your options organized without committing to buying anything right away.

Here's the feature I find particularly interesting. Universal Cart can monitor saved products and notify you when a price drops. It can also alert you when something that sold out becomes available again. Suppose you're considering a new television but aren't ready to spend the money. Rather than checking the same retailer every morning, you can save it and let Google's shopping system watch for changes. The alerts could be especially helpful heading into Black Friday and the holiday shopping season. Still, remember that a price reduction doesn't automatically guarantee the lowest price available.
IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR

This is where Google's AI starts doing some extra work. Universal Cart can surface relevant promotional codes and consider benefits associated with your payment cards. Let's say you have multiple credit cards but can't remember which one offers better rewards at a particular retailer. Universal Cart uses information from Google Wallet to understand supported credit card benefits and help you choose between payment methods. It can also show relevant promotional codes directly in your cart, potentially helping you find savings you might otherwise miss. However, I would still check the details before choosing a card. Rewards programs come with conditions, and the highest points offer may not always translate into the greatest savings.

Once you're ready to buy, Universal Cart offers a more streamlined checkout experience with participating retailers. In some cases, you can complete the purchase using Google Pay directly from the cart. Alternatively, Google can transfer your selected items to the retailer's website so you can finish your order there. Google says its simplified checkout experiences include retailers such as Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart and Wayfair, along with many Shopify merchants. However, the available checkout options depend on the retailer. Either way, the retailer remains the seller of record and handles order confirmations and customer support. That means you'll continue dealing with the merchant for delivery questions or returns.
119,000 FAKE SHOPS COULD STEAL YOUR CREDIT CARD DETAILS
Universal Cart highlights available promo codes, credit card rewards and shipping offers to help shoppers find savings before checkout. (Google)
How to get started with Google Universal Cart

Google began rolling out Universal Cart to U.S. users on Oct. 15. The feature works across Google Search and the Gemini app, although availability may vary as the rollout continues. To explore it, open Google Search or Gemini and look for products you're interested in buying. When Universal Cart becomes available in your shopping experience, you can save supported products from different retailers. Google says those items will remain in your cart when you return, allowing you to pick up where you left off. You can also use the cart to monitor price changes, discover promotional offers and review available checkout options. However, Google hasn't provided a single set of instructions that applies to every device. The appearance and placement of these features may vary.
NEW AMAZON AI SEARCH TURNS WORDS INTO SHOPPABLE IMAGES
Does Google's Universal Cart work with every retailer?

Not necessarily. Google says Universal Cart can organize products across retailers, but that doesn't mean every online store supports every feature. The products you can save depend on supported shopping experiences. Meanwhile, checkout options vary depending on the merchant. Some purchases can happen through Google Pay in the cart, while others require you to finish on the retailer's website. Google originally introduced Universal Cart in May with plans to bring it to Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail. However, its October 15 launch announcement specifically confirms availability across Search and Gemini in the U.S. Google has not announced a confirmed launch date for Universal Cart integration with Gmail or YouTube.
Google Universal Cart can send notifications when a saved product drops in price, helping shoppers spot deals without repeatedly checking stores. (Google)
What's powering Google's new shopping experience?

Behind the scenes, Google uses something called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It's a shared technical standard designed to help AI-powered shopping tools communicate with retailers and payment systems. For shoppers, the technical details are less important than what they make possible. UCP helps Google connect product discovery with checkout, reducing the need to jump between different shopping experiences. Google has also been expanding AI shopping beyond the cart. Its Let Google Call feature, for example, can use AI to contact nearby stores and check product availability. Amazon has been developing AI-powered shopping tools, while OpenAI offers AI agents that can assist with shopping-related tasks. The competition to become your digital shopping assistant is heating up.
What about your shopping privacy?

Having Google organize your shopping could be convenient, especially if you already use Search and Gemini. Still, it's worth considering how much shopping information you're comfortable keeping within your Google account. Universal Cart uses Google Wallet to help identify supported payment benefits and relevant offers. However, Google's launch announcement doesn't provide detailed information about how long Universal Cart shopping data is retained or exactly how it may be used for advertising. Before relying on the feature, review your Google account's privacy settings and Google's published privacy policies. For now, I would avoid assuming that adding something to Universal Cart keeps that shopping interest private. And if you're buying a surprise gift for someone who shares access to your Google account, think twice before saving it there. Of course, the usual online shopping precautions still apply. Before completing a purchase, check the final price and verify that you're buying from a legitimate seller. A familiar checkout experience shouldn't replace those basic habits. For more help spotting suspicious sellers, see our guide on how to tell whether an online store is real or a scam.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like the idea of having one place to keep track of everything I'm considering buying, especially when the holidays roll around. The price alerts could be genuinely helpful. And if Google's AI can find a discount code I would have otherwise missed, I'm all for it. But I'm also watching where this is heading. Google is making shopping increasingly convenient, and that convenience can be a double-edged sword. When a company knows what you're interested in buying and makes checkout easier, there's less time to reconsider a purchase. My advice? Use Universal Cart to do your homework and save money. Just don't let the technology do the deciding for you.
Would you trust Google's AI to help you shop and choose how to pay, or are we giving tech companies too much influence over what we buy? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Your phone can alert you when prices drop; here's how
summary: Safari's Notify Me feature and Google's price-tracking tools can monitor products and send alerts when prices drop on your iPhone or Android.
story: Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson explains how algorithms track browsing history and location to estimate what shoppers are willing to spend on ‘Fox & Friends.’

Have you ever found something you wanted to buy, only to wonder whether the price might drop next week? Maybe it's a new pair of headphones, a kitchen appliance or a gift you've had your eye on. You could keep checking the website every day, but who has time for that?

Here's something you may not realize. Your phone can help watch prices for you. Apple's Safari browser has a feature that monitors website changes, while Google's shopping tools offer price tracking on supported products.

That means you can spend less time refreshing product listings and more time deciding whether a deal is actually worth your money. I'll show you how to set up these alerts on an Apple iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel.
