“In prior trials, other drugs that were studied in combination with [this class of immunotherapies] led to significant, and eventually potentially permanent side effects, particularly side effects that triggered the immune system to attack our own body,” In, who wasn’t involved with the trial, wrote in an email.

Despite the positive results, investors reacted poorly when the findings were leaked on Thursday, causing Moderna’s stock price to fall. Bajaj said that this may be because while the trial’s results are a significant breakthrough for the field of cancer vaccines, the difference between taking Keytruda and the vaccine compared with Keytruda alone is still relatively modest.

“The reality is that on one hand, any difference you see is amazing because it’s one more option for a patient,” she said. “Is this likely helpful for a handful of patients? I would say yes, but it’s hard to say whether at this point we have data to suggest that this is actually the next blockbuster.”

The full data is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal, and Bajaj said that the patients in the trial still need to be followed for several more years to see whether the vaccine continues to offer additional benefits in terms of preventing the return and spread of melanoma as well as its effects on survival.

In addition, Bajaj said she had questions over the scalability of the treatment. She noted that of the 1,749 melanoma patients who were initially screened for participation in the trial, 17% did not have tumor samples that were big enough for a vaccine to be created.

“It’s amazing, but I think some of the logistics are going to need to be worked out,” she said. “But nothing that I saw from this study made me think that the logistics are infeasible. It’s just that it will be a hurdle to actually do this at a wide scale.”

However, Vonderheide described the results as a very welcome boost for the field of cancer vaccines. In recent months, the German company BioNTech announced clinical trial failures for experimental vaccines for colorectal and head and neck cancers.
He suggested that intismeran’s success may be because the Merck and Moderna trial focused on preventing melanoma recurrence rather than prolonging survival in later stage patients.

“The field of cancer vaccines has been filled with disappointments in treating patients with advanced disease,” Vonderheide said. “Some people look at those results and say, ‘cancer vaccines will never work.’ These results show that cancer vaccines are incredibly powerful when deployed in the right clinical setting. Vaccines work to prevent.”
Still, intismeran is being studied in a separate clinical trial in patients with advanced melanoma that has already spread to distant organs.
“This is just the proof of concept,” Long said. “We’re going into advanced melanoma, but we’re also doing work in many other cancers — bladder cancer, kidney cancer, lung cancer, using this concept.”
She said that researchers will also be actively working to understand more about why the vaccine worked to see if that can lead to further clues.

Vonderheide described the future possibilities for preventing cancer recurrence as being myriad. “One day, we might be able to think of how to use a cancer vaccine to prevent cancer in the first place,” he said. “That’s a very ambitious, far-off goal. But these results bring that goal even closer to reality than we might think.”

title: Russian diesel tanker heads to the U.S., the first since Trump’s deal with Putin
summary: A tanker loaded with diesel fuel set sail Friday from Russia for the United States, the first shipment since President Donald Trump agreed to a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more fuel into the global market.
story: A tanker loaded with diesel fuel set sail Friday from Russia for the United States, the first shipment since President Donald Trump agreed to a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more fuel into the global market.

Trump eased some sanctions on the Kremlin two weeks ago and has since waived more, reversing years of American policy despite Moscow’s ongoing illegal invasion of Ukraine in an apparent bid to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The ship’s departure for the U.S. was confirmed by the Kremlin. The tanker, a Malta-flagged ship named Agioi Fanendes, left a port in Russia’s Primorsk today, according to MarineTraffic tracking data reviewed by NBC News. The ship listed New York as its destination.
Energy Aspects, a market intelligence firm, said that it had confirmed with its industry sources that the ship loaded up 298,000 barrels of diesel in Primorsk.
The firm said that currently the ship plans to unload that fuel in New York. It is expected to arrive Nov. 10.

The ship’s expected arrival would put it just after the midterm elections. Trump’s Republican Party is on edge for potentially heavy losses in House and Senate seats its candidates are defending, driven in part by blowback from consumers facing soaring energy prices.

Trump and his administration have scrambled to try to bring down those prices, which have increased in the wake of supply shocks stemming from the Iran war launched by the U.S. and Israel, and the Russia-Ukraine war.
Trump has taken a number of steps to warm ties with the Kremlin and pressure Kyiv to agree to end the war, drawing outrage from Ukraine and its bipartisan backers in Congress.

“I believe there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has departed for its destinations and that further shipments will continue on a regular basis,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said early Friday.
Crude oil was headed for a third straight weekly gain. Brent, the most important global oil benchmark, traded around $114 per barrel, less than $13 away from its highest point this year.
Since the start of the year, the average price of diesel fuel has soared from $3.55 per gallon to $6.32, an unprecedented rise of 78%.
Energy Aspect’s analysts said the impact of the cargo’s arrival would likely be “limited.”

Diesel’s sky-high price has troubled economists more than the jump in the price of regular gasoline because, “the cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” as KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview.
“Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it,” she said.
Currently, U.S. daily diesel demand is about 3.8 million barrels, meaning that Friday’s shipment would satisfy not even a full day’s worth of usage.

“Global distillate markets have tightened sharply,” Bank of America’s head of global commodities, Francisco Blanch, wrote in a recent note, adding that it signals “an acute scarcity of refined products.”
Diesel is a distillate fuel, produced by refining crude oil.

“Geopolitical disruptions are exacerbating that shortage as attacks on shipping around Hormuz make energy flows more difficult and costly, while attacks on Russian refining capacity further restrict product availability,” he wrote.
Russia has historically been one of the world’s largest exporters of diesel.

In September and for some of October, the Kremlin restricted the export of diesel fuel amid a Ukrainian campaign of attacks on its energy infrastructure. It lifted those export restrictions after Putin’s diesel deal with Trump.
Easing sanctions on Russia to open up some previously-blocked diesel supplies was just the latest in a number of policy levers pulled by Trump.

In just the last few weeks, the president has also signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road variety of diesel. The administration also pressured European allies, particularly Germany and France, to urgently release some of their diesel reserves.
The administration has also reportedly pushed for a fresh release of crude and diesel reserves, though the International Energy Agency has rebuffed that request.
Experts say that even with all this put together, Trump’s actions will do little to help ease prices, which have continued to trend higher.
“Policy intervention can provide temporary relief, but there is no silver bullet for diesel,” Blanch wrote.

title: One person killed and 4 injured in suspected Islamophobic shooting near Paris
summary: At least one person was killed and four people were injured in a shooting near Paris that may have been motivated by Islamophobic hatred, French officials say.
story: At least one person was killed and four people were injured in a shooting near Paris that may have been motivated by Islamophobic hatred, French officials say.
French President Emmanuel Macron called the shooting a racist terror attack, saying people were targeted due to their religion and the color of their skin.

“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” Interior Minister ⁠Laurent Nuñez told reporters from the Yvelines ​district, about 20 miles west of Paris, where the attack took place.
For Subscribers

Officials said the 39-year-old suspect, who has not been named, drove through the town of Trappes, where he ⁠fired an automatic weapon at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.

Ali Rabeh, the mayor of Trappes, said it was “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic.” The official, whose parents came from Morocco, added: “The people ‌targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, ‌my brothers or my sisters-in-law.”
For Subscribers

One person has been arrested and charged on four counts, including murder and possession of a firearm, with the “aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed on the basis of actual or supposed membership in a particular race, ethnicity, a purported race, ethnic group, nation, or specific religion,” France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office told NBC News in a statement.
One of those injured was a 12-year-old girl, Rabeh told France’s BFM TV. Broadcaster ​BFM said ⁠the wounded girl had been ‌hit eight times and was in a serious condition.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: France’s Emmanuel Macron says ‘illegitimate’ protests will be banned as cities block demonstrations
summary: The French leader said “seditious” ultra-left groups as ‌well as vandals ​were behind ‌⁠Saturday’s riots and ⁠looting across France.
story: French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday that “illegitimate” protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend’s riots and looting.

Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organized by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to go ahead but could be diverted along alternative routes to protect businesses.
“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” Macron said.
His comments came as authorities across France prepared for fresh protests following some of the country’s worst urban unrest in years.
Authorities in multiple cities had already banned protests planned across the country Thursday.

The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response. Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored.
Demonstrations planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned, a move seen by some as an infringement on French people’s right to protest.
But high school and university student groups say they will continue to mobilize, even though the autumn school break started this week.

The Paris police prefecture said the ban was necessary given the risk of street violence that erupted over the weekend, when groups of masked youths clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars.

The ban in Paris will last until 8 p.m. local time and apply to areas including the Élysée presidential palace, both houses of Parliament and the city’s main train stations. Areas in downtown Paris that were severely hit by the looting are also covered.

title: Retired American teacher imprisoned by Russia returns to U.S.
summary: Steve Witkoff hailed the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” during talks with the release of Stephen Hubbard signaling warmer ties between the two countries.
story: Russia has released retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, 74, the latest sign of warmer ties between the two countries as Washington pressures Kyiv to agree to a deal to end Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
The jet carrying Hubbard touched down at Lackland Air Force Base, Texas, at about 10:49 p.m. Wednesday (11:49 p.m. ET), video  at the base showed.

U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff lauded Russian President Vladimir Putin for Hubbard’s release as they held peace talks early Wednesday in St. Petersburg. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Lawmakers from both parties criticized Witkoff’s use of the word “humanitarian,” with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, saying Putin is “the aggressor in the war against Ukraine.”

The U.S. has courted the Kremlin for weeks, and the release of Hubbard — a Michigan native detained in Ukraine in 2022 — will give President Donald Trump a victory to tout after backlash at home and abroad for his tilt away from Kyiv in the conflict.
Son of Stephen Hubbard says 'no evidence' his father was a mercenary
Trump hailed the news, telling reporters late Wednesday that Hubbard would visit the White House “over the next day or so.”

Earlier, Trump said on Truth Social that Hubbard was “on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia.”

Trump said he directly asked Putin in a phone call last week to release Hubbard, who was being held on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, which he denies. He was the last American designated as wrongfully detained in Russia by the State Department.
The Kremlin said the move was a goodwill gesture.

Hubbard’s family in a statement thanked “President Trump and his team for opening the dialog with Russia which led to this joyful day. Our family can attest that there are wonderful blessings to be found along the hard road to peace.”
Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov later said Hubbard was handed over to Witkoff at St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport.

In a video from the Russian state news agency RIA, Hubbard wears a green jacket and is smiling as he meets Witkoff. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” he tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding, “From today, it’s a new life.”

Martin De Luca, Hubbard’s lawyer, said in a phone interview Wednesday that he spoke with Hubbard as he was “getting ready to take off” on a plane bound for the U.S. and that his client was overjoyed to be released.

“He was overwhelmed with joy,” De Luca said. “The No. 1 thing he was excited about was seeing his children and family, who will be waiting for him when he arrives in the U.S. tonight. He was in a fragile state, so it wasn’t a long conversation, but he’s OK, which is what’s important.”
U.S. peace push

The meeting between Putin and Witkoff, which Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner was expected to join virtually, came after the American negotiators met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo.
Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals at the talks, a U.S. official told NBC News, adding that “meaningful progress” was made as the Trump administration intensifies its peace push.

Ushakov said Wednesday that Russia is ready to resume trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine from mid-November concerning “the establishment of a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict.”
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he would support talks involving himself, Trump and Putin, as well as direct Ukraine-Russia talks.
Meanwhile, Ushakov said a separate proposed meeting of leaders from Russia, China and the U.S. during next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, is “not rejected by any of the capitals.”

He said that Russia raised “several practical considerations regarding the content of possible trilateral talks” but that “if circumstances are favorable, they, our Chinese friends, will certainly include this meeting in the program of events.”

Diplomacy has made little headway for months, and the renewed American effort has drawn widespread criticism as Trump announced a series of moves to bolster Russia while Ukraine accused the U.S. of withdrawing crucial support.

“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday, intensifying a pressure campaign that has fueled concern the U.S. is no longer committed to Kyiv’s defense against the Russian invasion.
“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss,” Trump said.
Trump told reporters Wednesday that a deal to end the war might be close.
“We’re negotiating with Russia right now on Ukraine,” he said. “We are maybe close to a deal for the first time in a long time.”
Witkoff told Putin on Wednesday that “groundwork” had been laid to end the fighting and that he had brought documents outlining approaches to a possible deal.
Zelenskyy said a potential trilateral leaders’ meeting was “one of the important ideas” raised in Oslo after Tuesday’s talks, which also included the leaders of Norway and Finland.

Putin has so far insisted that any meeting with Zelenskyy could happen only once a deal is finalized and take place in Moscow, a nonstarter for Ukraine. The Kremlin has also shown little sign of shifting from its hard-line demands, which include seizing Ukraine’s entire eastern Donbas region.

Trump signed a diesel deal with Russia this month and waived new sanctions on Moscow, drawing bipartisan criticism. He claimed Wednesday that negotiations to free Hubbard “would have come to a complete and total halt” had he not waived the sanctions.

Kyiv, meanwhile, said that it received no warning about at least three major Russian attacks and that restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starshield satellite service continue to hamper its aerial defenses and battlefield operations.
After the talks with Witkoff on Tuesday, Zelenskyy told reporters the recent issues with intelligence sharing had been resolved.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks in Oslo “positive” but said “nothing unexpected” came out of them.

Rubio once again denied that the White House was behind any slowdown to Ukraine’s use of the internet service, saying it was an issue for Musk and SpaceX. Musk said last week that any decision was down to Trump.
Deadly Russian attacks continued to hit Ukraine, meanwhile, with at least nine civilians killed across the country Wednesday as Moscow ramps up its strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Authorities in Russia’s border Bryansk region said Wednesday that one person was killed in a Ukrainian strike.

title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, the retired American teacher freed by Russia?
summary: Hubbard, 74, who lived in eastern Ukraine, was detained in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion and was later convicted of serving as a mercenary.
story: Stephen James Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was released by Russia on Wednesday after nearly five years in detention in the midst of an apparent warming of ties between Washington and Moscow.

Hubbard, 74, of Michigan, had been living in eastern Ukraine for years when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. He was detained two months into the war as Russia captured swaths of Ukrainian territory. Two years later, a Russian court convicted him of serving as a mercenary.
The jet carrying Hubbard touched down at Lackland Air Force Base, Texas, at about 10:49 p.m. Wednesday (11:49 p.m. ET), video at the base showed.

The news of his release came out of a meeting between President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, when they were due to discuss an end to the Ukraine war.
Son of Stephen Hubbard says 'no evidence' his father was a mercenary
Witkoff thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard during their on-camera talks. He later met Hubbard in St. Petersburg before he boarded a flight back to the United States.

In a video from the Russian state news agency RIA, Hubbard is smiling as he meets Witkoff. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” he tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding, “From today, it’s a new life.”
During the meeting, Witkoff said on X, Trump “called Stephen to check on him and reaffirm his unwavering commitment to bringing all Americans wrongfully detained home.”
Witkoff shared an image of Hubbard on a plane next to the American flag and several other people, writing that he was “headed back home to his family.”

Martin De Luca, Hubbard’s lawyer, said in a phone interview Wednesday that he had spoken with Hubbard as he was getting ready to take off on a plane bound for the U.S. and that his client was overjoyed to be released.

“He was overwhelmed with joy,” De Luca said. “The No. 1 thing he was excited about was seeing his children and family, who will be waiting for him when he arrives in the U.S. tonight. He was in a fragile state, so it wasn’t a long conversation, but he’s OK, which is what’s important.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin released Hubbard “on humanitarian grounds.” Russia did not provide more details.
Hubbard’s family acknowledged Trump’s and Putin’s roles in securing his release.

“We have been gravely concerned for his safety and health since his 2022 detention,” Hubbard’s son, Joseph Coleman, said in a statement on behalf of the family. “Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” the statement said.
Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest who lives in Cyprus, wrote Putin “a long and very emotional letter” last month, De Luca said.

In the letter, Coleman said Hubbard’s family “feared he would die without ever seeing his kids or grandchildren,” De Luca said. Coleman also outlined his father’s background and family history and emphasized his faith.
NBC News’ Garrett Haake spoke Wednesday with Coleman, who again thanked Putin and Trump for his father’s release.
Coleman said it was his “understanding” that Putin had read his letter.
Asked about the Russian accusation that his father was a mercenary fighting for Ukraine, Coleman replied, “And I say the moon is made out of cheese.”
“There’s no evidence to that effect,” he added.
Coleman said his father is not political and may have been targeted because of his American nationality.
“I think my father was in the wrong place at the wrong time,” he said. “I think it served the interests of low-level military men to say, ‘Hey, we got this American.’ It’s a trophy.”
Coleman said his father had lived with him in Cyprus for a time before he decided to move to Ukraine to live with his girlfriend for economic reasons.
Coleman had only a brief conversation with his father while he was on the tarmac in Russia.
“He was just looking forward to seeing family,” Coleman said.
Trump cheered Hubbard’s return, framing it as a demonstration of the Kremlin’s “respect” for its American counterparts.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump said Wednesday on Truth Social, shortly after Witkoff announced Hubbard’s release. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia.”

There was no “swap” necessary for the release, Trump added, though in a later post he said “those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt” had the U.S. gone ahead with sanctions that he waived last week.
Hubbard was sentenced in a closed-door trial in 2024, with very little information about his case reported by Russian state media.

At the time, Russian prosecutors alleged that as the Kremlin launched its “special military operation” in Ukraine in February 2022, Hubbard voluntarily joined a territorial defense battalion in the eastern city of Izyum, where he had been living since 2014. The prosecutors said Hubbard took part in the Ukraine war and regularly received financial compensation before he was detained in April 2022 as advancing Russian forces captured the city.

“He was aware of the unlawful nature of his actions, yet — with the deliberate intent of personal enrichment — he carried out the orders of his superiors, which entailed direct participation in combat operations on the side of the Armed Forces of Ukraine against service members of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” according to Russia’s prosecutor general’s office.

Russian state media reported that he pleaded guilty. Following Hubbard’s release Wednesday, De Luca stood by his previous statements that Hubbard had told him that the charges were false and that he was not part of any combat or military unit.
The New York Times reported last year that Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, disputes that he fought for Ukraine, as do three former Ukrainian prisoners of war held with Hubbard.

The paper also cited Fox as saying her brother had a master’s degree in English and had lived in Japan and Cyprus before he moved to eastern Ukraine, where he had a Ukrainian partner. Fox also said Hubbard taught English online when he needed money and did not speak either Ukrainian or Russian.

Russia occupied Izyum, where Fox said her brother settled, for six months in 2022, but Ukraine later recaptured it in a major counteroffensive. It is currently held by Ukraine and is not part of the four Ukrainian oblasts Russia has illegally annexed.
Hubbard was released from Russian custody just months after former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who spent more than four years in a Russian prison, was set free in August.

Washington has accused Moscow of arbitrarily detaining American citizens in Russia for years, with their cases often used to negotiate prisoner swaps, including exchanges for state-backed intelligence operatives detained around the world.

In some of the higher-profile cases, U.S. journalist Evan Gershkovich was released in a swap in 2024, alongside Marine veteran Paul Whelan — both had been jailed on espionage charges. WNBA star Brittney Griner, detained on drug charges in 2022, was freed after the Biden administration negotiated her release in exchange for a Russian arms dealer.

John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine and the senior director of the Atlantic Council think tank’s Eurasia Center, said that despite the depiction of Hubbard’s release, “it was not a freebie. It was not a gift to the United States.”

He told NBC News’ “Here’s the Scoop” podcast that it came after the release of a prominent Russian war blogger, Mikhail Zvinchuk, who was detained in Montenegro in October and freed after the U.S. opted not to extradite him.
“Russia’s got back a bad guy who we should have taken into custody, and we got back an American who was innocent. That’s the pattern,” he said.
Meanwhile, on the day Hubbard was released, Russia said it had detained a German national accused of serving in the Ukrainian army.
Russia’s Federal Security Service did not release the man’s name or any other identifying details and did not say where or when he was taken into custody.

title: Pope Leo won’t require further treatment after lung surgery, doctors say
summary: The pope’s doctors said he had pulmonary adenocarcinoma, which was localized.
story: Pope Leo XIV will not need further treatment following lung cancer surgery, his doctors said Wednesday.
The Vatican’s press office said in an update from the pope’s doctors that final reports and analyses of tissue removed from his surgery were completed Wednesday.
Pope Leo rides popemobile for first time since surgery
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized,” said his doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora.
“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the statement said.
Leo, 71, had surgery this month at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a lung nodule found during recent routine medical tests. Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”
He was discharged Saturday and returned to his public duties Sunday with a prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica.
“This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are experiencing illness and a condition of frailty,” he said, thanking well-wishers.
“Having come through this delicate phase, as you know, I will now gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers,” he said.
The pope’s diagnosis and surgery left his upcoming trip to South America up in the air. He is still scheduled to depart Nov. 6 for the 12-day journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

The trip will be a demanding one, covering 19,000 miles on multiple flights and two helicopter rides. His itinerary includes a stopover in Cuzco in the Peruvian Andes, which is at an elevation of 11,000 feet.
Peru is a special place for Leo, where he was bishop of Chiclayo and holds citizenship.
The pope’s surgeon, Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that recovery from Leo’s type of surgery typically takes a couple of weeks.
“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.

title: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
summary: Ukraine’s president was meeting with American negotiators in Norway as Kyiv accused the U.S. of hampering the country’s defense against Russian attacks.
story: U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Washington’s backing is in doubt after Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo, and Kushner joined the talks remotely. Zelenskyy also held talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb before he met the U.S. delegation.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
A U.S. official told NBC News that the meetings among Witkoff, Kushner, Zelenskyy and the other officials were “very productive and constructive.”

“Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail. The parties made meaningful progress in aligning on a coordinated approach to engaging Russia and advancing the diplomatic process,” the official said.

“There is now strong alignment at the working level among the United States, Ukraine and Europe on the next steps. The teams are working exceptionally well together, with a shared commitment to finding practical solutions to end the war,” the official added.

A comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, was discussed, according to the official, along with a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability.
Rubio also said Wednesday that Witkoff’s meeting with Zelenskyy had been “positive,” with “nothing surprising.”
“He’ll now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let’s see if we can make some progress,” he told reporters in Mumbai, India.
Russian state media reported Witkoff’s arrival in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

He will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Kushner participating virtually, according to the U.S. official. The goal is to build on the progress made with Ukraine and Europe, discuss the proposals with Russia and create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations, the official said.

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed on a diesel deal with Russia, apparently in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate” in his latest rebuke.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years, that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters Monday. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Tuesday: “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office.”
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles Sunday for the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet service from Elon Musk’s SpaceX, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan congressional delegation.

Asked Wednesday about a Wall Street Journal report that Musk had ordered the Starlink slowdown, Rubio said Starlink was “a private company” and that “we cannot direct a private company as to the decisions they make or not make.”
“What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States, nor anyone in our system, ever requested that any changes to that system be made,” he said.

Zelenskyy also says the U.S. is delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies. He said early Tuesday that he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”

Zelenskyy said later Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice. The change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including the phone call with Rubio earlier in the day, he said.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said, the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements for what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he said earlier in his India trip. “We have our own needs, too.”

Ukrainian officials, including Zelenskyy, have made it clear that they accuse the U.S. of imposing restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks deadlier.
“That’s scandalous. That’s outrageous. That’s just simply not true,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a 1-year-old girl who they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

title: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
summary: Helen Haines was critical but stable after being struck by a car outside her office. Authorities charged the driver in what they said was a deliberate attack.
story: An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.

Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.

Local media reported that one of Haines’ legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker loses leg in car ramming attack

Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then did a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.

“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the network that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.

title: Dramatic images show violent unrest sweeping across France
summary: France unrest protest photos over the weekend Macron election buildup
story: Widespread violence erupted across France over the weekend, as rioters and looters ransacked storefronts, clashed with police and set fire to municipal buildings.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, the French Interior Ministry said, after some of the worst unrest the country has seen in years.
